Urgent treatment with high-dose parenteral thiamine (before glucose administration) is critical to prevent progression to irreversible Korsakoff Syndrome, characterized by severe memory impairment and confabulation. Labs may show thiamine deficiency, but treatment should not be delayed. Management aligns with international and Indian nutritional support guidelines.

clinical_hallmarks: chronic daily headache (often worse with Valsalva)
pulsatile tinnitus
transient visual obscurations
papilledema on fundoscopy
normal neurological exam except for possible CN VI palsy
pertinent_negatives: absence of mass lesion on imaging
normal CSF composition with elevated opening pressure
content: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH), or Pseudotumor Cerebri, is characterized by symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) without an identifiable cause, typically affecting obese young to middle-aged women. Presentation includes chronic daily headache, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, and most critically, papilledema. Physical examination focuses on fundoscopy for papilledema and cranial nerve assessment (especially CN VI palsy). Pertinent rule-outs include cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, brain tumor, hydrocephalus, and meningitis. Diagnostic workup involves neuroimaging (MRI brain with venography to rule out structural causes and CVST) and a lumbar puncture to measure elevated CSF opening pressure (>25 cm H2O) with normal CSF composition. Management includes weight loss, acetazolamide, and in severe cases, surgical interventions like optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunting to preserve vision, following international and Indian guidelines.

topic: Acute Necrotizing Pancreatitis (Balthazar CT Severity Index)
red_flags: severe epigastric pain radiating to back
clinical_hallmarks: severe epigastric pain radiating to back
nausea/vomiting
elevated lipase/amylase >3x ULN
CT evidence of necrosis
pertinent_negatives: absence of peritonitis in mild cases
content: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and fever. Physical examination may reveal epigastric tenderness, guarding, and in severe cases, signs of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) such as tachycardia, hypotension, and tachypnea. Cullen's or Grey Turner's signs indicate retroperitoneal hemorrhage but are rare. Pertinent rule-outs include perforated viscus, acute cholecystitis, myocardial infarction, and mesenteric ischemia. Diagnostic workup involves serum lipase and amylase (typically >3x upper limit of normal), CBC, LFTs, renal function tests, and inflammatory markers (CRP, procalcitonin). Abdominal CT with contrast is crucial for diagnosis, assessing severity (Balthazar CT Severity Index), and identifying necrosis or complications like pseudocyst or abscess. Management focuses on aggressive fluid resuscitation, pain control, nutritional support, and managing complications, often requiring ICU admission.

topic: Ascending Cholangitis (Charcot Triad & Reynolds Pentad Emergency)
clinical_hallmarks: Charcot's Triad (fever, RUQ pain, jaundice)
Reynolds' Pentad (Charcot's Triad + hypotension + altered mental status)
pertinent_negatives: absence of biliary duct dilation on imaging
content: Ascending cholangitis is an acute bacterial infection of the bile ducts, typically due to obstruction. Patients present with Charcot's Triad: fever, right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain, and jaundice. In severe cases, Reynolds' Pentad emerges, adding hypotension and altered mental status, indicating septic shock. Physical examination reveals RUQ tenderness, jaundice, and potentially signs of sepsis. Pertinent rule-outs include acute cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, and liver abscess. Diagnostic workup includes CBC (leukocytosis), LFTs (elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, GGT), inflammatory markers, and blood cultures. Imaging, starting with ultrasound, then CT or MRCP, identifies biliary obstruction (e.g., choledocholithiasis, stricture, mass) and ductal dilation. ERCP is therapeutic for stone extraction or stenting. Urgent management involves broad-spectrum antibiotics and prompt biliary decompression, often via ERCP, to prevent progression to multi-organ failure.

topic: Bleeding Esophageal Varices (Terlipressin / Endoscopic Band Ligation)
clinical_hallmarks: acute upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) in a patient with known or suspected cirrhosis/portal hypertension
signs of chronic liver disease
pertinent_negatives: absence of stigmata of chronic liver disease
normal coagulation profile (though often deranged in cirrhosis)
absence of portal hypertension signs on imaging
content: Bleeding esophageal varices present as acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, typically with hematemesis (bright red blood or coffee-ground emesis) and/or melena, in patients with portal hypertension, most commonly due to cirrhosis. Patients may exhibit signs of hemodynamic instability, including tachycardia, hypotension, and pallor. Physical examination often reveals stigmata of chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, spider angiomata, palmar erythema, encephalopathy). Pertinent rule-outs include peptic ulcer disease, Mallory-Weiss tear, and gastritis. Diagnostic workup involves CBC (hemoglobin drop), coagulation profile (INR/PT often elevated), LFTs, and renal function. Urgent upper endoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic (endoscopic band ligation). Initial management includes airway protection, fluid resuscitation, vasoactive drugs (e.g., terlipressin, octreotide) to reduce portal pressure, and prophylactic antibiotics. Transfusion support is guided by hemoglobin levels and clinical status.

clinical_hallmarks: Mallory-Weiss: hematemesis after forceful vomiting/retching
Boerhaave: severe retrosternal chest pain, dyspnea, subcutaneous emphysema (Mackler's Triad) after forceful vomiting
pertinent_negatives: absence of chest pain and systemic signs in Mallory-Weiss
absence of hematemesis in Boerhaave (though can occur)
normal mediastinum on imaging for Mallory-Weiss
content: Mallory-Weiss Syndrome involves a non-transmural esophageal mucosal tear, typically at the gastroesophageal junction, caused by forceful vomiting or retching. Patients present with hematemesis, often preceded by non-bloody emesis. Physical exam is usually benign, with stable hemodynamics. Boerhaave Syndrome is a transmural esophageal rupture, a life-threatening emergency, usually following forceful vomiting. Patients experience sudden, severe retrosternal chest pain, dyspnea, and often subcutaneous emphysema (Mackler's Triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema). Signs of shock and mediastinitis may develop rapidly. Rule-outs for Mallory-Weiss include peptic ulcer, variceal bleed. For Boerhaave, rule-outs include myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, and acute pancreatitis. Diagnosis for Mallory-Weiss is by endoscopy. For Boerhaave, chest X-ray may show pneumomediastinum or pleural effusion; CT chest with oral contrast confirms perforation. Urgent surgical repair is critical for Boerhaave.

topic: Gastric Outlet Obstruction (Peptic vs Malignant Antral Stricture)
clinical_hallmarks: recurrent postprandial vomiting of undigested food (often hours after eating)
early satiety
progressive weight loss
succussion splash on exam
pertinent_negatives: absence of weight loss (less likely malignant)
absence of succussion splash (rules out significant obstruction)
content: Gastric outlet obstruction (GOO) presents with recurrent postprandial vomiting of undigested food, often hours after eating, early satiety, and progressive weight loss. Peptic strictures typically result from chronic ulcer disease, while malignant strictures are often due to gastric adenocarcinoma or pancreatic head tumors. Physical examination may reveal a succussion splash, epigastric fullness, and in malignant cases, cachexia or a palpable epigastric mass. Pertinent rule-outs include gastroparesis, rumination syndrome, and high intestinal obstruction. Diagnostic workup includes electrolyte panel (hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis), CBC, and imaging. Upper endoscopy is crucial for direct visualization, biopsy (to differentiate peptic from malignant), and therapeutic dilation. Barium upper GI series can delineate the obstruction site and degree. CT abdomen helps assess for malignancy, nodal involvement, or pancreatic pathology. Management involves gastric decompression, fluid/electrolyte correction, and definitive treatment of the underlying cause.

topic: Acute Liver Failure (Fulminant Hepatic Failure Kings College Criteria)
clinical_hallmarks: rapid onset of severe liver dysfunction (jaundice, coagulopathy) with hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing liver disease
pertinent_negatives: absence of pre-existing chronic liver disease
content: Acute liver failure (ALF) is defined by severe acute liver injury with encephalopathy and coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) in a patient without pre-existing liver disease, occurring within 26 weeks of symptom onset. Common etiologies include acetaminophen overdose, viral hepatitis, and idiosyncratic drug reactions. Patients present with jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and rapidly progressive hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis, coma). Physical examination reveals jaundice, signs of encephalopathy, and potentially cerebral edema. Pertinent rule-outs include acute exacerbation of chronic liver disease, sepsis, and metabolic encephalopathies. Diagnostic workup includes LFTs (markedly elevated transaminases, bilirubin), coagulation profile (elevated INR), ammonia, glucose, and viral hepatitis serologies. Imaging (ultrasound, CT) assesses liver size and morphology. Kings College Criteria guide prognosis and liver transplant candidacy. Management focuses on supportive care, managing complications (cerebral edema, infection, renal failure), and urgent evaluation for liver transplantation.

red_flags: signs of toxic megacolon (abdominal distension, tenderness)
clinical_hallmarks: watery diarrhea (often foul-smelling) after antibiotic exposure
abdominal cramping
fever
leukocytosis
content: Clostridioides difficile colitis (CDI), or pseudomembranous colitis, typically presents with watery, often foul-smelling diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and fever, usually following antibiotic exposure. It can range from mild diarrhea to severe, life-threatening toxic megacolon. Physical examination may reveal abdominal tenderness, distension, and signs of dehydration. In severe cases, signs of systemic toxicity or peritonitis may be present. Pertinent rule-outs include other infectious colitides (e.g., viral, bacterial), inflammatory bowel disease flares, and irritable bowel syndrome. Diagnostic workup involves stool testing for C. difficile toxin (EIA) or gene (PCR). CBC typically shows leukocytosis. Abdominal X-ray may show colonic dilation in toxic megacolon. Colonoscopy can confirm pseudomembranes but is usually reserved for refractory cases or when diagnosis is unclear. Management includes discontinuing the inciting antibiotic, initiating specific anti-C. difficile therapy (e.g., oral vancomycin, fidaxomicin), and supportive care.

clinical_hallmarks: elevated transaminases (often >1000 U/L)
positive autoantibodies (ANA, SMA for Type 1; LKM-1 for Type 2)
interface hepatitis on liver biopsy
often insidious onset
content: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a chronic inflammatory liver disease, often insidious but can present acutely. Type 1 AIH (most common) is characterized by positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and/or anti-smooth muscle antibodies (SMA). Type 2 AIH, typically affecting children/young adults, involves anti-liver kidney microsomal type 1 (LKM-1) antibodies. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with fatigue, jaundice, anorexia, or signs of chronic liver disease (e.g., spider angiomata, hepatosplenomegaly). Physical examination may reveal jaundice, hepatomegaly, or stigmata of cirrhosis. Pertinent rule-outs include viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, and genetic liver diseases. Diagnostic workup involves LFTs (markedly elevated transaminases), immunoglobulin G (IgG) levels, and specific autoantibodies. Liver biopsy is essential for diagnosis, showing interface hepatitis, and for staging fibrosis. Treatment involves immunosuppression, typically with corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) and azathioprine, to achieve remission and prevent progression to cirrhosis.

red_flags: signs of decompensated cirrhosis (ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleed)
clinical_hallmarks: chronic fatigue
intractable pruritus
elevated alkaline phosphatase
positive antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA)
often associated with other autoimmune diseases
content: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic, progressive autoimmune liver disease characterized by immune-mediated destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts. It predominantly affects middle-aged women. Patients often present with insidious onset of fatigue and intractable pruritus, which can be debilitating. Jaundice is a late manifestation. Physical examination may reveal excoriations from scratching, hepatomegaly, or xanthelasmas. In advanced stages, signs of cirrhosis may be present. Pertinent rule-outs include other cholestatic liver diseases (e.g., primary sclerosing cholangitis, drug-induced cholestasis) and obstructive jaundice. Diagnostic workup involves LFTs (markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT), and the hallmark serological marker: positive antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA). Liver biopsy confirms the diagnosis and stages the disease, showing florid duct lesions. Treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) slows disease progression. Symptomatic management for pruritus and monitoring for complications like osteoporosis are crucial.

topic: Budd-Chiari Syndrome (Hepatic Venous Outflow Tract Obstruction)
clinical_hallmarks: classic triad of abdominal pain, ascites, and hepatomegaly
often acute or subacute onset
in absence of primary liver disease
often associated with hypercoagulable states
pertinent_negatives: absence of portal hypertension signs (e.g., varices) in early stages
content: Budd-Chiari Syndrome (BCS) results from obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, ranging from small intrahepatic veins to the inferior vena cava. It often presents with the classic triad of abdominal pain, ascites, and hepatomegaly, with acute, subacute, or chronic onset. Underlying hypercoagulable states (e.g., myeloproliferative neoplasms, oral contraceptives) are common etiologies. Physical examination reveals tender hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema. Jaundice is less common unless severe liver damage occurs. Pertinent rule-outs include congestive heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, cirrhosis with portal hypertension, and veno-occlusive disease. Diagnostic workup includes LFTs (variable), renal function, and screening for hypercoagulable disorders. Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins and IVC is the primary diagnostic tool, showing absent or abnormal flow. CT or MRI with contrast can further delineate obstruction. Angiography is used for definitive diagnosis and intervention. Management involves anticoagulation, diuretics for ascites, and potentially interventional radiology procedures (e.g., angioplasty, stenting, TIPS) or liver transplantation.

topic: Acute Compartment Syndrome (The 6 Ps Surgical Emergency)
clinical_hallmarks: severe pain out of proportion to injury
tense, swollen limb compartment
pain on passive stretch of muscles
paresthesia or numbness
content: Acute Compartment Syndrome is a surgical emergency characterized by increased pressure within a confined osteofascial compartment, leading to impaired tissue perfusion and potential irreversible muscle and nerve damage. It typically presents with the '6 Ps': Pain (disproportionate), Pallor, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Pulselessness, and Poikilothermia. Pain with passive stretch of muscles within the affected compartment is a highly sensitive sign. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by direct intracompartmental pressure measurement (delta pressure < 30 mmHg or absolute pressure > 30-40 mmHg). Urgent fasciotomy is the definitive treatment, aiming to decompress the compartment and restore blood flow. Delay can result in Volkmann's ischemic contracture, limb loss, or renal failure from rhabdomyolysis. Rule out DVT, cellulitis, or simple contusion.

topic: Hip Fracture in Elderly (Femoral Neck vs Intertrochanteric Fracture)
red_flags: inability to bear weight after fall
clinical_hallmarks: shortened and externally rotated lower limb
severe groin or hip pain
inability to ambulate
tenderness over greater trochanter
content: Hip fractures in the elderly typically result from low-energy falls, often in osteoporotic individuals. Presentation includes severe groin or hip pain, inability to bear weight, and a classic deformity of a shortened, externally rotated lower limb. Femoral neck fractures (intracapsular) carry a risk of avascular necrosis, while intertrochanteric fractures (extracapsular) are often more comminuted and associated with greater blood loss. Initial assessment includes ABCs, pain control, and neurovascular examination. Diagnosis is confirmed with AP and lateral X-rays of the hip. If X-rays are negative but suspicion remains high, MRI or CT scan is indicated. Urgent surgical fixation (e.g., hemiarthroplasty for displaced femoral neck, intramedullary nail for intertrochanteric) within 24-48 hours is crucial to reduce morbidity and mortality. Rule out pelvic fracture or soft tissue injury.

clinical_hallmarks: skin breach communicating with fracture site
visible bone fragments or marrow
wound contamination (dirt, debris)
significant soft tissue injury
pertinent_negatives: normal neurovascular status distal to injury
content: An open or compound fracture involves a break in the skin and underlying soft tissues, exposing the fracture site to the external environment, significantly increasing infection risk. These are classified by Gustilo-Anderson (Type I: <1cm wound, clean; Type II: 1-10cm wound, moderate contamination; Type III: >10cm wound, severe contamination, extensive soft tissue damage, often high-energy). Initial management includes sterile wound dressing, tetanus prophylaxis, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (e.g., cephalosporin + aminoglycoside for Type III), and pain control. Urgent surgical debridement and irrigation within 6-8 hours are paramount to remove contaminated tissue and bone. Fracture stabilization (internal or external fixation) follows debridement. Neurovascular assessment is critical. Rule out closed fracture or soft tissue laceration without bone involvement.

topic: Acute Anterior Shoulder Dislocation (Bankart & Hill-Sachs Lesion)
red_flags: severe pain and inability to move arm
visible deformity (flattened deltoid, prominent humeral head)
clinical_hallmarks: arm held in slight abduction and external rotation
flattened deltoid contour
prominent humeral head anteriorly
severe pain with attempted movement
content: Acute anterior shoulder dislocation typically results from indirect trauma with the arm in abduction and external rotation. Patients present with severe pain, inability to move the arm, and a characteristic deformity: a flattened deltoid contour and a prominent humeral head anteriorly. A thorough neurovascular examination, especially for axillary nerve function (deltoid sensation and contraction), is crucial. X-rays (AP, Y-view, and axillary views) confirm the diagnosis and rule out associated fractures (e.g., greater tuberosity, surgical neck). Bankart lesion (anterior labral tear) and Hill-Sachs lesion (posterolateral humeral head compression fracture) are common complications. Urgent closed reduction under sedation is performed, followed by post-reduction X-rays and immobilization. Rule out rotator cuff tear or AC joint injury.

topic: Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Tear & Meniscal Tear
clinical_hallmarks: positive Lachman test (ACL)
positive anterior drawer test (ACL)
joint line tenderness (meniscus)
positive McMurray test (meniscus)
content: ACL and meniscal tears are common knee injuries, often occurring together, typically from twisting or hyperextension sports injuries. Patients often report an audible 'pop' at the time of injury, followed by immediate swelling (hemarthrosis for ACL) and knee instability or 'giving way.' Meniscal tears can cause joint line pain, locking, or catching. Physical examination reveals a positive Lachman test and anterior drawer test for ACL injury, and positive McMurray test with joint line tenderness for meniscal tears. X-rays rule out fractures. MRI is the gold standard for definitive diagnosis of ligamentous and meniscal injuries. Initial management includes RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation). Definitive treatment varies from conservative management to surgical reconstruction (ACL) or repair/meniscectomy (meniscus), depending on patient activity level and tear characteristics. Rule out collateral ligament injury or patellar dislocation.

topic: Achilles Tendon Rupture (Thompson Squeeze Test Positive)
red_flags: inability to push off foot or stand on toes
clinical_hallmarks: positive Thompson squeeze test (absence of plantarflexion)
palpable gap in Achilles tendon
weakness in plantarflexion
inability to stand on toes
content: Achilles tendon rupture typically occurs during sudden plantarflexion or dorsiflexion, often in 'weekend warriors.' Patients describe a sudden sharp pain in the calf or heel, often feeling like they were kicked, accompanied by an audible 'pop' or 'snap.' They experience difficulty with push-off and inability to stand on their toes. The hallmark clinical sign is a positive Thompson squeeze test: squeezing the calf muscle does not produce plantarflexion of the foot. A palpable gap in the tendon may also be present. Ultrasound or MRI can confirm the diagnosis and assess the extent of the tear. Management options include non-operative treatment with casting/boot immobilization in equinus or surgical repair, depending on patient age, activity level, and tear characteristics. Rule out calf muscle strain or ankle sprain.

topic: Cauda Equina Syndrome (Saddle Anesthesia & Sphincter Disturbance)
red_flags: new onset urinary retention or incontinence
clinical_hallmarks: saddle anesthesia (loss of sensation in S2-S5 dermatomes)
bladder and/or bowel dysfunction
decreased anal sphincter tone
bilateral lower extremity motor and sensory deficits
content: Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES) is a rare but severe neurological emergency caused by compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots distal to the conus medullaris. It typically presents with a triad of symptoms: severe low back pain, saddle anesthesia (numbness in the perineal, perianal, and genital areas), and bladder/bowel dysfunction (urinary retention/incontinence, fecal incontinence). Other signs include bilateral lower extremity weakness, sensory deficits, and diminished anal tone. Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine is the diagnostic modality of choice. Immediate surgical decompression is critical, ideally within 24-48 hours of symptom onset, to prevent permanent neurological deficits. Delay in treatment can lead to irreversible bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction. Rule out simple disc herniation or peripheral neuropathy.

red_flags: acute onset monoarticular joint pain, swelling, warmth, erythema
inability to bear weight (in lower limb)
clinical_hallmarks: acute monoarticular arthritis (most commonly knee, hip)
fever and systemic signs of infection
elevated ESR and CRP
elevated synovial fluid WBC count (>50,000 cells/mm3, >75% PMNs)
content: Septic arthritis is a joint infection, typically bacterial, causing rapid joint destruction if untreated. It presents as acute onset monoarticular arthritis with severe pain, swelling, warmth, erythema, and restricted range of motion. Systemic symptoms like fever and chills are common. In children, Kocher criteria (non-weight bearing, ESR >40, fever, WBC >12,000) aid in diagnosing septic hip. Urgent joint aspiration for synovial fluid analysis (cell count, Gram stain, culture, glucose, protein) is critical. Blood cultures and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, WBC) are essential. X-rays may show soft tissue swelling, while MRI can detect early changes. Management involves prompt intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent surgical drainage (arthrotomy or arthroscopic lavage) to remove pus and debris, preventing irreversible cartilage damage. Rule out gout, pseudogout, or inflammatory arthritis.

topic: Acute Osteomyelitis (Pediatric Hematogenous vs Chronic Diabetic)
red_flags: persistent localized bone pain, tenderness, swelling
non-healing wound with exposed bone (diabetic foot)
clinical_hallmarks: localized bone pain and tenderness
fever (especially in pediatric hematogenous)
elevated ESR and CRP
positive probe-to-bone test (diabetic foot ulcer)
content: Acute osteomyelitis is a bone infection, often bacterial. Pediatric hematogenous osteomyelitis typically affects long bones, presenting with fever, localized bone pain, and refusal to bear weight. Chronic osteomyelitis, particularly in diabetics, often involves the foot, arising from contiguous spread from ulcers, presenting with a non-healing wound, erythema, and swelling, sometimes without fever. Diagnosis involves elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, WBC), blood cultures (especially for hematogenous), and imaging. X-rays show late changes (periosteal reaction, lucency). MRI is highly sensitive for early diagnosis. Bone scan can also be useful. Management requires prolonged intravenous antibiotics (4-6 weeks) and often surgical debridement of infected and necrotic bone, especially in chronic cases or those with abscess formation. Rule out cellulitis, stress fracture, or tumor.

topic: Pelvic Ring Fracture with Hemodynamic Instability (Tile / Young-Burgess)
red_flags: gross hematuria, rectal or vaginal bleeding
clinical_hallmarks: pelvic instability on examination (gentle compression/distraction)
signs of hypovolemic shock
positive FAST scan for free fluid in abdomen
associated genitourinary or gastrointestinal injuries
content: Pelvic ring fractures with hemodynamic instability are life-threatening injuries resulting from high-energy trauma. The primary concern is massive hemorrhage from venous plexuses or arterial injury. Patients present with severe pelvic pain, signs of hypovolemic shock (hypotension, tachycardia), and often pelvic instability on examination. Initial management focuses on ABCDE, aggressive fluid resuscitation, and immediate application of a pelvic binder or sheet to reduce pelvic volume and tamponade bleeding. AP pelvis X-ray is initial imaging; CT scan provides detailed fracture assessment and identifies hemorrhage sources. Angioembolization or preperitoneal packing may be required for arterial bleeding. External fixation or C-clamp application provides definitive stabilization and further hemorrhage control. Close monitoring for associated genitourinary, gastrointestinal, and neurological injuries is crucial. Rule out isolated hip fracture or sacral fracture without instability.

clinical_hallmarks: brawny induration of submandibular space
elevation of tongue
bilateral submandibular swelling
woody neck
content: Ludwig's Angina is a rapidly progressive, aggressive cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, typically arising from odontogenic infections. It is a medical emergency due to its potential for rapid airway compromise. Patients present with fever, malaise, severe neck pain, bilateral submandibular swelling, and a characteristic 'woody' induration of the floor of the mouth and neck. Physical examination reveals elevated tongue, drooling, and trismus. Pertinent rule-outs include deep neck abscesses and necrotizing fasciitis. Diagnostic workup involves urgent CT scan of the neck with contrast to assess the extent of infection and airway patency. Management includes aggressive broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (e.g., penicillin G plus metronidazole or clindamycin), meticulous airway monitoring, and potential for surgical airway (tracheostomy) if obstruction is imminent. Surgical drainage is generally not indicated unless a true abscess forms.

topic: Deep Neck Space Infection (Retropharyngeal & Parapharyngeal Abscess)
clinical_hallmarks: unilateral neck swelling
torticollis
trismus (parapharyngeal)
muffled voice
pharyngeal bulge (retropharyngeal)
content: Deep neck space infections, including retropharyngeal and parapharyngeal abscesses, are serious infections of the fascial planes of the neck, often originating from odontogenic, tonsillar, or pharyngeal infections. Patients typically present with fever, severe neck pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, and torticollis. Physical examination may reveal unilateral neck swelling, trismus (parapharyngeal), or a posterior pharyngeal bulge (retropharyngeal). These infections can rapidly spread, leading to life-threatening complications like airway obstruction, mediastinitis, or septic thrombophlebitis (Lemierre's syndrome). Pertinent rule-outs include simple cellulitis or lymphadenitis. Diagnostic workup necessitates an urgent CT scan of the neck with intravenous contrast to delineate the extent of infection and identify abscess formation. Management involves aggressive broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and often surgical incision and drainage, particularly for mature abscesses or those causing airway compromise.

topic: Malignant Otitis Externa (Skull Base Osteomyelitis in Diabetics)
red_flags: granulation tissue at bony cartilaginous junction
clinical_hallmarks: severe otalgia disproportionate to findings
granulation tissue in external auditory canal
purulent otorrhea
elevated ESR/CRP
pertinent_negatives: absence of typical fungal elements (though can be fungal)
content: Malignant Otitis Externa (MOE) is a severe, necrotizing infection of the external auditory canal and skull base, predominantly affecting elderly diabetic or immunocompromised patients. It is typically caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Patients present with unrelenting, deep-seated otalgia, purulent otorrhea, and often granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the external auditory canal. Progression can lead to cranial nerve palsies, particularly facial nerve paralysis, and osteomyelitis of the temporal bone and skull base. Pertinent rule-outs include simple otitis externa or cholesteatoma. Diagnostic workup includes high-resolution CT scan of the temporal bone to assess bone erosion, MRI for soft tissue and intracranial extension, and Technetium-99m bone scan for early diagnosis. Treatment involves prolonged courses (weeks to months) of high-dose intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics, with surgical debridement reserved for refractory cases or sequestrum formation.

topic: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL Golden Window Steroid Therapy)
clinical_hallmarks: acute onset (>30 dB SNHL over 3 contiguous frequencies within 72 hours)
often unilateral
absence of conductive component
tinnitus and/or vertigo
content: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL) is defined as an acute onset of hearing loss of at least 30 dB in three contiguous frequencies over a period of 72 hours or less. It is often idiopathic but can be caused by viral infections, vascular events, or autoimmune conditions. Patients typically present with unilateral hearing loss, often accompanied by tinnitus and sometimes vertigo. The 'golden window' for treatment is crucial, ideally within 2 weeks of onset. Physical examination should rule out conductive causes (e.g., cerumen impaction, middle ear effusion). Diagnostic workup includes urgent pure-tone audiometry to confirm SNHL. MRI of the internal auditory canal and brain is essential to rule out retrocochlear pathology, such as a vestibular schwannoma. Treatment involves systemic corticosteroids, with intratympanic steroid injections as an alternative or salvage therapy, and close follow-up.

topic: Severe Posterior Epistaxis (Sphenopalatine Artery Bleed / Epistaxis Packing)
clinical_hallmarks: blood dripping down posterior pharynx
inability to control bleeding with anterior pressure
significant blood loss
often associated with hypertension/anticoagulants
content: Severe posterior epistaxis typically originates from branches of the sphenopalatine artery in the posterior nasal cavity and can lead to significant blood loss and hemodynamic instability. Patients present with profuse bleeding, often perceived as blood dripping down the back of the throat, which is not controlled by anterior nasal pressure. Risk factors include hypertension, coagulopathies, and anticoagulant use. Initial management focuses on ABCs, vital sign stabilization, and assessment of blood loss. Physical examination involves careful anterior rhinoscopy after suctioning to identify the bleeding source. If anterior packing fails, posterior nasal packing (e.g., balloon catheter, gauze pack) is required. Pertinent rule-outs include trauma or underlying tumors. Diagnostic workup may include CBC, coagulation profile, and type and cross-match. Refractory cases may necessitate endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolization. Hospital admission is often required for observation and management of underlying causes.

topic: Foreign Body Bronchus vs Foreign Body Esophagus (Coin vs Button Battery)
clinical_hallmarks: sudden onset choking/coughing (bronchus)
dysphagia/odynophagia (esophagus)
unilateral wheeze/decreased breath sounds (bronchus)
refusal to eat (child)
content: Foreign body (FB) aspiration into the bronchus or ingestion into the esophagus are common pediatric emergencies. Bronchial FBs present with sudden choking, coughing, wheezing, or stridor, potentially leading to respiratory distress. Esophageal FBs cause dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling, or refusal to eat. Button battery ingestion is a critical emergency due to rapid liquefaction necrosis and perforation risk. Coins are common FBs. Physical examination includes assessing respiratory status and auscultating the chest for unilateral findings. Pertinent rule-outs include croup or asthma. Diagnostic workup begins with plain radiographs (AP and lateral neck/chest/abdomen) to localize the FB. Bronchial FBs appear vertically oriented on AP view, esophageal FBs appear horizontally. Management involves urgent endoscopic removal: rigid bronchoscopy for airway FBs and esophagoscopy for esophageal FBs. Button batteries require immediate removal.

clinical_hallmarks: postauricular erythema, tenderness, swelling, and fluctuance
protrusion of auricle
recent history of acute otitis media
fever, otalgia
content: Acute mastoiditis is an inflammatory process of the mastoid air cells, typically a complication of inadequately treated acute otitis media. When a subperiosteal abscess forms, it indicates pus accumulation beneath the mastoid periosteum. Patients present with persistent otalgia, fever, and postauricular pain, erythema, and swelling, often causing the auricle to protrude downwards and outwards. Physical examination reveals tenderness and fluctuance over the mastoid process. Pertinent rule-outs include cellulitis or lymphadenitis. Diagnostic workup includes a high-resolution CT scan of the temporal bone with contrast to confirm mastoiditis, identify bone erosion, and delineate any abscesses or intracranial complications. Management involves aggressive intravenous antibiotics. Surgical intervention, typically myringotomy with tympanostomy tube placement and/or cortical mastoidectomy with abscess drainage, is often required, especially with abscess formation or signs of intracranial spread.

topic: Vestibular Neuritis & Labyrinthitis (HINTS Exam Central vs Peripheral)
clinical_hallmarks: acute onset severe vertigo
nausea/vomiting
spontaneous horizontal nystagmus (unidirectional, suppressed by fixation)
positive head impulse test (peripheral), no hearing loss (neuritis)
content: Vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis are acute peripheral vestibulopathies causing sudden, severe vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. Labyrinthitis additionally involves hearing loss. The critical distinction is differentiating peripheral from central causes of vertigo, especially stroke, using the HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew). A 'HINTS-plus' exam (adding hearing loss) is highly sensitive for central lesions. Peripheral findings include a positive head impulse test, unidirectional horizontal nystagmus suppressed by fixation, and no skew deviation. Central findings include a negative head impulse, vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation. Pertinent rule-outs include posterior circulation stroke or cerebellar hemorrhage. Diagnostic workup involves clinical assessment; MRI brain is indicated if HINTS suggests a central lesion. Management is symptomatic (antiemetics, vestibular suppressants) and vestibular rehabilitation.

topic: Nasal Bone Fracture with Septal Hematoma
clinical_hallmarks: nasal deformity
crepitus on palpation
epistaxis
periorbital ecchymosis
intranasal examination revealing septal hematoma (bluish, boggy swelling)
content: Nasal bone fractures are the most common facial fractures, typically resulting from direct trauma. Patients present with nasal pain, swelling, epistaxis, and often visible deformity. The most critical complication to identify is a septal hematoma, which appears as a bluish, boggy swelling on intranasal examination. Untreated, a septal hematoma can lead to avascular necrosis of the septal cartilage and subsequent 'saddle nose' deformity or septal abscess. Physical examination involves palpation for crepitus and deformity, and careful anterior rhinoscopy. Pertinent rule-outs include other facial fractures or intracranial injury. Diagnostic workup is primarily clinical; imaging (CT facial bones) is reserved for suspected concomitant fractures, orbital involvement, or for surgical planning. Management includes urgent incision and drainage of any septal hematoma, pain control, and closed reduction of the nasal fracture, ideally within 7-14 days of injury.

topic: Vocal Cord Paralysis (Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Palsy)
clinical_hallmarks: hoarseness/dysphonia
breathy voice
vocal fatigue
aspiration/choking on liquids
direct visualization of immobile vocal cord on laryngoscopy
pertinent_negatives: no obvious mass on initial exam
content: Vocal cord paralysis, often due to recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) palsy, results in impaired vocal cord mobility. Unilateral paralysis typically presents with hoarseness, a breathy voice, and sometimes aspiration, particularly with liquids. Bilateral paralysis is a life-threatening emergency causing severe airway obstruction and stridor. Common etiologies include iatrogenic injury (e.g., thyroid or neck surgery), malignancy (lung, thyroid, esophageal), neurological disorders, or idiopathic causes. Physical examination includes flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy to directly visualize vocal cord mobility and identify the affected side. Pertinent rule-outs include vocal cord mass or cricoarytenoid joint fixation. Diagnostic workup involves imaging from the skull base to the diaphragm (CT neck and chest) to identify any lesion compressing or invading the RLN. Management includes voice therapy, and for persistent dysphonia or aspiration, surgical options like injection laryngoplasty or medialization thyroplasty.

clinical_hallmarks: biphasic illness: prodromal high fever followed by acute neurological deterioration
generalized convulsions
parkinsonian extrapyramidal signs (cogwheel rigidity, tremor, mask-like facies)
coma
pertinent_negatives: no neck stiffness characteristic of pyogenic bacterial meningitis
content: Flavivirus infection transmitted by Culex tritaeniorhynchus mosquitoes breeding in rural rice fields. Leading cause of Acute Encephalitis Syndrome (AES) in children in endemic zones. Diagnosis: CSF IgM capture ELISA. Treatment: ICU neuro-protective supportive care and antiepileptic therapy.

clinical_hallmarks: sudden high fever with chills and frontal headache
severe prostration and generalized muscle pain
biphasic course with hemorrhagic signs
marked leukopenia and thrombocytopenia
content: Tick-borne hemorrhagic viral disease caused by KFD virus transmitted by Haemaphysalis ticks. Features sudden high fever, intense myalgias, conjunctival suffusion, and bleeding diathesis. Diagnosis: RT-PCR / IgM ELISA. Treatment: Supportive care, blood/platelet transfusion as indicated.

red_flags: ascending cellulitis / necrotizing soft tissue infection
septic shock from secondary bacterial superinfection
clinical_hallmarks: acute adenolymphangitis (adl): high fever with retrograde ascending painful red streaks along lymphatics
tender inguinal lymphadenopathy
non-pitting progressive lymphedema of lower limbs or genitalia (scrotal hydrocele)
pertinent_negatives: no deep vein thrombosis on compression venous doppler
content: Parasitic infection caused by Wuchereria bancrofti transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Adult worms dwell in lymphatic channels causing mechanical obstruction. Diagnosis: Midnight peripheral blood smear, Filarial Antigenaemia Card Test. Treatment: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC 6 mg/kg/day for 12 days) + Albendazole 400 mg.

clinical_hallmarks: classic undulant pattern fever rising in afternoon
profuse nocturnal drenching diaphoresis with distinctive moldy odor
asymmetric sacroiliitis, spondylodiscitis, and peripheral arthritis
epididymo-orchitis in young men
content: Zoonotic bacterial infection caused by Brucella species acquired via unpasteurized dairy consumption or direct animal contact. Diagnosis: Standard Agglutination Test (SAT titer >= 1:160), blood culture (prolonged incubation). Treatment: Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 6 weeks PLUS Streptomycin 1g IM daily for 2-3 weeks.

topic: Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (WHO Category III Dog Bite)
red_flags: category iii transdermal bite with bleeding
lick over broken skin or mucosal contamination
clinical hydrophobia or aerophobia (100% fatal encephalitis)
clinical_hallmarks: fresh animal bite wound with tooth laceration or puncture
localized paresthesia at site of healed bite (prodrome)
hydrophobia (pharyngeal spasm triggered by attempting to swallow liquids)
aerophobia
pertinent_negatives: no previous complete rabies pre-exposure immunization
content: Lyssavirus infection transmitted via saliva of infected mammals. Protocolized PEP: 1. Immediate wound washing with soap and running water for 15 minutes; 2. Infiltrate Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG: ERIG 40 IU/kg or HRIG 20 IU/kg) into and around all wound margins STAT; 3. Modern Cell Culture Rabies Vaccine (CCRV) on Days 0, 3, 7, and 28.

topic: Rotaviral & Enteric Adenoviral Enteritis in Infants
red_flags: severe dehydration: sunken fontanelle, absent tears, prolonged capillary refill > 3s, lethargy, anuria
clinical_hallmarks: watery, non-bloody diarrhea with fever and vomiting lasting 3-8 days
rapid onset dehydration in infant aged 6-24 months
perianal excoriation from acidic loose stools
pertinent_negatives: no frank blood or mucus in stools (rules out bacterial dysentery)
content: Leading cause of severe dehydrating diarrhea in infants worldwide. Transmitted via fecal-oral route. Diagnosis: Stool rotavirus antigen detection (ELISA/immunochromatography). Treatment: Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) + Zinc supplementation (20 mg/day for 14 days) + continuation of breastfeeding; IV Ringer Lactate if severe shock.

clinical_hallmarks: the 3 cs: Cough, Coryza, and Conjunctivitis with prominent photophobia
pathognomonic Koplik spots (tiny bluish-white grains on erythematous buccal mucosa opposite molars)
erythematous maculopapular rash beginning at hairline/behind ears and spreading downward to face, trunk, and extremities (craniocaudal)
content: Highly contagious paramyxovirus infection transmitted by respiratory droplets. Diagnostic workup: Measles IgM serology, RT-PCR. Treatment: Supportive care, isolation, and Vitamin A supplementation (200,000 IU daily for 2 days) to prevent blindness and mortality.

red_flags: congenital rubella syndrome: microcephaly, sensorineural deafness, cataract, patent ductus arteriosus (pda) in fetus of infected pregnant mother
clinical_hallmarks: mild fever with distinctive tender suboccipital, postauricular, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy
discrete pink-rose maculopapular rash spreading from face downward, clearing by day 3
Forchheimer spots (petechiae on soft palate) and transient polyarthralgia in adult females
pertinent_negatives: rash fades much faster than measles (3-day measles)
content: Togavirus infection mild in children but catastrophic in early pregnancy (teratogenic Congenital Rubella Syndrome). Diagnosis: Rubella IgM antibodies. Treatment: Symptomatic supportive care; prevention via universal MMR vaccination.

red_flags: acute testicular atrophy and subfertility from post-pubertal mumps orchitis
acute pancreatitis with severe epigastric pain
clinical_hallmarks: acute bilateral or unilateral tender, painful swelling of parotid salivary glands obscuring the angle of the jaw and elevating the earlobe
pain accentuated by chewing or consuming sour/acidic foods (lemon juice test)
erythema and edema of Stensen duct orifice on buccal mucosa
pertinent_negatives: no purulent discharge from stensen duct on massage (rules out bacterial suppurative parotitis)
content: Paramyxovirus infection spread by respiratory droplets affecting salivary glands, gonads, pancreas, and CNS. Diagnosis: Mumps IgM, elevated serum amylase. Treatment: Supportive analgesia, cold/warm compresses, scrotal support and bed rest for orchitis.

red_flags: apnea episodes and cyanosis in infants < 6 months
clinical_hallmarks: violent paroxysmal coughing spasms followed by high-pitched inspiratory whoop
post-tussive emesis (vomiting after coughing fit)
subconjunctival hemorrhages and facial petechiae
pertinent_negatives: no wheezing or crackles on auscultation between coughing spasms
content: Respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis. Dangerous in infants under 6 months where whoop is absent, presenting with apnea. Diagnosis: Nasopharyngeal swab PCR, marked absolute lymphocytosis. Treatment: Azithromycin (10 mg/kg/day for 5 days); post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts.

topic: Acute Lower Extremity Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
red_flags: phlegmasia cerulea dolens: massive limb cyanosis and impending gangrene
concomitant sudden chest pain or dyspnea (PE)
clinical_hallmarks: acute unilateral swelling of calf (> 3 cm difference measured 10 cm below tibial tuberosity)
tenderness along deep venous distribution (popliteal/femoral)
erythema, warmth, and prominent superficial collateral veins
pertinent_negatives: no bilateral symmetrical edema characteristic of heart failure or cirrhosis
content: Blood clot in deep leg veins governed by Virchow triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability). Diagnosis: Venous Duplex Compression Ultrasound, D-dimer. Treatment: Therapeutic anticoagulation with DOACs (Apixaban, Rivaroxaban) or LMWH bridging to Warfarin; graduated compression stockings.

red_flags: acute severe valvular regurgitation with pulmonary edema
conduction block (prolonged PR / complete heart block) from aortic ring abscess
clinical_hallmarks: prolonged unexplained fever with chills and night sweats
new regurgitant cardiac murmur or changing character of preexisting murmur
stigmata: subungual splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, splenomegaly
pertinent_negatives: no negative blood cultures after proper collection prior to antibiotics
content: Microbial infection of cardiac endothelial lining and valves (Staph aureus, Viridans strep). Diagnosis: Modified Duke criteria; 3 sets of blood cultures; Transthoracic and Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE). Treatment: Prolonged bactericidal IV antibiotics (4-6 weeks); urgent surgical valve replacement if refractory heart failure or large vegetations.

topic: Hypertensive Emergency with Acute Target-Organ Damage
red_flags: hypertensive encephalopathy (altered mental status, papilledema, seizures)
clinical_hallmarks: severe acute elevation in blood pressure: SBP >= 180 and/or DBP >= 120 mmHg
PRESENCE of acute, progressive target-organ dysfunction
severe occipital headache, blurred vision, bilateral retinal flame hemorrhages and papilledema
pertinent_negatives: absence of end-organ damage defines Hypertensive Urgency
content: Severe blood pressure elevation accompanied by acute life-threatening target-organ compromise. Therapeutic principle: Lower MAP by NO MORE than 20-25% in the first hour to prevent cerebral/renal hypoperfusion. Treatment: Titratable IV antihypertensives (IV Labetalol, IV Nicardipine, IV Nitroglycerin).

red_flags: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (fever and abdominal pain in ascites)
clinical_hallmarks: stigmata: ascites with fluid wave, spider nevi, palmar erythema, jaundice
asterixis (flapping tremor of dorsiflexed hands)
reversal of sleep-wake cycle and confusion
pedal edema and sarcopenia
pertinent_negatives: no focal neurological deficits typical of stroke
content: End-stage hepatic fibrosis complicated by portal hypertension and synthetic failure. Diagnosis: Diagnostic paracentesis (neutrophil count >= 250/uL confirms SBP; SAAG >= 1.1 g/dL confirms portal HTN), LFT, ultrasound with portal Doppler. Treatment: Lactulose + Rifaximin for encephalopathy; sodium restriction and diuretics for ascites; IV Cefotaxime + Albumin for SBP.

red_flags: hernia mass becomes exquisitely painful, firm, erythematous, and completely irreducible
bowel obstruction: bilious vomiting, obstipation, distension
clinical_hallmarks: preexisting reducible groin bulge that suddenly becomes intensely painful and cannot be pushed back
tenderness localized to groin lump with absence of expansile cough impulse
colicky abdominal cramps
pertinent_negatives: no manual reducibility with gentle taxis
content: Surgical emergency where abdominal viscera trapped in hernia neck develop compromised vascular supply leading to bowel gangrene and perforation. Forceful taxis is strictly contraindicated. Protocol: Strict NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, NG decompression, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and STAT emergency inguinal herniotomy.

topic: Acute Ascending Cholangitis (Charcot's Triad & Reynolds' Pentad)
red_flags: Reynolds' Pentad: Charcot triad PLUS hypotension/shock and altered mental status
severe biliary septic shock refractory to fluid resuscitation
bilirubin > 5 mg/dL with acute renal failure
clinical_hallmarks: Charcot Triad in 70%: high spiking fever with rigors, obstructive jaundice, and RUQ abdominal pain
dark amber urine and pale clay stools
RUQ guarding and positive Murphy sign
pertinent_negatives: absence of pneumoperitoneum on chest x-ray
content: Life-threatening bacterial infection of biliary tree superimposed on biliary outflow obstruction (CBD stones, strictures). Diagnosis: Ultrasound abdomen (dilated CBD > 8 mm, choledocholithiasis), MRCP, elevated cholestatic enzymes (ALP, GGT, bilirubin), blood cultures. Treatment: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (Piperacillin-Tazobactam) AND emergency biliary decompression via ERCP sphincterotomy/stenting within 24h.

red_flags: deep rapid labored breathing (Kussmaul) with fruity acetone odor
altered sensorium or coma (cerebral edema risk)
clinical_hallmarks: triad: Hyperglycemia (glucose > 250 mg/dL), Ketosis (positive serum/urine ketones >= 3+), and High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (pH < 7.30, HCO3 < 18, anion gap > 12)
nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain mimicking surgical abdomen
polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, dehydration
pertinent_negatives: no focal neurological signs prior to fluid resuscitation
content: Acute metabolic decompensation from insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormone excess. Protocol: 1. Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (Normal Saline 1-1.5 L in first hour); 2. Potassium repletion BEFORE insulin if K+ < 3.3 mEq/L; 3. Regular Insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hr IV) to close anion gap; 4. Treat precipitating infection.

red_flags: continuous convulsive seizure activity lasting >= 5 minutes
patient does not regain baseline consciousness between seizures
clinical_hallmarks: generalized tonic phase (sustained contraction, apnea, cyanosis, tongue biting) followed by clonic phase (rhythmic jerking of limbs)
frothing at mouth, incontinence
postictal stupor with deep stertorous breathing
pertinent_negatives: no pseudo-seizure features: eyes tightly closed, pelvic thrusting, out-of-phase thrashing
content: Neurological emergency defined as continuous seizure >= 5 min or recurrent seizures without full recovery. Protocol: 0-5 min: Airway, oxygen, glucose check. 5-10 min (First-line): IV Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg or IM Midazolam 10mg. 10-20 min (Second-line): IV Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg or IV Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg. > 30 min (Refractory): Intubation and general anesthesia infusion (Propofol/Midazolam) with continuous EEG.

red_flags: ECLAMPSIA: new-onset generalized tonic-clonic convulsions in pre-eclamptic patient
severe hypertension: SBP >= 160 and/or DBP >= 110 mmHg
HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets < 100k)
clinical_hallmarks: new-onset hypertension (BP >= 140/90) occurring AFTER 20 weeks gestation in previously normotensive female
PLUS proteinuria (>= 300 mg/24h or dipstick 1+) or organ dysfunction
brisk hyperactive deep tendon reflexes (patellar clonus)
pertinent_negatives: no history of chronic hypertension prior to 20 weeks
content: Multisystem pregnancy disorder driven by abnormal placentation and endothelial dysfunction. Definitive cure is delivery. Management: Seizure prophylaxis with IV Magnesium Sulfate (Pritchard/Zuspan regimen: 4g IV loading + 1-2 g/hr maintenance; continue 24h postpartum); Antihypertensives (IV Labetalol, oral Nifedipine); Expedited delivery for eclampsia, HELLP, or gestational age >= 37 weeks.

red_flags: bilateral ptosis (earliest and most sensitive sign of neurotoxicity)
bulbar palsy: dysphagia, pooling of saliva, inability to speak
respiratory muscle paralysis (intercostal/diaphragmatic weakness causing asphyxia)
krait bite often presents with early morning abdominal pain and paralysis without visible bite mark
clinical_hallmarks: history of snake bite or sleeping on rural floor
rapidly descending flaccid motor paralysis: ptosis -> ophthalmoplegia -> facial/palatal weakness -> neck weakness (broken neck sign) -> respiratory arrest
cobra bite has painful local swelling and necrosis; krait bite has zero local swelling
pertinent_negatives: normal 20-Minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20WBCT confirms non-hemotoxic)
content: Neurotoxic snake envenomation (Common Krait, Cobra) blocking neuromuscular junction transmission. Protocol: 1. Immobilize bitten limb (splint, no tourniquet/cutting); 2. Polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV: 10 vials in 100 mL NS over 30-60 min STAT); 3. Atropine 0.6mg + Neostigmine 1.5mg IV test for cobra bites; 4. Early endotracheal intubation for impending respiratory arrest.

topic: Snake Envenomation - Hemotoxic Viperine (Russell's & Saw-Scaled Viper)
red_flags: spontaneous systemic bleeding: hematuria, hemoptysis, gum bleeding
rapidly progressive local swelling crossing two major joints
acute kidney injury / oliguria from tubular necrosis
clinical_hallmarks: two distinct fang marks with immediate agonizing localized burning pain
rapid local edema, hemorrhagic bullae, ecchymosis, and tissue necrosis spreading up the limb
bleeding from gingival margins and continuous ooze from punctures
hypotension and shock
pertinent_negatives: no bilateral ptosis or descending paralysis
content: Viperine snake envenomation (Russell's Viper, Saw-Scaled Viper) containing hemorrhagins and procoagulants causing Venom-Induced Consumption Coagulopathy (VICC) and acute tubular necrosis. Diagnostic workup: 20-Minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20WBCT: dry glass tube undisturbed for 20 min; failure to clot indicates coagulopathy), PT/INR, Serum Creatinine. Treatment: Polyvalent ASV (10 vials in 100 mL NS over 1 hr); Repeat 10 vials after 6h if non-clotting (max 30 vials); Hemodialysis for acute renal failure.

clinical_hallmarks: positive Nikolsky sign (epidermis easily separates and slips off dermis with gentle lateral pressure)
targetoid atypical cutaneous lesions with central dusky purpura
severe involvement of at least two mucosal sites (oral stomatitis, hemorrhagic lip crusting, severe conjunctivitis, genital erosions)
history of culprit drug ingestion 1-3 weeks prior (allopurinol, carbamazepine, sulfonamides, oxicams)
pertinent_negatives: no preceding history of burn trauma
content: Rare life-threatening severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR) characterized by widespread epidermal necrosis and detachment. Score of Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (SCORTEN) determines mortality. Immediate cessation of culprit drug; transfer to Burn ICU; supportive fluid resuscitation, wound care with non-adherent dressings; IVIG or Cyclosporine.

red_flags: erythrodermic psoriasis (> 90% body surface area involvement with hypothermia and high-output heart failure)
generalized pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch) with high fever and leukocytosis
clinical_hallmarks: sharply demarcated erythematous plaques covered by coarse, layered, silvery-white lamellar scales
predilection for extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, scalp, lumbosacral region)
pathognomonic Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding spots upon scraping off silvery scale due to tortuous dermal capillaries)
Koebner phenomenon (appearance of new lesions at sites of mechanical trauma)
nail changes: pitting, oil drop sign, subungual hyperkeratosis
pertinent_negatives: no vesicles or pustules in chronic plaque psoriasis
content: Chronic inflammatory immune-mediated papulosquamous skin disease driven by hyperproliferation of keratinocytes and T-cell mediated cytokines (IL-17, IL-23, TNF-alpha). Treatment: Topical corticosteroids + Vitamin D3 analogues (Calcipotriol); Phototherapy (NB-UVB); Systemic disease-modifying agents (Methotrexate) or targeted Biologics (Secukinumab, Ustekinumab).

red_flags: crusted norwegian scabies in immunocompromised (millions of mites, highly contagious, thick hyperkeratotic crusts)
secondary bacterial glomerulonephritis from streptococcal impetiginization
clinical_hallmarks: intense, agonizing nocturnal pruritus that keeps patient awake, disproportionate to visible cutaneous findings
pathognomonic burrows (short, wavy, grey-white threadlike linear tracks ending in a tiny vesicle where female mite resides)
predilection for interdigital web spaces of fingers, flexor wrists, axillae, periumbilical area, buttocks, and male genitalia (penile papules)
multiple family members or cohabitants simultaneously affected with identical nocturnal itching
pertinent_negatives: sparing of head and neck in immunocompetent adults
content: Parasitic infestation of the epidermis by the microscopic mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. Transmitted via prolonged direct skin-to-skin contact. Diagnosis: Skin scraping with mineral oil demonstrating mites, ova, or scybala (fecal pellets) under microscopy. Treatment: Permethrin 5% cream applied thoroughly from neck down to soles, left on for 8-14 hours and washed off, repeated after 7 days; Oral Ivermectin (200 mcg/kg single dose, repeated in 1-2 weeks); Simultaneous treatment of ALL household contacts and hot washing of bedding/clothes.

red_flags: herpes zoster ophthalmicus with Hutchinson sign (vesicle on tip/side of nose indicating nasociliary nerve involvement risking corneal blindness)
Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy + ear vesicles + vertigo)
sacral zoster causing neurogenic bladder dysfunction
clinical_hallmarks: unilateral, grouped vesicular eruption strictly confined to a single cutaneous dermatome (most commonly thoracic T3-L2 or trigeminal V1), NOT crossing the anatomical midline
preceded 2-4 days by intense localized dermatomal burning, tingling, dysesthesia, or lancinating neuropathic pain
clear fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base that become pustular and crust over within 7-10 days
content: Reactivation of latent Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) residing in dorsal root or cranial nerve sensory ganglia following prior chickenpox. Inciting factors include aging, cellular immunosuppression, or severe stress. Treatment: Oral Valacyclovir (1000 mg TID for 7 days) or Acyclovir (800 mg 5 times daily) initiated within 72 hours of rash onset accelerates healing and reduces Post-Herpetic Neuralgia (PHN) risk; Pregabalin or Gabapentin for acute neuropathic pain.

red_flags: cervical spine fracture following minor trauma (rigid fused spine is brittle)
acute anterior uveitis (red painful photophobic eye)
restrictive pulmonary defect from chest wall rigidity
clinical_hallmarks: insidious onset of chronic low back and buttock pain in young males (< 40 years) lasting > 3 months
inflammatory back pain hallmarks: morning stiffness lasting > 30 minutes, IMPROVES with exercise, DOES NOT improve with rest, frequent nighttime waking
alternating buttock pain from bilateral sacroiliitis
loss of spinal mobility in all planes (reduced Schober test < 5 cm expansion) and reduced chest expansion (< 2.5 cm)
content: Chronic inflammatory arthritis primarily affecting the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints, strongly associated with HLA-B27 antigen (> 90%). Leads to syndesmophyte formation, calcification of interspinous ligaments, and eventual 'bamboo spine' fusion. Diagnostic workup: Pelvic X-ray / MRI showing bilateral sacroiliitis (bone marrow edema, erosions, sclerosis), HLA-B27 genetic testing, elevated ESR/CRP. Treatment: First-line: Regular daily physical therapy/swimming PLUS continuous NSAIDs (Naproxen, Indomethacin); Second-line: Biologics (TNF inhibitors: Infliximab, Adalimumab; IL-17 inhibitors: Secukinumab).

topic: Lumbar Disc Herniation with Cauda Equina Syndrome Triage
red_flags: CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME (SURGICAL EMERGENCY): new-onset urinary retention or overflow incontinence
saddle anesthesia (loss of sensation over perineum, buttocks, inner thighs, and perianal S3-S5 distribution)
lax anal sphincter tone on digital rectal examination
bilateral lower extremity motor weakness or progressive foot drop
clinical_hallmarks: unilateral sharp, shooting, electric-shock lancinating pain radiating from lower back down the buttock, posterior/lateral thigh, calf, and into the foot along a specific lumbar/sacral dermatome (sciatica)
pain aggravated by coughing, sneezing, bending forward, or straining
positive Straight Leg Raise (SLR / Lasegue test: radiating pain reproduced between 30 and 70 degrees of passive leg elevation)
diminished ankle reflex (S1) or knee reflex (L4)
pertinent_negatives: absence of saddle sensory loss and normal bladder scan rules out cauda equina in simple sciatica
content: Protrusion or extrusion of lumbar intervertebral disc nucleus pulposus through a torn annulus fibrosus, most commonly L4-L5 or L5-S1, compressing the traversing or exiting nerve root. Cauda equina syndrome requires emergency MRI and surgical decompression within 24-48 hours. Simple sciatica: 90% improve with conservative care (oral NSAIDs, short course oral steroids, physical therapy, epidural steroid injections).

red_flags: irreversible neuromuscular necrosis within 6-8 hours leading to permanent contracture (Volkmann ischemic contracture) or amputation
rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuric acute renal failure
clinical_hallmarks: pain completely OUT OF PROPORTION to the underlying injury, refractory to opioid analgesia
exquisite, agonizing pain upon PASSIVE STRETCH of muscles traversing the affected compartment (most sensitive early clinical sign)
tense, woody, stony-firm induration of the muscular compartment on palpation
paresthesias and hypoesthesia in distribution of traversing sensory nerves (early sign)
pulselessness and pallor are late terminal findings indicating established tissue death
pertinent_negatives: distal pulses may remain palpable even in advanced compartment syndrome (do not rely on pulses to exclude)
content: Elevated osteofascial compartment pressure (> 30 mmHg or delta pressure < 30 mmHg from diastolic BP) compromising capillary perfusion and tissue viability, commonly following tibia/forearm fractures, crush injuries, or tight circumferential casts. Orthopedic emergency. Protocol: Immediately split and remove all circumferential casts, splints, and dressings down to skin; keep limb level with heart (do NOT elevate, as elevation decreases perfusion pressure); STAT emergency surgical double-incision decompressive fasciotomy of all involved compartments.

keywords: tall thin young man chest pain
red_flags: TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX: tracheal deviation away from affected side, severe hypotension/shock, distended neck veins, cyanosis
clinical_hallmarks: sudden onset sharp, stabbing, unilateral pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea occurring at rest
markedly decreased or absent breath sounds on affected side
hyper-resonance upon percussion over affected hemithorax
decreased tactile vocal fremitus on affected side
pertinent_negatives: absence of tracheal shift indicates simple, non-tension pneumothorax
content: Accumulation of air within pleural cavity causing lung collapse. Primary spontaneous occurs in tall, thin young adult males without lung disease due to rupture of subpleural apical blebs. Secondary spontaneous occurs in preexisting lung disease (COPD, bullae, TB). Tension pneumothorax is a clinical emergency requiring immediate needle thoracostomy (14G needle in 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line or 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line) followed by formal intercostal chest tube insertion (ICD) with underwater seal drainage.

red_flags: empyema (frank pus in pleural space: requires immediate chest tube drainage)
loculated complicated parapneumonic effusion (pH < 7.20, glucose < 40 mg/dL)
massive effusion causing mediastinal shift and respiratory failure
clinical_hallmarks: stony dullness on percussion over affected lower lung field
markedly decreased or absent breath sounds and absent vocal resonance over fluid area
egophony (e-to-a change) at superior border of fluid level
dull aching pleuritic chest pain that improves as fluid accumulates and separates pleural layers
pertinent_negatives: no bronchial breath sounds over the fluid itself
content: Excessive accumulation of fluid between parietal and visceral pleura. Light's criteria differentiates exudate from transudate (effusion protein/serum protein > 0.5, effusion LDH/serum LDH > 0.6). Parapneumonic effusions and TB are leading exudative causes. Diagnostic workup: Diagnostic thoracentesis / pleural tap, chest ultrasound, CT thorax. Treatment: Therapeutic aspiration; Intercostal chest drain (ICD) for empyema or complicated parapneumonic effusion; Intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy (tPA + DNase) for loculated collections.

red_flags: massive life-threatening hemoptysis (> 200-400 mL/24h risking airway asphyxiation)
acute respiratory failure with severe hypoxia and hypercapnia
clinical_hallmarks: chronic, daily cough producing copious amounts of thick, foul-smelling, purulent, three-layered sputum (top frothy, middle turbid, bottom thick sediment)
recurrent episodes of hemoptysis (streaky blood in sputum)
coarse, loud, wet crackles and expiratory squeaks heard over affected lung bases that persist after coughing
digital clubbing in chronic cases
pertinent_negatives: no reversible bronchospasm completely normalizing spirometry
content: Irreversible abnormal dilation and destruction of major bronchi and bronchioles caused by recurrent chronic infection and inflammation (post-TB, cystic fibrosis, measles, immunodeficiency). Diagnostic workup: High-Resolution CT Thorax (HRCT: gold standard showing 'tram-track' sign, 'signet ring' sign where bronchial diameter exceeds adjacent pulmonary artery), sputum culture (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, H. influenzae), pulmonary function tests. Treatment: Daily airway clearance techniques (chest physiotherapy, oscillatory positive expiratory pressure devices, postural drainage); Targeted antibiotics (e.g. Ciprofloxacin for Pseudomonas); Bronchial artery embolization for massive hemoptysis.

clinical_hallmarks: frequent small-volume stools with frank blood and mucus
severe colicky lower abdominal cramping
tenesmus (painful ineffectual straining)
absence of high spiking fever characteristic of bacillary dysentery
pertinent_negatives: no massive watery dehydration typical of cholera
content: Invasive intestinal infection by Entamoeba histolytica causing flask-shaped mucosal ulcers. Treatment: Oral Metronidazole (750 mg TID for 7-10 days) followed by luminal Diloxanide furoate (500 mg TID for 10 days).

red_flags: chronic malabsorption with profound weight loss
clinical_hallmarks: profuse, pale, greasy, foul-smelling diarrhea that floats in toilet (steatorrhea)
rotten-egg sulfurous eructations / burping
excessive abdominal flatulence, distension, and bloating
absence of blood or pus in stool
content: Flagellated protozoan infection of duodenum and jejunum by Giardia lamblia cysts from contaminated water. Diagnosis: Stool microscopy for cysts/trophozoites or stool Giardia antigen ELISA. Treatment: Metronidazole (400 mg TID for 5-7 days) or Tinidazole (2g single dose).

red_flags: secondary bacterial perianal excoriation and cellulitis
clinical_hallmarks: intense, troublesome nocturnal perianal and perineal pruritus disturbing sleep
restlessness, teeth grinding (bruxism), and enuresis in children
tiny white thread-like worms visible around anus or on stool surface at night
pertinent_negatives: no diarrhea or weight loss in simple pinworm
content: Nematode infestation by Enterobius vermicularis where gravid female worms migrate out of anus at night to deposit ova on perianal skin. Diagnosis: Cellophane tape / Scotch tape test applied to perianal skin early in morning before bathing. Treatment: Single dose Albendazole 400 mg (or Mebendazole 100 mg), MUST BE REPEATED in 2 weeks; treat all household members simultaneously.

red_flags: mechanical bowel obstruction from worm bolus in ileocecal valve
clinical_hallmarks: passage of live 15-30 cm smooth, creamy-white roundworm in stool or vomitus
Loeffler syndrome (pulmonary phase: dry cough, wheezing, transient infiltrates, marked peripheral eosinophilia as larvae migrate through lungs)
abdominal distension and protein-energy malnutrition in children
content: Common intestinal nematode infection by Ascaris lumbricoides via ingestion of embryonated eggs in contaminated soil/vegetables. Diagnosis: Stool microscopy for characteristic bile-stained mammillated eggs. Treatment: Single dose Albendazole 400 mg or Mebendazole 100 mg BID for 3 days; Conservative or surgical relief for mechanical bolus obstruction.

topic: Hookworm Infection & Severe Iron Deficiency Anemia
red_flags: severe high-output congestive heart failure from profound anemia (Hb < 4-5 g/dL)
impaired cognitive and physical growth in children
clinical_hallmarks: 'Ground itch' (pruritic maculopapular dermatitis at site of larval skin penetration on bare feet)
profound microcytic hypochromic iron deficiency anemia (severe pallor, fatigue, exertional dyspnea, koilonychia) caused by chronic intestinal blood loss
epigastric pain and geophagia (pica / eating dirt)
content: Intestinal nematode infection by Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus whose adult worms attach to small bowel mucosa and consume 0.2 mL blood/worm/day. Diagnosis: Stool microscopy for hookworm ova, CBC showing severe microcytic anemia and eosinophilia. Treatment: Albendazole 400 mg single dose PLUS oral iron therapy (Ferrous sulfate 200 mg TID) for 3-6 months to replenish marrow iron stores.

keywords: liver cyst with water lily sign
red_flags: anaphylactic shock and acute peritonitis secondary to hydatid cyst rupture
biliary tract obstruction / cholangitis from daughter cyst rupture
tension pneumothorax from pulmonary cyst rupture
clinical_hallmarks: large, painless, slowly expanding cystic mass in right hepatic lobe (> 70%) or lung
dull right upper quadrant heaviness or chronic cough with hemoptysis
pathognomonic 'water lily sign' (floating collapsed endocyst membranes) or daughter cysts on ultrasound/CT
pertinent_negatives: asymptomatic for years due to slow growth (1-5 cm/year)
content: Zoonotic larval cestode infection caused by Echinococcus granulosus tapeworms whose definitive hosts are canines. Man is an accidental intermediate host. Diagnostic workup: Ultrasound / CT abdomen showing multilocular cystic lesion with calcified rim (Gharbi classification), Echinococcus IgG ELISA serology. Treatment: PAIR technique (Puncture, Aspiration, Injection of scolicidal agent [hypertonic saline], Re-aspiration) for selected cysts, radical surgical pericystectomy, combined with Albendazole (400 mg BID for 1-6 months).

red_flags: Type 1 reversal reaction (acute neuritis with rapid motor loss / foot drop)
Type 2 erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL: painful red subcutaneous nodules, fever, uveitis)
corneal ulceration and blindness from lagophthalmos
clinical_hallmarks: hypopigmented or erythematous cutaneous macules / plaques with DEFINITE LOSS OF SENSATION (to light touch, pinprick, or temperature)
thickened, enlarged, tender peripheral nerves (great auricular, ulnar, common peroneal)
motor deformities: claw hand, wrist drop, trophic non-healing plantar ulcers
lepromatous signs: diffuse cutaneous infiltration, leonine facies, madarosis (loss of eyebrows)
pertinent_negatives: sensory loss distinguishes from vitiligo or fungal tinea
content: Chronic granulomatous mycobacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae, primarily targeting cooler tissues: skin, peripheral nerves, and upper respiratory mucosa. Classified by WHO into Paucibacillary (PB: 1-5 skin lesions) and Multibacillary (MB: > 5 lesions). Diagnosis: Slit-skin smear for acid-fast bacilli, nerve biopsy. Treatment: WHO Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT): Rifampicin + Dapsone (+ Clofazimine for MB) for 6-12 months.

red_flags: airway obstruction from membrane detachment causing sudden asphyxiation
diphtheritic myocarditis (arrhythmias, heart failure on day 7-14)
neuropathy (palatal paralysis with nasal regurgitation, polyneuritis)
clinical_hallmarks: dense, dirty-grey, adherent fibrinous pseudomembrane firmly attached to tonsils, uvula, and pharynx that BLEEDS PROFUSELY when dislodged
massive tender bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and soft tissue edema producing pathognomonic 'bull-neck' appearance
brassy barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and low-grade fever with disproportionate toxic prostration
pertinent_negatives: firm adherence of membrane distinguishes from easily scrapable candida thrush
content: Acute toxin-mediated infection by Corynebacterium diphtheriae producing diphtheria exotoxin which inhibits cellular protein synthesis. Statutory emergency. Treatment: Immediate Diphtheria Antitoxin (DAT: 20,000 - 100,000 units IV depending on extent) STAT without waiting for lab confirmation; IV Aqueous Penicillin G or oral Erythromycin for 14 days; Strict droplet isolation; Close monitoring for airway compromise and ECG monitoring for myocarditis.

red_flags: traumatic or spontaneous splenic rupture (sudden severe LUQ pain and hemorrhagic shock)
airway compromise from massive tonsillar enlargement
clinical_hallmarks: classic triad: 1. High fever; 2. Severe exudative pharyngitis with enlarged tonsils; 3. Symmetrical posterior cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy
splenomegaly (present in > 50%) and hepatomegaly with mild transaminase elevation
pathognomonic maculopapular rash appearing 5-7 days after taking Ampicillin or Amoxicillin
pertinent_negatives: absence of bacterial response to beta-lactams
content: Acute viral illness caused by Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV / Human Herpesvirus 4) spread by saliva ('kissing disease') infecting B-lymphocytes. Diagnostic workup: Heterophile antibody test (Monospot test), CBC showing absolute lymphocytosis with > 10% atypical reactive lymphocytes (Downey cells), EBV viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM. Treatment: Supportive care (hydration, analgesia); STRICT AVOIDANCE of contact sports and heavy lifting for minimum 3-4 weeks to prevent catastrophic splenic rupture; Systemic steroids indicated only for airway obstruction or severe thrombocytopenia.

red_flags: superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome (facial edema, neck vein distension, upper extremity plethora)
malignant spinal cord compression from vertebral metastasis
hypercalcemia of malignancy (confusion, polyuria, qt shortening)
clinical_hallmarks: new-onset persistent cough or change in character of chronic smoker cough lasting > 3 weeks
recurrent hemoptysis (coughing blood) and progressive exertional dyspnea
unexplained rapid weight loss, anorexia, and digital clubbing
Pancoast tumor (apical sulcus): shoulder/arm pain (C8-T1 distribution) PLUS Horner syndrome (unilateral ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, enophthalmos)
pertinent_negatives: absence of acute infective fever or sputum response to antibiotics
content: Malignant epithelial tumor of the bronchopulmonary tree (Non-Small Cell [NSCLC 85%] vs Small Cell [SCLC 15%]), strongly correlated with tobacco smoking. Diagnostic workup: Contrast CT thorax/upper abdomen, bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy or CT-guided core biopsy, PET-CT staging, molecular profiling (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, PD-L1). Treatment: Surgical resection (lobectomy) for early stage NSCLC; Chemoradiotherapy, targeted Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (Osimertinib), or Immunotherapy (Pembrolizumab).

red_flags: acute complete large bowel obstruction (vomiting, distension, obstipation)
colonic perforation with acute fecal peritonitis
clinical_hallmarks: Right-sided (caecal/ascending): insidious occult bleeding producing profound microcytic iron deficiency anemia, unexplained fatigue, and palpable right iliac fossa mass

Left-sided (descending/sigmoid): progressive change in bowel habits (alternating constipation and diarrhea), narrowing of stool caliber ('pencil stools'), and visible hematochezia / red blood mixed with stool
unintentional weight loss and tenesmus in rectal cancer
pertinent_negatives: absence of painful external anal pathology (differentiates from hemorrhoids/fissure)
content: Adenocarcinoma arising from epithelial lining of colon or rectum, predominantly progressing through adenoma-carcinoma sequence (APC, KRAS, p53 mutations) or Lynch syndrome (MSI-H). Diagnostic workup: Complete colonoscopy with biopsy (gold standard), CEA tumor marker, Contrast CT chest/abdomen/pelvis staging, MRI pelvis for rectal cancer. Treatment: Oncological resection (hemicolectomy / low anterior resection) with regional lymphadenectomy + adjuvant FOLFOX chemotherapy.

red_flags: inflammatory breast carcinoma (rapid fiery erythema, edema, peau d'orange mimicking mastitis but refractory to antibiotics)
pathological fracture or spinal cord compression from bone metastasis
clinical_hallmarks: painless, hard, irregular, solitary breast mass that is fixed to underlying pectoralis muscle or overlying skin
skin tethering, dimpling, or nipple retraction / inversion
peau d'orange (coarse orange-peel pitting of breast skin from dermal lymphatic invasion)
unilateral spontaneous bloody or serous nipple discharge
hard matted non-tender axillary lymphadenopathy
Paget disease: persistent eczema-like, crusting, scaling lesion of the nipple-areolar complex
pertinent_negatives: distinct from cyclic bilateral tender nodularity of fibrocystic disease
