content: Malignant neoplasm of breast epithelial tissue (Invasive Ductal Carcinoma 80%, Invasive Lobular 10-15%). Triple Assessment (The Gold Standard): 1. Clinical breast examination; 2. Imaging (Bilateral Digital Mammography + High-Resolution Breast Ultrasound; Breast MRI in young/dense breasts); 3. Pathological confirmation via Core Needle Biopsy with ER, PR, HER2-neu, and Ki-67 immunohistochemistry. Treatment: Breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) or modified radical mastectomy + Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB); Adjuvant/neoadjuvant chemotherapy, targeted Trastuzumab (HER2+), and hormonal therapy (Tamoxifen, Anastrozole).

topic: Multiple Myeloma (Plasma Cell Dyscrasia - CRAB Criteria)
red_flags: spinal cord compression from pathological vertebral collapse
acute hyperviscosity syndrome (retinal hemorrhages, stroke, mucosal bleeding)
acute light-chain cast nephropathy / myeloma kidney
clinical_hallmarks: the CRAB diagnostic criteria: 1. Calcium elevation (serum calcium > 11 mg/dL); 2. Renal insufficiency (creatinine > 2 mg/dL); 3. Anemia (normocytic normochromic Hb < 10 g/dL); 4. Bone lesions (lytic 'punched-out' bone lesions or pathological fractures, persistent deep back/rib pain)
erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) markedly elevated (> 100 mm/hr)
recurrent bacterial infections (pneumonia, pyelonephritis from hypogammaglobulinemia)
Rouleaux formation on peripheral blood smear
pertinent_negatives: absence of blastic/sclerotic bone lesions (lytic only)
content: Clonal neoplastic proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow producing excess monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein: IgG 50%, IgA 20%, or free light chains). Diagnostic workup: Serum and Urine Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP/UPEP) showing dense monoclonal M-spike, Serum Free Light Chain (sFLC) ratio, Bone Marrow Biopsy (> 10% clonal plasma cells), Whole-body low-dose CT or skeletal survey. Treatment: Triplet induction therapy (Bortezomib + Lenalidomide + Dexamethasone [VRd]); Autologous Stem Cell Transplantation (ASCT); Bisphosphonates (Zoledronic acid) for bone disease; Dialysis for myeloma kidney.

red_flags: ADDISONIAN CRISIS: severe refractory hypotensive shock unresponsive to vasopressors and fluids
clinical_hallmarks: striking bronze hyperpigmentation of skin in sun-exposed areas and friction zones, accompanied by dark pigmentation of palmar creases, buccal mucosa, and surgical scars (due to high ACTH stimulating melanocytes)
severe persistent orthostatic postural hypotension, salt craving, and chronic fatigue
lab derangements: hyponatremia (low Na+), hyperkalemia (high K+), and non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from aldosterone deficiency
pertinent_negatives: hyperpigmentation is absent in secondary adrenal insufficiency (low ACTH)
content: Destruction of all layers of the adrenal cortex, most commonly autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison's) in developed nations or tuberculosis (adrenal TB) in developing countries. Diagnostic workup: Morning 8 AM serum cortisol (< 3 mcg/dL), plasma ACTH (markedly elevated), ACTH stimulation test (Synacthen test: failure of cortisol to rise > 18 mcg/dL). Acute Crisis Management: 1. STAT IV Hydrocortisone (100 mg IV bolus followed by 100 mg q8h); 2. Aggressive IV resuscitation with 0.9% Normal Saline with 5% Dextrose (treats hypotension, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia); 3. Oral Fludrocortisone (0.1 mg daily) added for chronic maintenance.

red_flags: irreversible Korsakoff amnesic confabulatory dementia if thiamine delayed
acute high-output wet beriberi heart failure and shock
clinical_hallmarks: classic Wernicke triad: 1. Encephalopathy (acute confusion, apathy, disorientation); 2. Oculomotor dysfunction (bilateral horizontal nystagmus, lateral rectus / CN VI palsy, conjugate gaze palsy); 3. Gait ataxia (wide-based unsteady gait)
history of chronic alcohol abuse, hyperemesis gravidarum, prolonged fasting, or bariatric surgery
Wet Beriberi: high-output congestive heart failure, bounding pulses, peripheral edema; Dry Beriberi: symmetrical peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy
content: Critical nutritional emergency caused by deficiency of Vitamin B1 (thiamine pyrophosphate), a key coenzyme in cerebral carbohydrate metabolism. Medical imperative: Thiamine MUST ALWAYS be administered BEFORE any intravenous glucose solutions to prevent acute cerebral metabolic collapse. Protocol: High-dose IV Thiamine (Pabrinex: 500 mg IV TID for 3-5 days, then 250 mg daily); prompt reversal of ophthalmoplegia within hours confirms diagnosis.

topic: Pernicious Anemia & Subacute Combined Degeneration of Cord
red_flags: irreversible spastic paraparesis and permanent spinal cord ataxia
clinical_hallmarks: triad: 1. Megaloblastic anemia symptoms (fatigue, lemon-yellow pallor, dyspnea); 2. Atrophic glossitis (smooth, painful, beefy-red raw tongue / Hunter glossitis); 3. Neurological dysfunction (Subacute Combined Degeneration: loss of vibration and proprioception / joint position sense, sensory ataxia, positive Romberg sign, spasticity, and extensor plantar responses)
hypersegmented neutrophils (>= 5 lobes in > 5% of PMNs) on peripheral blood smear
pertinent_negatives: folate deficiency DOES NOT cause neurological degeneration (crucial distinction)
content: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells leading to loss of Intrinsic Factor (IF) and inability to absorb Vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum. CRITICAL PEARL: Treating B12 deficiency with folic acid alone corrects anemia while allowing neurological destruction to progress irreversibly. Diagnostic workup: Serum Vitamin B12 (< 200 pg/mL), elevated serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine, Anti-Intrinsic Factor and Anti-Parietal Cell antibodies. Treatment: Intramuscular Cyanocobalamin / Hydroxocobalamin (1000 mcg IM daily for 1 week, then weekly for 1 month, then monthly for life).

keywords: severe eye pain with runny nose
red_flags: severe behavioral agitation, pacing, and suicidal ideation during agonizing attacks
clinical_hallmarks: excruciating, strictly unilateral orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain described as a 'hot poker in the eye', lasting 15-180 minutes

accompanied by ipsilateral cranial parasympathetic autonomic features: conjunctival injection, lacrimation (eye tearing), nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, forehead sweating, and partial Horner syndrome (ptosis/miosis)
striking circadian and circannual periodicity (attacks strike at same hour each night, clustering for weeks followed by remission)
patient is intensely agitated and paces the room (differentiates from migraineur who prefers dark quiet stillness)
pertinent_negatives: absence of nausea and vomiting in typical attacks
content: Severe primary headache disorder classified under Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalgias (TACs), predominantly affecting males. Acute abortive treatment: 100% High-Flow Oxygen (12-15 L/min via non-rebreather mask for 15-20 min - response within 10 min is diagnostic) PLUS subcutaneous Sumatriptan (6 mg). Prophylactic maintenance: Oral Verapamil (high-dose 240-960 mg daily with ECG PR-interval monitoring).

red_flags: injury or fractures sustained from sudden violent fall during positional turn
clinical_hallmarks: brief, violent, episodic rotational vertigo (room spinning) lasting LESS THAN 60 SECONDS
triggered strictly by changes in head position relative to gravity: turning over in bed, looking up at ceiling, or bending forward
Dix-Hallpike positional maneuver reproduces the vertigo AND elicits pathognomonic torsional geotropic nystagmus with latency (2-5s) and fatigability
complete absence of hearing loss, tinnitus, or neurological focal deficits
pertinent_negatives: no hearing loss or ear fullness (differentiates from Meniere disease)
content: Most common cause of peripheral vertigo, caused by free-floating calcium carbonate otoconia (canalithiasis) dislodged from the utricle into the posterior semicircular canal. Definitive bedside treatment: Particle repositioning maneuvers (Epley Maneuver for posterior canal; Semont maneuver) achieves > 85-90% instant cure without medications.

red_flags: Tumarkin drop attacks (sudden catastrophic fall without loss of consciousness from otolithic crisis)
clinical_hallmarks: classic clinical tetrad: 1. Spontaneous recurrent episodes of rotational vertigo lasting 20 minutes to several hours; 2. Fluctuating low-frequency Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SNHL documented on audiometry); 3. Low-pitched roaring tinnitus in affected ear; 4. Aural fullness (sensation of pressure or plugging in affected ear)
symptoms fluctuate, with hearing deteriorating during attacks and partially improving in early stages
pertinent_negatives: vertigo lasts hours (not seconds like BPPV)
content: Inner ear disorder characterized by excessive accumulation of endolymphatic fluid (endolymphatic hydrops) causing distension and periodic micro-ruptures of the membranous labyrinth. Treatment: Acute attacks: Vestibular suppressants (Betahistine, Dimenhydrinate); Long-term prevention: Low-salt diet (< 1.5-2 g/day), caffeine and alcohol restriction, oral Thiazide diuretics, intratympanic dexamethasone or gentamicin for refractory disease.

topic: Acute Aortic Dissection (Stanford Type A / B)
keywords: ripping chest pain radiating to back
clinical_hallmarks: abrupt onset of excruciating, sharp, 'tearing' or 'ripping' substernal chest pain radiating between shoulder blades into interscapular back
marked blood pressure differential (> 20 mmHg systolic) between left and right arms
new diastolic decrescendo murmur of aortic insufficiency
radio-femoral pulse delay or absent radial/femoral pulses
pertinent_negatives: no st-elevation on ecg typical of transmural myocardial infarction
content: Intimal tear allowing high-pressure arterial blood to cleave aortic media. Stanford Type A involves ascending aorta (surgical emergency); Type B is confined to descending aorta. Diagnosis: Emergent CT Aortogram with contrast (CT Angiography thorax/abdomen) is gold standard; Transesophageal Echocardiogram (TEE) if unstable. Management: Type A requires STAT emergent open surgical repair (graft replacement). Type B: aggressive medical BP and shear stress control with IV beta-blockers (Esmolol / Labetalol targeting systolic BP 100-120 mmHg and HR < 60 bpm) +/- vasodilators (Nitroprusside) and TEVAR for complicated cases.

red_flags: absent pedal pulses with pale cold foot
clinical_hallmarks: intermittent claudication: reproducible cramping, ache, or fatigue in calves/thighs triggered by walking a set distance and relieved within 2-5 minutes of standing still
cool, pale, shiny skin on feet with loss of hair and thick brittle toenails
diminished or absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses with delayed capillary refill (> 3s)
Leriche syndrome triad: bilateral buttock claudication, absent femoral pulses, and erectile dysfunction from aortoiliac occlusion
pertinent_negatives: no venous stasis dermatitis or medial malleolar hyperpigmentation
content: Atherosclerotic narrowing of peripheral arteries causing reduced perfusion to extremities. Diagnosis: Resting Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI <= 0.90 confirms PAD; < 0.4 indicates critical limb ischemia); Arterial Duplex Doppler ultrasound and CT Angiography of lower limbs. Treatment: Supervised exercise walking program, Smoking cessation, high-intensity Statin, antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin 75-100 mg or Clopidogrel 75 mg), Cilostazol (100 mg BID for claudication relief); Endovascular angioplasty/stenting or surgical bypass for lifestyle-limiting or limb-threatening ischemia.

topic: Brugada Syndrome (Sodium Channelopathy - Sudden Cardiac Death)
clinical_hallmarks: coved-type ST segment elevation (>= 2 mm / 0.2 mV) followed by a negative T wave in >= 1 right precordial leads (V1-V2) positioned in 2nd, 3rd, or 4th intercostal spaces (Type 1 Brugada pattern)
episodes of unexplained syncope or nocturnal agonal gasping in young, otherwise structurally healthy individuals
family history of sudden unexplained nocturnal death in young relatives (< 45 years)
pertinent_negatives: no structural heart disease on echocardiogram
content: Autosomal dominant cardiac channelopathy (most commonly loss-of-function SCN5A mutation encoding Nav1.5 cardiac sodium channel) predisposing to malignant ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death during sleep or fever. ECG diagnosis: Type 1 coved ST-segment elevation in V1-V2 (spontaneous or unmasked by fever or sodium channel blockers like Ajmaline/Flecainide). Management: Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator (ICD) is the only proven preventive therapy for high-risk patients. Strict avoidance of Brugada-triggering drugs (BrugadaDrugs.org), prompt antipyretic treatment of fever, Quinidine for electrical storms.

clinical_hallmarks: sudden abrupt onset and termination of rapid, regular, intense palpitation ('flip-flop' switch sensation in chest)
heart rate typically 150-250 bpm with regular rhythm
narrow QRS complex (< 120 ms) with absent or retrograde P waves buried within or immediately after QRS (pseudo-r' in V1)
polyuria following attack due to atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) release
pertinent_negatives: regular rhythm differentiates from atrial fibrillation
narrow QRS differentiates from ventricular tachycardia
content: Re-entrant supraventricular tachyarrhythmia, most commonly AV Nodal Re-entrant Tachycardia (AVNRT 60%) involving dual AV nodal pathways (slow and fast), or AV Reciprocating Tachycardia (AVRT 30% via accessory pathway). Acute management: 1. Hemodynamically unstable: Synchronized DC cardioversion (50-100 J); 2. Hemodynamically stable: Vagal maneuvers (Modified Valsalva maneuver with leg elevation achieves > 40% reversion); if unsuccessful: Rapid IV Adenosine (6 mg rapid IV push followed by 20 mL saline flush; repeat 12 mg if no response); second-line: IV Verapamil or Diltiazem. Long-term definitive cure: Electrophysiology study (EPS) and catheter ablation of slow pathway (> 95% curative).

clinical_hallmarks: regular, rapid wide complex tachycardia (QRS > 120-140 ms, rate 140-250 bpm)
pathognomonic ECG signs: AV dissociation (P waves marching independently through QRS), capture beats, and fusion beats (Dressler beats)
extreme axis deviation ('northwest axis'), concordance of QRS polarity across all precordial leads V1-V6
Torsades de Pointes: polymorphic VT with twisting of QRS peaks around the isoelectric line in patients with prolonged QT interval
pertinent_negatives: absence of typical bundle branch block morphology favors VT over SVT with aberrancy
content: Potentially lethal ventricular tachyarrhythmia originating distal to the bundle of His, most frequently secondary to prior myocardial infarction scar, cardiomyopathy, channelopathy, or QT prolongation. Protocol: 1. Pulseless VT: Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation (200 J biphasic) + ACLS; 2. Unstable with pulse: Immediate synchronized cardioversion (100 J); 3. Stable monomorphic VT: IV Amiodarone (150 mg IV over 10 min, then 1 mg/min for 6 hours) or IV Procainamide; 4. Torsades de Pointes: IV Magnesium Sulfate (2 g IV bolus), correct hypokalemia, overdrive pacing/Isoproterenol. Long-term: ICD implantation and antiarrhythmic therapy.

clinical_hallmarks: classic Beck's triad: 1. Hypotension with narrowed pulse pressure; 2. Jugular venous distension (elevated JVP with prominent x descent and absent y descent); 3. Muffled, distant heart sounds
pulsus paradoxus: an abnormally large drop in systolic blood pressure (> 10 mmHg) during inspiration
ECG shows low-voltage QRS complexes and electrical alternans (beat-to-beat alternation of QRS amplitude due to heart swinging within fluid)
bedside ultrasound/echo: large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse and dilated IVC without respiratory collapse
pertinent_negatives: no lung crackles/edema (distinguishes from cardiogenic shock caused by LV failure)
content: Life-threatening mechanical compression of the heart chambers caused by rapid accumulation of pericardial fluid, impairing diastolic filling and reducing stroke volume. Diagnostic workup: Bedside focused cardiac ultrasound (POCUS) confirms pericardial effusion and chamber collapse. Treatment: Immediate emergency Pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid needle decompression with catheter drainage) or emergent surgical subxiphoid pericardial window. Aggressive volume loading with IV normal saline bolus as temporary temporizing measure to augment preload.

clinical_hallmarks: acute onset ischemic chest pain, dyspnea, and syncope immediately preceded by profound emotional distress (grief, divorce, panic) or severe physical trauma/surgery
ECG mimicking acute STEMI: anterior ST-segment elevation, subsequent deep symmetrical T-wave inversions, and prolonged QT interval
echocardiogram reveals pathognomonic apical ballooning with hypercontractile basal segments and akinesia of the mid and apical left ventricle
absence of obstructive coronary artery disease on urgent coronary angiography
pertinent_negatives: angiography shows clear coronary arteries with no plaque rupture or acute thrombus
content: Transient systolic dysfunction of apical and mid-ventricular myocardial segments mimicking acute myocardial infarction, triggered by massive catecholamine surge and microvascular spasm. Predominantly affects postmenopausal women (> 90%). Diagnosis: Mayo Clinic Criteria (transient LV hypokinesis, absence of angiographic obstructive CAD, new ECG changes, modest troponin rise disproportionately low for extent of wall motion abnormality). Management: Supportive hemodynamics, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors; avoid inotropes if LVOT obstruction is present. Prognosis is generally excellent with recovery of LV function within 4-8 weeks.

red_flags: massive pulmonary hemorrhage from bronchial vein rupture (apoplexy)
acute thromboembolic stroke from left atrial thrombus
clinical_hallmarks: opening snap (OS) followed by a low-pitched, rumbling mid-diastolic murmur with presystolic accentuation, best heard at apex in left lateral decubitus position with the bell of stethoscope
loud first heart sound (S1)
malar flush (pinkish-purple plum discoloration over malar prominences from cutaneous vasoconstriction and cyanosis)
exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, nocturnal cough, and pink frothy hemoptysis
frequently complicated by new-onset irregular pulse of Atrial Fibrillation
pertinent_negatives: no systolic ejection murmur or carotid thrill typical of aortic stenosis
content: Progressive mechanical narrowing of the mitral valve orifice, overwhelmingly caused by post-streptococcal Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) resulting in commissural fusion and calcification. Diagnostic workup: Transthoracic and Transesophageal Echocardiography with Wilkins score (valve area < 1.5 cm2 indicates clinically significant stenosis; < 1.0 cm2 severe). Management: Rate control (Beta-blockers, Digoxin) to prolong diastolic filling time; Anticoagulation (Warfarin, INR 2-3) MANDATORY if atrial fibrillation or prior embolic event; Percutaneous Transvenous Mitral Commissurotomy (PTMC / balloon valvuloplasty) if favorable valve anatomy, or surgical mitral valve replacement.

clinical_hallmarks: classic episodic triphasic digital color changes triggered by cold exposure or emotional stress: 1. Pallor / white (severe arteriolar vasospasm and ischemia); 2. Cyanosis / blue (tissue hypoxia and deoxygenated venous pooling); 3. Rubor / red (reactive hyperemia with throbbing pain and tingling on rewarming)
sharply demarcated blanching of distal digits of hands and feet
primary Raynaud (Raynaud disease): symmetric, adolescent onset, normal nailfold capillaroscopy, negative ANA
secondary Raynaud (Raynaud syndrome): older onset, asymmetric, digital ulcers, abnormal nailfold capillary drop-out, positive ANA (suggests Scleroderma or SLE)
pertinent_negatives: absence of persistent ischemic pain between attacks in primary Raynaud
content: Reversible paroxysmal digital vasospasm of small muscular arteries and arterioles. Diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; Nailfold video-capillaroscopy and autoimmune serology (ANA, Anti-Scl-70, Anti-Centromere) to distinguish primary from secondary Raynaud. Treatment: Lifestyle measures (thermal insulation, hand warmers, avoidance of smoking and sympathomimetics); First-line pharmacotherapy: Dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers (oral Nifedipine 30-60 mg daily or Amlodipine); Topical nitroglycerin; Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (Sildenafil) or IV Iloprost for refractory or ulcerating secondary Raynaud.

topic: Deep Vein Thrombosis & Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens
red_flags: phlegmasia cerulea dolens (massive cyanotic edema with threatened arterial perfusion)
acute shortness of breath indicating pulmonary embolism
clinical_hallmarks: acute, unilateral, painful calf or entire lower extremity swelling (> 3 cm difference in calf circumference measured 10 cm below tibial tuberosity)
erythema, warmth, and localized tenderness along deep venous system distribution
pitting edema restricted to affected extremity
Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens: catastrophic fulminant ileofemoral venous thrombosis presenting with massive taut edema, profound violaceous cyanosis, agonizing pain, and impending venous gangrene
pertinent_negatives: absence of bilateral symmetric ankle edema typical of congestive heart failure
content: Thrombus formation in deep veins of lower extremity (popliteal, femoral, iliac), governed by Virchow's triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability). Clinical stratification via Wells Score for DVT. Diagnostic workup: High-sensitivity D-Dimer (rules out DVT if low risk); Compression Duplex Venous Ultrasonography (loss of vein compressibility confirms DVT). Treatment: Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs: Apixaban, Rivaroxaban) or LMWH bridged to Warfarin for minimum 3-6 months; Emergent catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical thrombectomy for Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens.

topic: Chronic Venous Insufficiency & Venous Stasis Ulcer
clinical_hallmarks: chronic bilateral lower extremity heaviness, dull ache, and dependent edema worsening at end of day and relieved by elevation
dilated, tortuous superficial varicose veins in saphenous distribution

cutaneous changes: hemosiderin hyperpigmentation (brownish discoloration of lower third of leg), stasis dermatitis (erythematous pruritic scale), and 'champagne bottle' leg (lipodermatosclerosis with wooden induration)
Venous stasis ulcer: large, shallow, irregular-bordered, exudative ulcer located OVER THE MEDIAL MALLEOLUS with granulating base
pertinent_negatives: punched-out, deep, painful lateral foot ulcer suggests arterial ulcer, not venous
content: Venous hypertension and reflux resulting from incompetent valves in superficial, perforator, or deep leg veins. CEAP classification (C1-C6). Diagnostic workup: Duplex Doppler ultrasound mapping of lower extremity venous reflux (> 0.5 sec reflux in superficial veins). Treatment: Graduated compression stockings (30-40 mmHg) is the cornerstone; Leg elevation; Moist wound dressings; Endovenous thermal ablation (EVLA / RFA) or foam sclerotherapy of incompetent saphenous trunks.

red_flags: left ventricular apical mural thrombus with stroke
clinical_hallmarks: progressive exertional dyspnea, orthopnea (pillow elevation needed to sleep), and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)
laterally and inferiorly displaced diffuse apex beat (hyperdynamic or sustained PMI)
pathognomonic S3 ventricular filling gallop ('Kentucky' cadence)
bilateral basal lung crackles, elevated JVP with hepatojugular reflux, and bilateral dependent pitting pedal edema
echocardiogram reveals four-chamber cardiac enlargement with severe diffuse left ventricular systolic hypokinesis (LVEF < 40%)
pertinent_negatives: no significant coronary artery stenosis on angiography (non-ischemic etiology)
content: Myocardial disorder characterized by left ventricular or biventricular enlargement and impaired systolic contractile function not explained by abnormal loading conditions or CAD. Etiologies: genetic (titin/TTN), viral myocarditis, alcohol, peripartum, chemotherapy (doxorubicin). Diagnostic workup: Echocardiography, cardiac MRI (late gadolinium enhancement for fibrosis), BNP/NT-proBNP. Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT - The 4 Pillars): 1. ARNI (Sacubitril-Valsartan) or ACEi; 2. Evidence-based Beta-blocker (Carvedilol, Bisoprolol, Metoprolol succinate); 3. Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonist (Spironolactone); 4. SGLT2 inhibitor (Dapagliflozin/Empagliflozin); Loop diuretics for congestion; Primary prevention ICD.

red_flags: family history of premature sudden cardiac death
clinical_hallmarks: harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at left sternal border that INTENSIFIES WITH VALSALVA MANEUVER and standing (decreased preload), and SOFTENS WITH SQUATTING or handgrip (increased preload/afterload)
bifid carotid pulse (pulsus bisferiens) and prominent 'a' wave in jugular venous pulse

echocardiogram demonstrates asymmetric septal hypertrophy (interventricular septum to posterior wall ratio > 1.3-1.5) and Systolic Anterior Motion (SAM) of the anterior mitral leaflet producing dynamic LVOT gradient
pertinent_negatives: murmur differs from aortic stenosis which softens with Valsalva and radiates to carotids
content: Autosomal dominant genetic cardiac disease caused by sarcomeric protein mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3) causing marked, unexplained myocardial hypertrophy and myofibrillar disarray. Leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young competitive athletes. Treatment: First-line medical: Non-vasodilating Beta-blockers (Metoprolol, Atenolol) or non-dihydropyridine CCBs (Verapamil) to prolong diastole and decrease gradient; Novel cardiac myosin inhibitor (Mavacamten); Surgical septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation for drug-refractory gradients >= 50 mmHg; ICD for high-risk sudden death prevention.

clinical_hallmarks: profound, fixed bradycardia (typically heart rate 25-45 bpm) refractory to atropine
intermittent pathognomonic 'cannon a waves' in the jugular venous pulse occurring when atrium contracts against closed tricuspid valve
varying intensity of the first heart sound (S1) and fluctuating systolic blood pressure

ECG shows complete AV dissociation: regular P waves marching at one rate, and independent regular wide or narrow QRS complexes marching at a much slower escape rate with NO relationship between P waves and QRS
pertinent_negatives: no constant PR interval (distinguishes from first or second degree block)
content: Complete electrical disruption of impulse conduction from atria to ventricles, caused by degenerative conduction disease (Lenegre-Lev disease), acute inferior or anterior MI, hyperkalemia, or drug toxicity (Digoxin, Beta-blockers). Acute emergency management: STAT transcutaneous pacing pads applied; IV Atropine (0.5 mg - 1 mg; often ineffective in infra-nodal block); IV Isoproterenol or Dopamine infusion; Emergency temporary transvenous pacemaker insertion. Definitive long-term treatment: Permanent dual-chamber (DDD) pacemaker implantation.

specialty: Emergency Medicine / Trauma Surgery / Critical Care
red_flags: tracheal deviation away from affected side
clinical_hallmarks: sudden onset severe sharp unilateral pleuritic chest pain and rapidly worsening dyspnea in setting of trauma or positive pressure mechanical ventilation
hyperresonance to percussion and total absence of vesicular breath sounds over affected hemithorax
tracheal deviation to the CONTRALATERAL (opposite) side
distended jugular neck veins, tachycardia, severe hypotension, and cyanosis caused by vena caval compression
pertinent_negatives: CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS: DO NOT DELAY LIFE-SAVING TREATMENT TO OBTAIN CHEST RADIOGRAPH
content: One-way valve mechanism allowing air into the pleural space during inspiration without escape during expiration, producing progressive intrapleural pressure rise, lung collapse, mediastinal shift, and inferior vena cava compression leading to fatal obstructive shock. Immediate Life-Saving Action: Emergency Needle Decompression (14-16G large-bore cannula inserted into 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line, or 5th intercostal space anterior-axillary line) STAT, instantly converting tension into open pneumothorax. Follow immediately by definitive tube thoracostomy (Chest Tube / Intercostal Drain in 5th intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line connected to underwater seal).

topic: Farmer's Lung & Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis)
clinical_hallmarks: acute form: abrupt onset of fever, chills, malaise, dry cough, and dyspnea developing 4-8 hours following intense exposure to organic antigens (moldy hay [thermophilic actinomycetes], bird droppings [avian antigens])
symptoms resolve spontaneously over 24-48 hours upon removal from exposure, but recur upon re-exposure
chest auscultation reveals diffuse fine bibasilar inspiratory crackles and mid-inspiratory squeaks
HRCT thorax: diffuse centrilobular ground-glass opacities, mosaic attenuation, and pathognomonic 'headcheese sign' (combination of ground-glass, normal lung, and air trapping on expiratory CT)
pertinent_negatives: no wheezing or eosinophilia (differentiates from IgE-mediated asthma)
content: Immunologically mediated lung disease caused by repetitive inhalation of specific organic aeroantigens in sensitized individuals, involving Type III (immune-complex) and Type IV (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity. Diagnostic workup: Antigen exposure history, serum precipitating IgG antibodies, HRCT, Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) showing marked lymphocytosis (often > 50% with low CD4/CD8 ratio). Treatment: Complete and strict antigen avoidance is paramount and often curative in early stages; Oral Corticosteroids (Prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day tapered over 4-8 weeks) for severe acute/subacute disease to accelerate symptom and physiologic recovery.

red_flags: lung abscess formation with putrid sputum
clinical_hallmarks: acute cough, fever, dyspnea, and hypoxemia in a patient with impaired consciousness (alcohol intoxication, stroke, seizures, general anesthesia) or chronic neurogenic dysphagia

chest radiography: focal infiltrates located classically in the dependent bronchopulmonary segments (superior segment of lower lobes or posterior segment of upper lobes in recumbent patients; right lower lobe basilar segments in upright patients)
putrid, foul-smelling sputum strongly indicates secondary anaerobic bacterial pulmonary gangrene or abscess
Mendelson syndrome: acute chemical pneumonitis from massive acidic gastric juice aspiration producing abrupt bronchospasm, cyanosis, and pulmonary edema within 2-4 hours
pertinent_negatives: no anterior upper lobe predominance (atypical for simple gravity-dependent aspiration)
content: Pulmonary consequence resulting from inhalation of colonized oropharyngeal secretions (aspiration pneumonia) or sterile acidic gastric contents (chemical pneumonitis / Mendelson syndrome). Polymicrobial etiology including oral streptococci and anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, Prevotella). Treatment: Chemical pneumonitis: supportive oxygen and suctioning (prophylactic antibiotics NOT indicated immediately); Aspiration pneumonia: IV Ampicillin-Sulbactam (1.5-3g q6h) or Amoxicillin-Clavulanate, or Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole (or Clindamycin); Swallowing assessment and speech therapy.

topic: Legionnaires' Disease (Legionella Pneumophila - Severe Atypical Pneumonia)
clinical_hallmarks: history of exposure to aerosolized mist from contaminated water reservoirs: hotel cooling towers, air-conditioning systems, hot tubs, or cruise ships
high remittent fever with relative bradycardia (Faget sign: pulse rate slower than expected for the degree of hyperpyrexia)
striking extrapulmonary manifestations: prominent watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and early neurological confusion or encephalopathy out of proportion to fever
characteristic laboratory abnormalities: profound hyponatremia (serum Na+ < 130 mEq/L from SIADH), elevated transaminases, microhematuria, and marked hypophosphatemia
pertinent_negatives: sputum Gram stain reveals numerous neutrophils but NO predominant bacterial organisms (poorly staining intracellular bacillus)
content: Severe form of atypical pneumonia caused by Legionella pneumophila, an intracellular Gram-negative flagellated bacterium. Diagnostic workup: Urine Legionella Antigen test (rapid, detects serogroup 1 with > 95% specificity), sputum Legionella PCR or BCYE agar culture, CBC, electrolytes. Treatment: First-line pharmacotherapy: Fluoroquinolones (IV/oral Levofloxacin 750 mg daily) or Macrolides (IV/oral Azithromycin 500 mg daily) for 7-14 days (21 days in immunocompromised patients). Beta-lactam antibiotics are completely ineffective.

topic: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency & Early-Onset Panacinar Emphysema
clinical_hallmarks: early-onset chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD / emphysema) presenting in young patients (< 40-45 years) or in non-smokers or minimal smokers
progressive exertional dyspnea, wheezing, and hyperinflated barrel chest

chest radiograph and HRCT thorax demonstrate severe panacinar (panlobular) emphysematous destruction with marked PREDILECTION FOR LOWER LUNG BASES (in contrast to upper-lobe centrilobular emphysema of cigarette smoking)
concomitant unexplained chronic liver disease, neonatal cholestasis, or cryptogenic cirrhosis
pertinent_negatives: absence of heavy smoking history or advanced age typical of standard copd
content: Autosomal co-dominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene, resulting in deficiency of the protease inhibitor Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT). Uninhibited neutrophil elastase degrades alveolar elastin, destroying alveolar architecture. Phenotypes: PiMM (normal), PiMZ (carrier), PiZZ (severe deficiency). Diagnostic workup: Serum AAT quantitative level (< 11 mcmol/L or < 57 mg/dL confirms deficiency), SERPINA1 genotype/phenotype testing. Treatment: Standard COPD bronchodilators, smoking cessation (smoking drastically accelerates lung destruction); Weekly IV augmentation therapy with human pooled Alpha-1 Proteinase Inhibitor for patients with FEV1 35-65%.

clinical_hallmarks: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA): poorly controlled, steroid-dependent severe asthma or cystic fibrosis with recurrent episodic wheezing, fever, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, and expectoration of brownish mucus plugs
marked peripheral blood eosinophilia (> 500-1000 cells/mcL) and massively elevated total serum IgE (typically > 1000 IU/mL)

Aspergilloma (Fungus Ball): preexisting tuberculosis or sarcoid cavity colonized by Aspergillus fumigatus, presenting with recurrent hemoptysis and pathognomonic chest radiograph/CT showing a mobile, rounded intracavitary mass surrounded by a crescent of air ('Monod sign' or 'Air-crescent sign')
pertinent_negatives: no invasive tissue necrosis in immunocompetent host
content: Hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus colonization (ABPA) or saprophytic growth within pre-existing pulmonary cavities (Aspergilloma). Diagnostic workup: Total serum IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG, serum galactomannan, HRCT thorax (central bronchiectasis). Treatment: ABPA: Oral Systemic Corticosteroids (Prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day tapered over 3-6 months) + Oral Itraconazole (200 mg BID for 16 weeks); Aspergilloma: Surgical cavity resection (lobectomy) for recurrent severe hemoptysis, or bronchial artery embolization.

topic: Boerhaave Syndrome (Spontaneous Esophageal Perforation - Mackler Triad)
keywords: vomiting followed by severe chest pain
clinical_hallmarks: classic Mackler triad: 1. Repeated violent vomiting / retching; 2. Sudden, catastrophic, excruciating retrosternal or epigastric tearing pain; 3. Cervical or thoracic subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus on palpation of neck)
Hamman sign: crunching, rasping sound synchronous with the heartbeat heard on precordial auscultation due to mediastinal emphysema
left-sided pleural effusion (frequently showing low pH < 6.0 and high salivary amylase on thoracentesis)
chest CT with oral contrast: pneumomediastinum, extravasation of water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) from distal esophagus
pertinent_negatives: Mackler triad distinguishes Boerhaave from simple myocardial infarction or Mallory-Weiss tear
content: Spontaneous full-thickness transmural rupture of the esophagus, most frequently occurring in the left posterolateral wall of the distal intrathoracic esophagus, caused by a sudden massive increase in intraluminal pressure against a closed glottis during violent retching. Statutory surgical emergency with mortality approaching 50% if treatment delayed > 24 hours. Diagnosis: Water-soluble Gastrografin swallow or Contrast CT chest. Protocol: NPO, STAT IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, ICU resuscitation; Emergent open thoracotomy or VATS with primary esophageal repair and mediastinal debridement/drainage within 24 hours.

red_flags: acute fulminant hepatic failure with coombs-negative hemolytic anemia
clinical_hallmarks: bimodal presentation: hepatic disease in children/adolescents (unexplained acute hepatitis, cirrhosis) vs neuropsychiatric manifestations in young adults (tremor, dystonia, parkinsonism, dysarthria, behavioral changes)

pathognomonic Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings: golden-brown or greenish copper pigmentation in the Descemet membrane of the corneal limbus on slit-lamp examination (present in > 95% with neurological symptoms)
'wing-beating' coarse postural tremor of upper limbs

laboratory tetrad: 1. Low serum ceruloplasmin (< 20 mg/dL); 2. Markedly elevated 24-hour urinary copper excretion (> 100 mcg/day); 3. High free serum copper; 4. Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with acute liver failure
pertinent_negatives: negative autoimmune markers and viral hepatitis serologies
content: Autosomal recessive inborn error of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13, impairing biliary copper excretion and incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin, causing toxic accumulation in liver, basal ganglia, and cornea. Diagnostic workup: Slit-lamp examination, serum ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, liver biopsy for quantitative dry-weight copper. Treatment: Copper chelating agents: D-Penicillamine or Trientine hydrochloride (taken away from meals); Oral Zinc acetate (blocks intestinal copper absorption via metallothionein induction) for maintenance; Liver transplantation is curative for fulminant liver failure.

clinical_hallmarks: the classic triad (advanced disease): 1. Bronze cutaneous hyperpigmentation ('slate-grey' or bronze metallic skin); 2. Diabetes mellitus ('bronze diabetes' due to pancreatic islet iron deposition); 3. Cirrhosis / hepatomegaly
severe chronic fatigue, loss of libido, and erectile dysfunction (due to pituitary iron accumulation causing secondary hypogonadotropic hypogonadism)
arthropathy characteristically targeting 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints with chondrocalcinosis (pseudogout)
laboratory hallmarks: Transferrin Saturation > 45-50% (earliest and most sensitive screening test) and Markedly elevated serum Ferritin (> 1000 ng/mL indicates risk of cirrhosis)
pertinent_negatives: absence of secondary iron overload (no multiple blood transfusions)
content: Autosomal recessive iron overload disorder caused by mutations in the HFE gene (most commonly homozygous C282Y or compound heterozygous C282Y/H63D) causing inappropriately low hepcidin production and unregulated excessive intestinal iron absorption. Diagnostic workup: Fasting transferrin saturation, serum ferritin, HFE gene mutation analysis, Liver MRI (T2* sequence for quantitative iron quantification). Treatment: Therapeutic Phlebotomy (removal of 500 mL blood weekly or biweekly until serum ferritin reaches 50-100 ng/mL); Iron-chelation therapy (Deferasirox) if phlebotomy contraindicated; Dietary iron restriction.

clinical_hallmarks: multiple, recurrent, severe, refractory peptic ulcers occurring in unusual locations (distal duodenum or jejunum)
ulcers recur immediately despite high-dose PPI or H2-blocker therapy or after surgical ulcer repair
chronic watery, secretory diarrhea that improves with high-dose acid suppression (diarrhea caused by massive acid volume overloading intestine and inactivating pancreatic lipase)
25% of cases occur as part of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN-1: Parathyroid, Pancreas/Gastrinoma, Pituitary)
laboratory hallmark: Fasting serum gastrin markedly elevated (> 1000 pg/mL in presence of gastric pH < 2.0)
pertinent_negatives: absence of h. pylori infection and negative nsaid use
content: Gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma), typically located within the 'gastrinoma triangle' (confluence of cystic/common bile ducts, 2nd/3rd duodenum, and neck/body of pancreas), driving autonomous hypersecretion of gastric hydrochloric acid. Diagnostic workup: Fasting serum gastrin, gastric pH, Secretin stimulation test (paradoxical rise in gastrin > 120 pg/mL confirms gastrinoma), Somatostatin Receptor Scintigraphy (68Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT). Treatment: High-dose oral PPIs (Omeprazole 60-120 mg daily) to control acid secretion; Surgical exploratory laparotomy and oncological enucleation/resection of gastrinoma.

clinical_hallmarks: constant, severe, aching pain localized to the LEFT LOWER QUADRANT (LLQ) of the abdomen (the 'left-sided appendicitis')
fever, localized tenderness, muscular guarding, and sometimes a tender palpable inflammatory mass in left iliac fossa
nausea, anorexia, constipation (50%) or diarrhea (30%), and dysuria/frequency if inflamed sigmoid abuts the bladder
Contrast-enhanced CT of abdomen/pelvis (gold standard): colonic diverticula with sigmoid wall thickening (> 4 mm), pericolic fat stranding, and absence or presence of extraluminal air/abscess
pertinent_negatives: COLONOSCOPY IS STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in acute episode due to high risk of bowel perforation
content: Micro- or macro-perforation of a colonic diverticulum (most commonly sigmoid colon) leading to localized inflammation, pericolic abscess, or generalized peritonitis. Classified by modified Hinchey criteria (Stage I pericolic abscess to Stage IV feculent peritonitis). Diagnostic test of choice: Contrast CT abdomen/pelvis. Management: Uncomplicated: bowel rest, oral/IV antibiotics covering Gram-negatives and anaerobes (Ciprofloxacin + Metronidazole or Amoxicillin-Clavulanate); Complicated: CT-guided percutaneous drainage for abscess > 3-4 cm (Hinchey II); Emergent Hartmann's procedure or primary resection with anastomosis for generalized peritonitis (Hinchey III/IV); Elective colonoscopy recommended 6-8 weeks after recovery to exclude malignancy.

topic: Anal Fissure (Acute vs Chronic - Sphincter Hypertonicity)
specialty: General Surgery / Colorectal Surgery / Primary Care
red_flags: off-midline lateral fissure (raises suspicion of Crohn's, TB, HIV, or anal carcinoma)
clinical_hallmarks: excruciating, sharp, tearing, burning anal pain during defecation, described as 'passing shards of broken glass'
pain persists as an intense, throbbing spasm for several minutes to hours after defecation due to internal anal sphincter hypertonicity
scant, bright red blood on toilet paper or streaking the outside of hard stool
physical examination (gentle parting of buttocks): visible longitudinal tear located in the POSTERIOR MIDLINE (> 90%) or anterior midline (10%)
chronic fissure triad: visible fissure base showing circular internal sphincter fibers, an external 'sentinel' skin tag at anal verge, and an enlarged hypertrophied anal papilla at proximal apex
pertinent_negatives: DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION (DRE) SHOULD NOT BE FORCED acutely due to intolerable sphincter spasm
content: Longitudinal tear in the anoderm distal to the dentate line, overwhelmingly caused by trauma from passage of hard, dry stool combined with localized microvascular ischemia from internal anal sphincter hypertonicity. Treatment: 1. Conservative (high-fiber diet, stool softeners, warm sitz baths); 2. Chemical Sphincterotomy (first-line medical): Topical 0.2-0.4% Glyceryl Trinitrate (GTN) ointment or topical 2% Diltiazem cream applied BID for 6-8 weeks (promotes healing in 60-70%); 3. Botulinum toxin injection into internal sphincter; 4. Lateral Internal Sphincterotomy (LIS surgery - gold standard cure > 95% for refractory chronic fissures).

red_flags: high transsphincteric / suprasphincteric fistula (risk of fecal incontinence with surgery)
multiple complex fistulae indicating Crohn's disease
clinical_hallmarks: persistent or intermittent, malodorous, purulent, serosanguinous discharge from an external opening on the perineal skin around the anus
history of previous acute perianal abscess that was either surgically drained or ruptured spontaneously
perianal pruritus, excoriation, and recurrent painful swelling that is temporarily relieved when pus bursts and drains

Goodsall's Rule: fistulae with external openings POSTERIOR to the transverse anal line follow a curved path to the posterior midline crypt; anterior openings <= 3 cm from verge follow a straight radial tract to the nearest crypt
palpable fibrous, cord-like tract extending from external skin opening toward anal canal
pertinent_negatives: no deep rectal mass or pelvic bone erosion on MRI
content: Hollow, chronic, epithelialized fibrous tract connecting an internal opening in the anal canal (arising from infected anal cryptoglandular glands) to an external opening on the perianal skin. Park's classification (intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric). Diagnostic gold standard: Pelvic MRI with endoanal coil for complex or recurrent fistulae. Treatment: Low intersphincteric/subcutaneous fistulae: Fistulotomy (laying open the tract); High or complex fistulae involving significant sphincter muscle: Loose Seton placement, LIFT procedure (Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract), mucosal advancement flap, or VAAFT to preserve fecal continence.

red_flags: severe dehydration and electrolyte derangements (hypokalemic alkalosis)
clinical_hallmarks: persistent postprandial fullness, early satiety (inability to finish normal-sized meal), nausea, and bloating
vomiting of recognizable, undigested food consumed many hours or even days earlier
history of long-standing diabetes mellitus with microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, peripheral neuropathy) or prior vagotomy/gastric surgery
unexplained erratic, brittle blood glucose fluctuations with frequent unpredictable postprandial hypoglycemia (insulin peaks before food is emptied and absorbed from stomach)
succussion splash audible over epigastrium > 3-4 hours after food intake
pertinent_negatives: upper endoscopy reveals NO mechanical gastric outlet obstruction or peptic stenosis
content: Symptomatic delayed gastric emptying of solid food in the absence of mechanical gastric outlet obstruction, caused by autonomic neuropathy, loss of interstitial cells of Cajal, or enteric neural nitric oxide synthase deficiency. Diagnostic gold standard: 4-Hour Solid-Phase Gastric Emptying Scintigraphy (retention of > 10% of radiolabeled meal at 4 hours is diagnostic). Treatment: Dietary modification (small, frequent, low-fat, low-insoluble-fiber meals); Optimization of glycemic control; Prokinetic pharmacotherapy: Oral Metoclopramide (10 mg 30 min before meals - limited to 12 weeks due to tardive dyskinesia risk) or oral Erythromycin (motilin receptor agonist) or Domperidone; Gastric electrical stimulation (Enterra) for refractory cases.

red_flags: anuric acute renal failure needing dialysis
clinical_hallmarks: classic pulmonary-renal presentation: acute onset of hemoptysis (coughing fresh blood), dyspnea, and bilateral alveolar infiltrates combined with rapidly progressive acute glomerulonephritis (macroscopic hematuria, oliguria, rapid serum creatinine rise)
frequently triggered by respiratory infections or hydrocarbon/cigarette smoke exposure in HLA-DRB1*1501 positive individuals
laboratory hallmark: circulating high-titer Anti-GBM (anti-alpha-3 chain of Type IV collagen) antibodies in serum

renal biopsy (pathognomonic): light microscopy shows extensive cellular crescent formation (> 50% crescents); Direct Immunofluorescence reveals continuous, linear ribbon-like deposition of IgG and C3 along glomerular capillary basement membranes
pertinent_negatives: negative ANCA (distinguishes from GPA or MPA, though double-positive variants exist)
content: Life-threatening autoimmune small vessel vasculitis caused by circulating pathogenic antibodies directed against the non-collagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen present in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. Urgent Medical Protocol: 1. STAT Daily Plasmapheresis (Plasma Exchange: 4 L exchanges daily for 14 days) to rapidly clear pathogenic circulating anti-GBM antibodies; 2. High-dose pulse IV Methylprednisolone (1 g IV daily for 3 days) followed by oral Prednisone (1 mg/kg/day); 3. Oral or IV Cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg/day for 2-3 months) to halt autoantibody synthesis.

red_flags: acute pulmonary edema from fluid overload
clinical_hallmarks: classic nephritic syndrome triad: 1. Macroscopic hematuria (dark, tea-colored, cola-colored, or smoky urine with dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts); 2. Hypertension; 3. Oliguria with periorbital morning facial puffiness and mild dependent edema

latent period: typically develops 1-2 weeks following streptococcal pharyngitis, or 3-6 weeks following streptococcal pyoderma / impetigo (caused by nephritogenic Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus strains)
laboratory hallmarks: Markedly depressed serum Complement C3 level (normalizes within 6-8 weeks) with normal C4, accompanied by elevated Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer or anti-DNase B titer
renal biopsy (if performed): diffuse endocapillary proliferative glomerulonephritis with pathognomonic large subepithelial electron-dense 'humps' on electron microscopy
pertinent_negatives: no persistent low C3 beyond 8 weeks (persistent low C3 indicates MPGN or lupus nephritis)
content: Immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis triggered by nephritogenic streptococcal antigens (SpeB, NAPlr) that deposit in glomeruli and activate the alternative complement pathway. Overwhelmingly favorable prognosis in children (> 95% complete spontaneous recovery). Treatment: Supportive care is key: Strict fluid restriction, sodium-restricted diet, Loop diuretics (IV Furosemide) for volume overload and hypertension, Calcium Channel Blockers (Amlodipine) for severe hypertension; Course of oral Penicillin or Amoxicillin to eradicate residual streptococcal colonization.

topic: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD & Berry Aneurysms)
red_flags: ruptured cerebral berry aneurysm (sudden thunderclap headache)
clinical_hallmarks: strong family history of autosomal dominant kidney disease (PKD1 on chromosome 16 in 85%, PKD2 on chromosome 4 in 15%)
bilateral palpable, huge, nodular, non-tender flank or abdominal masses
early, refractory hypertension developing in young adults (often preceding renal decline)
dull, chronic flank or low back pain punctuated by acute bouts of sharp pain from cyst hemorrhage, cyst infection, or nephrolithiasis
extrarenal manifestations: hepatic cysts (in > 80% by age 30), intracranial saccular 'berry' aneurysms in Circle of Willis (10-15%), mitral valve prolapse (25%), and colonic diverticulosis
pertinent_negatives: absence of medullary cysts alone on ultrasound
content: Progressive systemic genetic disorder characterized by the development and relentless expansion of multiple fluid-filled bilateral renal cysts, resulting in massive kidney enlargement, parenchymal destruction, and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) typically by the 5th or 6th decade. Diagnostic gold standard: Renal ultrasound (Ravine unified criteria based on age and bilateral cyst count). Treatment: Rigorous BP control (target < 110-120/75-80 mmHg with ACE inhibitors or ARBs); High water intake (> 3 L/day) to suppress endogenous vasopressin; Vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist (Tolvaptan) slows cyst growth and eGFR decline in rapidly progressing ADPKD; Hemodialysis/Peritoneal dialysis and Renal Transplantation for ESRD.

topic: Renal Cell Carcinoma (Clear Cell & Classical Triad)
red_flags: inferior vena cava (ivc) tumor thrombus extension into right atrium
clinical_hallmarks: classic clinical triad (present simultaneously in < 10% of cases, usually late stage): 1. Gross macroscopic painless hematuria; 2. Dull, aching flank pain; 3. Palpable abdominal/flank mass
new-onset, non-reducing LEFT VARICOCELE (does not collapse when patient lies supine) caused by left renal vein occlusion by tumor thrombus blocking left testicular vein drainage
paraneoplastic syndromes: polycythemia (excess erythropoietin secretion), hypercalcemia (PTHrP production), hypertension (renin), or Stauffer syndrome (reversible non-metastatic hepatic dysfunction)
most common subtype: Clear Cell RCC (75-80%), strongly linked to VHL gene inactivation on chromosome 3p
pertinent_negatives: no fever or pyuria (distinguishes from acute pyelonephritis or renal abscess)
content: Malignant neoplasm arising from renal tubular epithelial cells, predominantly clear cell histopathology. Over 60% are now discovered incidentally on abdominal imaging for unrelated reasons ('incidentaloma'). Diagnostic workup: Triphasic Contrast CT of abdomen and pelvis with nephrographic and excretory phases (solid, enhancing renal cortical mass with necrotic/cystic areas); Chest CT for pulmonary metastasis staging. Treatment: Localized disease (Stage I-III): Surgical resection (Radical or Partial Nephrectomy / nephron-sparing surgery); Advanced/Metastatic disease: Dual immunotherapy (Nivolumab + Ipilimumab) or VEGF-tyrosine kinase inhibitor combination (Pembrolizumab + Axitinib / Cabozantinib); RCC is notoriously resistant to conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

topic: Testicular Torsion (Spermatic Cord Twisting & Bell-Clapper Deformity)
red_flags: ischemic testicular infarction / necrosis if untreated beyond 6 hours
clinical_hallmarks: sudden, abrupt, excruciating, severe unilateral scrotal pain, often awakening the patient from sleep or following vigorous exercise/minor trauma
frequently accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and lower quadrant abdominal pain (often misdiagnosed as appendicitis)
physical examination: affected testis is swollen, tender, HIGH-RIDING (elevated towards inguinal ring) with a HORIZONTAL LIE due to cord shortening and twisting
pathognomonic sign: ABSENCE OF THE IPSILATERAL CREMASTERIC REFLEX (light stroking of superior inner thigh fails to cause normal ipsilateral testicular elevation)
Negative Prehn's sign: manual elevation of the scrotum DOES NOT relieve the pain (and often worsens it)
pertinent_negatives: CLINICAL EMERGENCY: DO NOT DELAY SURGICAL EXPLORATION FOR IMAGING IF TORSION IS SUSPECTED
content: Mechanical twisting of the spermatic cord along its axis, interrupting venous drainage and subsequently arterial blood supply to the testicle, predisposing to complete testicular necrosis within 6-8 hours. Anatomic predisposition: high investing tunica vaginalis ('bell-clapper deformity'). Diagnostic imaging: Emergent Scrotal Color Doppler Ultrasound (shows absent or severely decreased intratesticular blood flow with twisted cord 'whirlpool sign'). Treatment: STAT Emergency Surgical Exploration without delay: intraoperative detorsion and assessment of viability; Bilateral three-point Orchiopexy (fixation of BOTH testes to prevent future torsion of contralateral side) or orchiectomy if non-viable.

clinical_hallmarks: gradual, progressive onset (developing over 24-48 hours) of unilateral scrotal aching pain, swelling, and localized tenderness
associated symptoms: fever, dysuria, urethral discharge, urinary frequency, and pyuria
physical examination: exquisitely tender, indurated, swollen epididymis distinctly palpable posterior to testis in early stages, progressing to diffuse scrotal enlargement and erythema
pathognomonic sign: POSITIVE PREHN'S SIGN (manual gentle elevation of the affected hemiscrotum PROVIDES MARKED RELIEF of pain)
cremasteric reflex is PRESERVED and normal
pertinent_negatives: normal horizontal lie is absent (testis remains in normal vertical orientation)
content: Acute inflammation of the epididymis and adjoining testis, caused by retrograde ascent of pathogens from the urethra or bladder. Etiology: in sexually active men < 35 years: overwhelmingly Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae; in older men > 35 years or post-instrumentation: enteric urinary coliforms (Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas). Diagnostic workup: Scrotal Doppler ultrasound (shows hyperemia and massively increased blood flow to epididymis with normal or increased testicular perfusion), First-void urine NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia, urine culture. Treatment: 1. Sexually transmitted: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose PLUS Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 10-14 days (treat partner!); 2. Enteric: Levofloxacin 500 mg daily or Ofloxacin for 10-14 days; Scrotal elevation, ice packs, and NSAIDs.

clinical_hallmarks: progressive, insidious diminution of urinary stream: thin, narrow caliber, spraying, or splayed urinary stream with prolonged micturition time
history of previous straddle injury to perineum, urethral catheterization, transurethral instrumentation/endoscopy, or prior gonococcal urethritis
post-void urinary dribbling and sensation of incomplete bladder evacuation
secondary complications: recurrent urinary tract infections, prostatitis, and bladder calculi
flow rate evaluation: uroflowmetry shows flat, plateau-shaped curve with severely depressed peak flow rate (Qmax < 10-12 mL/s)
pertinent_negatives: normal non-enlarged prostate on DRE and ultrasound
content: Fibrotic narrowing of the urethral lumen caused by contraction of dense spongiofibrosis within the corpus spongiosum following ischemic, traumatic, or infectious injury. Diagnostic gold standard: Retrograde Urethrography (RUG) combined with Voiding Cystourethrography (VCUG) to delineate stricture length, location, and degree of spongiofibrosis. Treatment: Short (< 1 cm) bulbar strictures: Direct Vision Internal Urethrotomy (DVIU) or dilatation (high recurrence rate); Definitive surgical gold standard: Open Urethroplasty (excision and primary end-to-end anastomosis for short strictures, or Buccal Mucosa Graft [BMG] substitution urethroplasty for longer strictures, achieving > 85-90% permanent cure rate).

topic: Acute Urinary Retention (Bladder Catheterization & Post-Obstructive Diuresis)
red_flags: post-obstructive severe polyuric shock and hypokalemia
clinical_hallmarks: sudden, agonizing, complete inability to pass urine despite urgent, painful straining and urge
excruciating, severe suprapubic abdominal pain and restless agitation
physical examination: visible and palpable, tense, exquisitely tender, smooth, globular suprapubic mass that is DULL TO PERCUSSION and extends upward towards the umbilicus (distended urinary bladder)
bedside ultrasound / bladder scan: massive retained urine volume typically > 500-1500 mL
precipitating factors: constipation, cold weather, anticholinergic or sympathomimetic medications (decongestants, antihistamines), or post-operative general anesthesia
pertinent_negatives: complete absence of urine output with agonizing urge differentiates from anuric renal failure (no urge)
content: Acute, painful inability to voluntarily void urine, representing the most common urological emergency. Etiology: BPH (50%), urethral stricture, blood clots, prostate cancer, neurological injury, or anticholinergic drugs. Immediate Emergency Treatment: STAT Urethral Catheterization with a 14-16 Fr Foley catheter (or emergency Suprapubic Cystostomy if urethral catheterization fails or is contraindicated); Record initial drained urine volume. Critical Post-Catheterization Care: Monitor for Post-Obstructive Diuresis (defined as urine output > 200 mL/hr for > 2 consecutive hours), replacing 50-75% of hourly urinary fluid and electrolyte losses (0.45% Saline) to prevent hypovolemic shock and fatal hypokalemia.

topic: Subdural Hematoma (Acute vs Chronic - Bridging Vein Tear)
clinical_hallmarks: Acute SDH: high-energy head trauma presenting with immediate coma or progressive neurological deterioration, hemiparesis, and ipsilateral pupil dilation

Chronic SDH: insidious presentation weeks to months after trivial head bump in elderly or alcoholic individuals, mimicking dementia, transient ischemic attacks, progressive headache, unsteady gait, or personality changes

Non-Contrast Head CT: pathognomonic CRESCENT-SHAPED (crescentic, concavo-convex) extra-axial hyperdense (acute) or hypodense/isodense (chronic) hemorrhage that CROSSES SUTURE LINES but is limited by the dural reflections (falx and tentorium)
pertinent_negatives: hematoma crosses suture lines (distinguishes decisively from biconvex epidural hematoma)
content: Accumulation of blood beneath the inner layer of the dura mater and above the arachnoid membrane, caused by shearing rupture of the fragile cortical bridging veins that traverse the subdural space to drain into the superior sagittal sinus. Brain atrophy in the elderly stretches these veins, creating marked vulnerability. Management: Acute SDH with thickness > 10 mm or midline shift > 5 mm or declining GCS: Emergent decompressive craniotomy and hematoma evacuation; Chronic symptomatic SDH: Burr hole trephination and closed-system drainage, or mini-craniotomy; Correction of coagulopathies and antiepileptic prophylaxis.

topic: Epidural Hematoma (Middle Meningeal Artery & Lucid Interval)
clinical_hallmarks: classic clinical sequence: 1. Impact blunt head trauma to temporal fossa (pterion fracture); 2. Brief initial loss of consciousness; 3. Temporary 'LUCID INTERVAL' (patient awakens, feels normal or complains of headache for several minutes to hours); 4. Sudden, catastrophic neurological collapse with coma, ipsilateral mydriasis (fixed dilated pupil), and contralateral hemiparesis

Non-Contrast Head CT (pathognomonic): BICONVEX, LENS-SHAPED (lenticular), sharply demarcated hyperdense extra-axial collection that DOES NOT CROSS SUTURE LINES (where dura is firmly adherent to the skull table)
pertinent_negatives: hematoma does NOT cross cranial sutures (distinguishes from subdural hematoma)
content: Arterial hemorrhage into the potential space between the inner table of the skull and the outer periosteal layer of the dura mater, overwhelmingly (> 85%) caused by a temporal bone fracture tearing the Middle Meningeal Artery at the pterion. High arterial pressure produces rapid hematoma expansion and life-threatening uncal herniation compressing the brainstem and CN III. Management: Surgical emergency: Emergent Craniotomy and surgical evacuation of the hematoma with coagulation of the bleeding middle meningeal vessel. Patients treated before herniation achieve near-complete neurological recovery.

clinical_hallmarks: sudden, explosive, instantaneous onset of excruciating headache reaching MAXIMUM INTENSITY WITHIN 1 MINUTE ('thunderclap headache'), universally described as 'THE WORST HEADACHE OF MY ENTIRE LIFE'
frequently accompanied by neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity), photophobia, nausea, projectile vomiting, and transient loss of consciousness
subhyaloid / preretinal flame hemorrhages on fundoscopy (Terson syndrome)
Non-Contrast Head CT (within 6 hours sensitivity > 99%): hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns, sylvian fissures, and subarachnoid spaces

Lumbar Puncture (indicated if CT is negative but clinical suspicion persists): shows persistent blood in all 4 tubes and pathognomonic XANTHOCHROMIA (yellowish supernatant due to oxyhemoglobin/bilirubin breakdown) on spectrophotometry
pertinent_negatives: no preceding mild gradual headache; onset is instantaneous like a clap of thunder
content: Rupture of an intracranial saccular ('berry') aneurysm (85% located in the Circle of Willis: ACom, PCom, MCA) releasing arterial blood under systemic pressure into the subarachnoid space. Hunt and Hess clinical scale. Diagnostic workup: Emergent Non-Contrast Head CT -> Lumbar Puncture if CT normal -> CT Angiography (CTA) or Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA). Protocol: 1. STAT aneurysm securing within 24 hours (Endovascular Coiling or Microsurgical Clipping); 2. Enteral Nimodipine (60 mg q4h for 21 days) to prevent delayed ischemic neurological deficits from vasospasm; 3. Strict systolic BP control (< 140 mmHg) before clipping; 4. External Ventricular Drain (EVD) for hydrocephalus.

topic: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS - Motor Neuron Disease)
red_flags: aspiration pneumonia from severe bulbar dysphagia
clinical_hallmarks: pathognomonic hallmark: SIMULTANEOUS UPPER MOTOR NEURON (UMN) AND LOWER MOTOR NEURON (LMN) SIGNS in the same limb or body segment, with progressive spread to adjacent segments
LMN signs: muscle weakness, asymmetric wasting / atrophy, and diffuse widespread fasciculations (spontaneous muscle twitches, especially pathognomonic tongue fasciculations)
UMN signs: hyperreflexia, spasticity, clonus, and extensor plantar responses (Babinski sign) in an atrophied limb
Bulbar onset (25%): progressive dysarthria ('hot-potato' or slurred speech), dysphagia, sialorrhea, and pseudobulbar affect (inappropriate, involuntary laughing or crying)
STRICT PRESERVATION OF: sensory examination, extraocular eye movements, and bowel/bladder sphincter function
pertinent_negatives: sensory exam is completely normal (any sensory deficit argues strongly against ALS)
content: Fatal, relentlessly progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of upper motor neurons in the primary motor cortex and lower motor neurons in the brainstem and anterior horns of the spinal cord (El Escorial diagnostic criteria). Diagnostic workup: Electromyography and Nerve Conduction Studies (EMG/NCS: widespread active denervation and chronic reinnervation), Brain and Cervical MRI (rules out cervical spondylotic myelopathy). Treatment: Multidisciplinary palliative care; Disease-modifying pharmacotherapy: Riluzole (50 mg BID - antiglutamatergic, prolongs tracheostomy-free survival by 2-3 months), Edaravone (free radical scavenger); Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIV / BiPAP) when FVC drops; Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy (PEG) tube for dysphagia.

red_flags: myasthenic crisis (respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation)
clinical_hallmarks: cardinal feature: PATHOLOGICAL, FATIGABLE MUSCLE WEAKNESS that WORSENS WITH REPETITIVE USE OR TOWARDS THE END OF THE DAY and IMPROVES PROMPTLY WITH REST
ocular manifestations (> 85%): fluctuating, asymmetric ptosis (drooping eyelids) and binocular diplopia (double vision)
bulbar symptoms: nasal slurred speech with prolonged talking, chewing fatigue, and difficulty swallowing liquids
Ice Pack Test: placing an ice pack over ptotic eyelid for 2 minutes produces significant resolution of ptosis (sensitivity > 90% due to cold inhibiting acetylcholinesterase)
associated with Thymic Hyperplasia (65%) or Thymoma (10-15%)
pertinent_negatives: pupillary reflexes are completely normal and spared
deep tendon reflexes are brisk and preserved
content: Autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction caused by pathogenic autoantibodies directed against the postsynaptic nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor (Anti-AChR 85%) or Muscle-Specific Tyrosine Kinase (Anti-MuSK), leading to complement-mediated destruction of junctional folds and receptor loss. Diagnostic workup: Serum Anti-AChR and Anti-MuSK antibodies, Repetitive Nerve Stimulation (RNS: decremental response > 10%), Single-Fiber EMG, Contrast CT chest for thymoma. Treatment: 1. Symptomatic: Oral Pyridostigmine (60 mg q4-6h - acetylcholinesterase inhibitor); 2. Immunosuppression: Oral Prednisone + Azathioprine / Mycophenolate; 3. Thymectomy (improves long-term remission even in non-thymomatous AChR+ patients); 4. Myasthenic Crisis: IVIG or Plasmapheresis + ICU mechanical ventilation; AVOID beta-blockers, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and magnesium (which aggravate weakness).

topic: Giant Cell Arteritis & Polymyalgia Rheumatica (Temporal Arteritis)
red_flags: acute irreversible blindness (anterior ischemic optic neuropathy)
clinical_hallmarks: new-onset, severe, persistent, unilateral or bitemporal throbbing headache in an older patient (> 50 years, mean age 72)
pathognomonic sign: JAW CLAUDICATION (ischemic pain and fatigue in masseter muscles upon chewing food or prolonged talking, with > 90% specificity for GCA)
scalp tenderness (pain upon combing hair or resting head on pillow)
palpation of temporal artery: thick, tender, nodular, tortuous, cord-like vessel with diminished or absent pulse
visual disturbances: transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) or sudden catastrophic painless visual loss due to Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (A-AION)
strongly associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica (50%: morning stiffness and aching in bilateral shoulders and hips)
laboratory hallmarks: marked elevation of ESR (typically > 50-100 mm/hr) and CRP
pertinent_negatives: DO NOT WITHHOLD HIGH-DOSE CORTICOSTEROIDS while waiting for temporal artery biopsy
content: Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis predominantly affecting the temporal arteries and other cranial branches of the external carotid artery and aorta. Immediate Clinical Mandate: If GCA is suspected, IMMEDIATELY initiate high-dose systemic corticosteroids to prevent irreversible contralateral blindness. Diagnostic gold standard: Unilateral or bilateral Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB: showing transmural granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and disruption of internal elastic lamina); Color Doppler ultrasound (hypoechoic 'halo sign'). Treatment: Without visual loss: Oral Prednisone (40-60 mg daily); With impending/active visual loss: STAT IV pulse Methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days) followed by high-dose oral steroids; IL-6 receptor antagonist (Tocilizumab) as a steroid-sparing agent.

red_flags: hypoxic brain injury and neuronal death after 30 minutes
clinical_hallmarks: modern operational definition (ILAE): continuous, unremitting generalized convulsive seizure activity lasting GREATER THAN 5 MINUTES (t1 time point), OR two or more discrete seizures without complete recovery of consciousness between episodes
tonic-clonic motor convulsions: sustained muscular contraction followed by violent rhythmic symmetric clonic jerking of all extremities
autonomic surge: tachycardia, severe hypertension, hyperthermia, pupillary dilation, and copious oral secretions
subtle status: in prolonged or sedated patients, visible motor jerks may dwindle to subtle rhythmic eye twitching or nystagmoid jerks despite continuous electrographic seizure activity on EEG
pertinent_negatives: no purposeful movements or response to voice during ictal state
content: Life-threatening neurological emergency characterized by failure of the endogenous mechanisms responsible for seizure termination or initiation of mechanisms leading to abnormally prolonged seizures. Protocol (Time-Sensitive): Phase 1 (0-5 min): ABCs, high-flow O2, IV access, bedside capillary glucose (IV 50% Dextrose if hypoglycemic); Phase 2 (5-20 min - First-line Benzodiazepines): IV Lorazepam (0.1 mg/kg, typically 4 mg IV bolus) OR IM Midazolam (10 mg); repeat once if seizing continues; Phase 3 (20-40 min - Second-line Antiepileptics): IV Levetiracetam (60 mg/kg, max 4500 mg) OR IV Fosphenytoin (20 mg PE/kg) OR IV Valproate (40 mg/kg); Phase 4 (> 40 min - Refractory Status): General anesthesia and endotracheal intubation with IV continuous infusion of Propofol, Midazolam, or Ketamine with continuous EEG monitoring.

topic: Migraine with Aura (Scintillating Scotoma & Cortical Spreading Depression)
red_flags: headache reaching peak in < 1 minute (thunderclap - rules out SAH)
aura lasting > 60 minutes or acute onset with negative symptoms
clinical_hallmarks: classic visual aura (in 25-30% of migraineurs): fully reversible focal neurological symptoms developing gradually over 5-20 minutes and lasting less than 60 minutes

pathognomonic visual aura features: Scintillating Scotoma (a luminous, shimmering blind spot with jagged, flickering zigzag borders resembling walls of a medieval fortress / 'fortification spectra' spreading across visual field)
followed within 60 minutes by a moderate-to-severe, unilateral, pulsating/throbbing headache
pain is characteristically aggravated by routine physical activity (walking, climbing stairs)
associated with intense photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, and vomiting; patient seeks dark, quiet room to lie motionless
pertinent_negatives: visual aura evolves gradually over minutes (distinguishes from sudden instantaneous vascular TIA/stroke)
content: Neurovascular brain disorder driven by Cortical Spreading Depression (a wave of neuronal and glial depolarization) activating the trigeminovascular system and releasing calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), neurokinin A, and Substance P. Treatment: 1. Acute abortive: 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists (Triptans: oral Sumatriptan 50-100 mg, Rizatriptan) taken at onset of headache (NOT during aura); CGRP receptor antagonists (Gepants: Rimegepant); NSAIDs/Acetaminophen; 2. Prophylaxis (for >= 4 headache days/month): Beta-blockers (Propranolol), Topiramate, Amitriptyline, or monthly subcutaneous CGRP monoclonal antibodies (Erenumab, Fremanezumab).

topic: Transient Ischemic Attack (ABCD2 Score & Carotid Stenosis)
red_flags: high ABCD2 score (>= 4-6 indicates high 48-hour stroke risk)
clinical_hallmarks: transient, reversible episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, WITHOUT ACUTE INFARCTION on neuroimaging
typical symptoms resolve completely within minutes to an hour (most last < 15-30 minutes)

clinical manifestations: sudden unilateral arm/leg weakness, facial drooping, dysarthria, expressive aphasia, or monocular transient painless visual blackout ('amaurosis fugax' - transient curtain descending over one eye)

ABCD2 Clinical Risk Score (predicts 2-day stroke risk up to 8%): Age >= 60 (1 pt); BP >= 140/90 (1 pt); Clinical features: unilateral weakness (2 pts) or speech disturbance without weakness (1 pt); Duration: >= 60 min (2 pts) or 10-59 min (1 pt); Diabetes (1 pt)
pertinent_negatives: complete resolution of neurological deficits on physical examination upon presentation
content: Tissue-based definition: transient ischemia without structural tissue infarction. Represents an urgent harbinger of impending disabling ischemic stroke (10-15% of strokes occur within 90 days of a TIA, half within 48 hours). Diagnostic workup: STAT Brain MRI with Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) + MRA/CTA of head and neck, ECG, continuous telemetry for atrial fibrillation, Transthoracic/Transesophageal Echo. Protocol: 1. STAT Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT: Aspirin + Clopidogrel for 21 days, then monotherapy); 2. High-intensity Statin (Atorvastatin 80 mg); 3. Anticoagulation (DOAC) if atrial fibrillation; 4. Urgent Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA within 7-14 days) for symptomatic carotid stenosis 70-99%.

red_flags: perioperative hemodynamic collapse if beta-blocked alone
clinical_hallmarks: the classic symptom triad during paroxysms: 1. Pounding, severe headache; 2. Profuse diaphoresis (drenching sweats); 3. Palpitations with marked tachycardia
severe, paroxysmal or sustained refractory hypertension
attacks last minutes to hours, accompanied by severe pallor, tremulousness, and impending doom sensation
precipitated by postural change, abdominal palpation, urination (bladder paraganglioma), or drugs (beta-blockers, metoclopramide)
the famous '10% Rule': 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal (paragangliomas), 10% malignant, 10% familial (MEN-2A/2B, VHL, NF-1)
pertinent_negatives: CARDINAL RULE: NEVER ADMINISTER BETA-BLOCKERS BEFORE ADEQUATE ALPHA-BLOCKADE (avoids unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction and fatal hypertensive crisis)
content: Catecholamine-secreting tumor arising from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla (or sympathetic paraganglia). Diagnostic gold standard: Fractionated Plasma Free Metanephrines (high sensitivity > 97%) or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines; Localization: Contrast CT/MRI abdomen, 123I-MIBG scan or 68Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT. Preoperative Medical Optimization (MANDATORY): Non-competitive alpha-blockade (Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BID titrated for 10-14 days) PLUS high-salt diet and hydration; Beta-blocker (Propranolol) added ONLY AFTER full alpha-blockade achieved. Definitive cure: Laparoscopic adrenalectomy.

topic: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA - High Anion Gap Ketosis)
red_flags: cerebral edema (especially in pediatric patients receiving rapid fluids)
fatal hypokalemic cardiac arrest during insulin infusion
clinical_hallmarks: classic diagnostic triad: 1. Hyperglycemia (blood glucose > 250 mg/dL, though euglycemic DKA can occur with SGLT2 inhibitors); 2. High anion gap metabolic acidosis (arterial/venous pH < 7.30, serum bicarbonate < 18 mEq/L, anion gap > 10-12); 3. Positive serum and urine ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate > 3.0 mmol/L)

clinical signs: rapid, deep sighing Kussmaul respirations (respiratory compensation blowing off CO2), sweet fruity acetone breath odor, diffuse abdominal pain mimicking surgical abdomen, nausea, vomiting, and profound dehydration (sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, hypotension)
pertinent_negatives: anion gap is elevated (distinguishes from non-anion gap metabolic acidosis)
content: Life-threatening acute metabolic complication of diabetes (predominantly Type 1, but occurs in Type 2 under severe stress/infection) characterized by absolute insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormone excess. Protocol (Order of Operations): 1. Aggressive IV Fluid Resuscitation (0.9% Normal Saline 1-1.5 L in 1st hour, switch to 0.45% NaCl based on corrected sodium); 2. POTASSIUM MANAGEMENT FIRST: If serum K+ < 3.3 mEq/L, HOLD INSULIN and give IV KCl until K+ > 3.3; if K+ 3.3-5.2, add 20-30 mEq KCl per liter of IV fluid; 3. IV Regular Insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hr); 4. Add 5% Dextrose when glucose reaches 200-250 mg/dL to prevent hypoglycemia while clearing ketoacidosis (continue insulin until anion gap closes and bicarbonate > 18).

red_flags: arterial / venous thromboembolism from extreme hyperviscosity
clinical_hallmarks: predominantly occurs in elderly Type 2 diabetic patients, evolving insidiously over days to weeks

diagnostic triad: 1. Extreme, profound hyperglycemia (plasma glucose > 600 mg/dL, often 800-1200 mg/dL); 2. High effective serum osmolality (> 320 mOsm/kg); 3. Absence of significant ketoacidosis (arterial pH > 7.30, serum bicarbonate > 18 mEq/L, negative or trace ketones)
massive fluid deficit (typically 8 to 12 Liters / 100-200 mL/kg): severe hypotension, skin turgor loss, dry axillae, tachycardia
prominent neurological impairment directly correlating with osmolality: lethargy, confusion, hemichorea, focal seizures, and deep coma
pertinent_negatives: absence of significant ketoacidosis (endogenous basal insulin is sufficient to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis but insufficient for glucose uptake)
content: Acute metabolic crisis of Type 2 diabetes with severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and profound dehydration without substantial ketosis. Mortality is 10-20% (significantly higher than DKA). Emergency Management: 1. MASSIVE, CAREFUL FLUID REHYDRATION is the single most critical intervention (0.9% Normal Saline initially, switching to 0.45% Saline based on corrected sodium, replacing estimated 9L deficit over 24-48 hours); 2.
