Low-dose IV Regular Insulin (0.05-0.1 units/kg/hr) initiated only AFTER aggressive fluid resuscitation has started; 3. Vigorous potassium replacement; 4. Prophylactic LMWH anticoagulation (hyperosmolality induces extreme thrombophilia).

topic: Graves' Disease & Thyroid Eye Disease (TSHR Antibodies)
clinical_hallmarks: signs of hyperthyroidism: heat intolerance, unexplained weight loss despite ravenous appetite, fine resting hand tremor, hyperdefecation, palpitations, emotional lability
diffusely enlarged, smooth, non-tender goiter with an AUDIBLE SYSTOLIC BRUIT AND PALPABLE THRILL over the superior thyroid poles

Graves' Orbitopathy / Exophthalmos (pathognomonic): bilateral proptosis, eyelid retraction (Dalrymple sign), lid lag on downgaze (von Graefe sign), periorbital edema, and diplopia from extraocular muscle enlargement
Pretibial Myxedema (thyroid dermopathy): non-pitting, orange-peel, violaceous indurated plaques over the anterior shins
laboratory hallmark: completely suppressed TSH (< 0.01 mIU/L), elevated Free T4 and Free T3, and positive Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulin (TSI / TRAb in > 98%)
pertinent_negatives: radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) shows diffuse, homogeneous high uptake (distinguishes from thyroiditis or toxic adenoma)
content: Autoimmune disorder caused by circulating autoantibodies (TRAb/TSI) directed against the thyroid follicular TSH receptor, stimulating autonomous thyroid hormone hypersecretion and follicular hyperplasia. Treatment: 1. Beta-blockers (Propranolol 20-40 mg TID) for immediate adrenergic symptom relief; 2. Thionamides (Antithyroid drugs): Methimazole (10-30 mg daily) or Propylthiouracil (PTU - preferred in first trimester of pregnancy and thyroid storm); 3. Radioactive Iodine (RAI - 131I) ablation; 4. Total or near-total Thyroidectomy; Active moderate-to-severe orbitopathy: IV Methylprednisolone or Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor).

red_flags: bitemporal hemianopsia from optic chiasm compression
obstructive sleep apnea with respiratory failure
clinical_hallmarks: insidious, progressive soft tissue and acral overgrowth: widening of hands and feet requiring increasing ring, shoe, and glove sizes ('spade-like hands')

characteristic craniofacial changes: coarse facial features, frontal bossing, enlarged nose and lips, macroglossia (enlarged tongue with teeth indentations), and mandibular prognathism with dental malocclusion and widened teeth spacing
deep, hollow, resonant voice and excessive oily skin (hyperhidrosis and seborrhea)
mass effect from pituitary macroadenoma: bitemporal hemianopsia (compression of optic chiasm) and dull frontal headache
comorbidities: secondary hypertension, diabetes mellitus, severe OSA, and colonic polyps/adenocarcinomas
pertinent_negatives: normal age-adjusted IGF-1 completely excludes acromegaly
content: Syndrome of chronic autonomous Growth Hormone (GH) hypersecretion, > 95% caused by a benign pituitary somatotroph macroadenoma. Elevated GH stimulates excessive hepatic synthesis of Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1), which mediates peripheral tissue overgrowth. Diagnostic workup: 1. Serum IGF-1 (single best screening test; elevated confirms excess); 2. Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT: 75g glucose fails to suppress GH < 1.0 ng/mL); 3. Contrast MRI pituitary sella. Treatment: First-line definitive therapy: Endoscopic Transsphenoidal Pituitary Adenoma Resection; Medical therapy for residual disease: Long-acting Somatostatin receptor ligands (Octreotide LAR, Lanreotide), GH-receptor antagonist (Pegvisomant), or Dopamine agonist (Cabergoline).

topic: Diabetes Insipidus (Central vs Nephrogenic & Water Deprivation)
red_flags: hypovolemic shock / coma if water access restricted
clinical_hallmarks: massive, relentless polyuria (> 3 Liters/24 hours, often 8-15 L/day) of clear, pale, dilute water-like urine
intense, unquenchable polydipsia with a striking preference for ice-cold water
nocturia occurring multiple times each night
laboratory hallmark: low urine osmolality (< 300 mOsm/kg) and low urine specific gravity (< 1.005) in the presence of elevated or high-normal serum osmolality (> 295 mOsm/kg) and hypernatremia

Water Deprivation Test followed by Desmopressin (DDAVP) Challenge: Central DI shows marked rise in urine osmolality (> 50-100% increase after DDAVP); Nephrogenic DI shows NO or minimal (< 50%) response to DDAVP
pertinent_negatives: urine glucose is negative (distinguishes from osmotic diuresis of diabetes mellitus)
content: Disorder of water homeostasis characterized by the excretion of abnormally large volumes of dilute urine, resulting from either deficient pituitary Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH / Vasopressin) synthesis/release (Central DI: head trauma, pituitary surgery, craniopharyngioma) or renal tubular insensitivity to ADH (Nephrogenic DI: Lithium toxicity, hypercalcemia, hereditary AVPR2 mutation). Diagnostic test of choice: Water Deprivation Test followed by DDAVP challenge, or plasma Copeptin measurement. Treatment: Central DI: Desmopressin (DDAVP: oral 0.1-0.2 mg BID/TID or intranasal spray 10-20 mcg); Nephrogenic DI: Discontinue Lithium, low-sodium/low-protein diet, Thiazide diuretics (paradoxical antidiuresis) + Amiloride / Indomethacin.

clinical_hallmarks: neuromuscular excitability: circumoral paresthesias (tingling/numbness around mouth), numbness in fingertips and toes, and painful muscle cramps

pathognomonic latent tetany signs: 1. TROUSSEAU SIGN (carpopedal spasm: flexion of wrist and MCP joints with extension of IP joints and adduction of thumb ['main d'accoucheur'] provoked by inflating a BP cuff > 20 mmHg above systolic BP for 3 minutes); 2. CHVOSTEK SIGN (twitching of ipsilateral facial muscles provoked by tapping Cranial Nerve VII anterior to the ear)
ECG hallmark: PROLONGED QT INTERVAL (ST segment prolongation) predisposing to polymorphic ventricular arrhythmias
most common etiology: accidental damage, devascularization, or excision of parathyroid glands during total thyroidectomy or neck dissection
laboratory triad: Low serum ionized and total calcium, Low or inappropriately normal intact PTH, and HIGH serum phosphate
pertinent_negatives: absence of elevated PTH (elevated PTH with low calcium indicates Vitamin D deficiency or pseudohypoparathyroidism)
content: Deficiency of parathyroid hormone (PTH) causing impaired renal calcium reabsorption, decreased renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activation of Vitamin D, and reduced bone resorption. Emergency Protocol for Acute Symptomatic Hypocalcemia: 1. STAT IV Calcium Gluconate (1-2 ampules of 10% Calcium Gluconate in 50-100 mL 5% Dextrose infused over 10-20 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring); 2. Correct concurrent Hypomagnesemia (low Mg impairs PTH secretion and induces end-organ resistance); 3. Chronic Maintenance: Oral Calcium carbonate/citrate (1-3 g elemental calcium daily) + Active Vitamin D (Calcitriol 0.25-1.0 mcg daily); Recombinant human PTH (Natpara) for refractory cases.

topic: Osteomalacia & Rickets (Severe Vitamin D Deficiency & Looser Zones)
red_flags: hypocalcemic tetany or seizures in infants
clinical_hallmarks: Osteomalacia (Adults): diffuse, dull, aching bone pain and exquisite bone tenderness (especially over spine, pelvis, ribs, and anterior tibiae); proximal muscle weakness causing a characteristic 'waddling gait' and difficulty climbing stairs or standing from chair

Rickets (Children): delayed fontanelle closure, craniotabes (ping-pong ball skull softness), 'rachitic rosary' (beading of costochondral junctions), Harrison groove, and progressive bowing of weight-bearing long bones (genu varum or genu valgum)

radiographic hallmarks: generalized osteopenia, cortical thinning, and pathognomonic LOOSER'S ZONES (pseudofractures: narrow, radiolucent bands perpendicular to bone cortex, typically at pubic rami, femoral neck, and scapula)

laboratory tetrad: Markedly low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (< 10-12 ng/mL), low or low-normal serum calcium, low serum phosphate, and ELEVATED BONE ALKALINE PHOSPHATASE (ALP) with secondary hyperparathyroidism
pertinent_negatives: bone pain and proximal myopathy are absent in pure uncomplicated osteoporosis
content: Defective mineralization of newly formed osteoid matrix in cortical and trabecular bone (osteomalacia) and cartilaginous growth plates (rickets), overwhelmingly caused by severe, prolonged Vitamin D deficiency, dietary calcium lack, or chronic renal phosphate wasting. Diagnostic workup: Serum 25(OH)D, calcium, phosphate, ALP, intact PTH, skeletal radiographs. Treatment: High-dose Ergocalciferol (Vitamin D2: 50,000 IU orally once weekly for 8-12 weeks) or Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3: 60,000 IU weekly) followed by maintenance (1,000-2,000 IU daily); Concurrent oral elemental Calcium supplementation (1,000-1,500 mg daily) to prevent 'hungry bone' hypocalcemia during rapid remineralization.

clinical_hallmarks: Primary Hypogonadism / Klinefelter Syndrome (47,XXY - most common congenital form, 1 in 600 live male births): tall stature with eunuchoid body proportions (long limbs, arm span exceeding height by > 5 cm), bilateral painless gynecomastia, sparse facial and body hair with female pubic hair distribution, small, firm, fibrotic testes (< 4 mL volume), and azoospermia/infertility
Adult-onset secondary hypogonadism: progressive loss of libido, erectile dysfunction, decreased spontaneous morning erections, chronic fatigue, muscle mass loss, and depressed mood

laboratory hallmarks: Primary (Hypergonadotropic) shows Low morning total/free testosterone with HIGH LH and FSH; Secondary (Hypogonadotropic) shows Low testosterone with LOW or inappropriately normal LH/FSH
karyotype analysis confirms 47,XXY in Klinefelter syndrome
pertinent_negatives: elevated gonadotropins distinguish primary testicular failure from pituitary failure
content: Failure of the testes to produce physiological levels of testosterone and/or normal numbers of spermatozoa. Diagnostic workup: Morning (8-10 AM) fasting total testosterone on two separate mornings (diagnostic if < 300 ng/dL), LH, FSH, prolactin, karyotype analysis, semen analysis, bone mineral density (DEXA scan). Treatment: Klinefelter and primary hypogonadism: Lifelong Testosterone Replacement Therapy (TRT: transdermal gels, injectable testosterone cypionate/enanthate 100-200 mg q2 weeks, or testosterone undecanoate 1000 mg q10-14 weeks) to restore secondary sexual characteristics, muscle mass, bone density, and mood; TRT is contraindicated in active prostate or breast cancer.

clinical_hallmarks: the clinical paradox: SIMULTANEOUS WIDESPREAD SYSTEMIC MICROVASCULAR THROMBOSIS (causing multiorgan failure) AND PROFUSE BLEEDING (due to consumption of platelets and clotting factors)
spontaneous, persistent, continuous oozing of blood from IV venipuncture sites, surgical wounds, mucosal membranes, and catheter insertion points
petechiae, widespread ecchymoses, and Purpura Fulminans (cutaneous microvascular thrombosis and hemorrhagic skin necrosis)

triggered by a catastrophic underlying condition: severe sepsis / septic shock (Gram-negative endotoxemia), obstetric catastrophes (abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism), massive trauma, or malignancy (APL)

diagnostic laboratory tetrad: 1. Markedly elevated D-Dimer / Fibrin Degradation Products (FDPs); 2. Prolonged Prothrombin Time (PT/INR) and prolonged aPTT; 3. Progressive thrombocytopenia; 4. Severely depressed serum Fibrinogen level (< 100-150 mg/dL)
pertinent_negatives: prolonged PT and aPTT distinguish DIC decisively from TTP (where PT/aPTT are normal)
content: Systemic thrombohemorrhagic syndrome characterized by uncontrolled systemic activation of the extrinsic coagulation cascade (tissue factor release), resulting in widespread microvascular fibrin deposition and consumptive depletion of platelets and coagulation factors. Management: 1. TREAT THE UNDERLYING PRIMARY TRIGGER IMMEDIATELY (antibiotics for sepsis, emergent delivery for placental abruption, chemotherapy); 2. Supportive replacement therapy guided by active bleeding: Platelet transfusion (target > 50,000 /mcL if bleeding); Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP: 15-30 mL/kg for prolonged PT/aPTT); Cryoprecipitate (target fibrinogen > 150 mg/dL); 3. Heparin infusion considered only in predominant thrombotic phenotype (purpura fulminans, solid tumor).

topic: Sickle Cell Disease & Acute Vaso-Occlusive Bone Crisis
red_flags: acute chest syndrome (fever, chest pain, new lung infiltrate, hypoxemia)
splenic sequestration crisis in young child (hypovolemic shock, massive spleen)
ischemic stroke in pediatric sickle patient
clinical_hallmarks: recurrent, unpredictable episodes of severe, agonizing, deep bone or joint pain (commonly affecting back, ribs, femora, and tibiae) triggered by cold, hypoxia, dehydration, stress, or infection

Dactylitis ('hand-foot syndrome'): symmetrical, exquisitely painful, warm, non-erythematous swelling of dorsal hands and feet in infants (6-18 months) - frequently the first clinical manifestation of sickle cell disease
chronic hemolytic anemia: jaundice, scleral icterus, pigmented gallstones, and non-healing malleolar skin ulcers
functional asplenia: early autosplenectomy by age 5 due to repeated splenic micro-infarctions, predisposing to fatal encapsulated bacterial infections (Streptococcus pneumoniae)
diagnostic confirmation: Hemoglobin Electrophoresis or High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) showing predominant Hemoglobin S (HbS > 80-90%) with absence of normal HbA in homozygous HbSS
pertinent_negatives: presence of sickled, crescent-shaped erythrocytes and Howell-Jolly bodies on peripheral blood smear
content: Autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathy caused by a point mutation in the beta-globin gene (GAG to GTG, replacing glutamic acid with valine at codon 6 of beta-globin chain). Deoxygenation causes HbS polymerization into rigid, insoluble fibers that distort RBCs into sickle shapes, causing microvascular occlusion and hemolysis. Protocol for Acute Vaso-Occlusive Crisis: 1. Prompt, aggressive opioid analgesia (IV Morphine or Hydromorphone administered within 30-60 minutes); 2. Aggressive oral or IV hydration with hypotonic fluids (D5W or 0.45% Saline); 3. Supplemental oxygen ONLY IF SpO2 < 95%; 4. Preventative disease-modifying therapy: Hydroxyurea (induces fetal hemoglobin HbF synthesis, reducing crises by > 50%); L-glutamine, Voxelotor, Crizanlizumab.

red_flags: severe high-output cardiac failure in infancy
clinical_hallmarks: infant presents between 6 and 24 months of age (as fetal hemoglobin HbF production wanes) with severe, progressive, life-threatening pallor, failure to thrive, feeding difficulties, and irritability
profound microcytic, hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin typically 2-6 g/dL) with target cells, anisopoikilocytosis, basophilic stippling, and nucleated RBCs on blood smear

MASSIVE EXTRAMEDULLARY HEMATOPOIESIS signs: 1. Striking 'chipmunk facies' (prominent frontal bossing, maxillary hypertrophy, depressed nasal bridge); 2. Skeletal X-ray showing widening of diploic space with classic 'hair-on-end' skull appearance; 3. Massive hepatosplenomegaly causing huge protuberant abdomen
hemoglobin electrophoresis: profound deficiency or COMPLETE ABSENCE OF HbA, with compensatory elevation of HbF (> 90-95%) and variable HbA2
pertinent_negatives: normal or elevated serum ferritin and iron levels (decisively excludes iron deficiency anemia)
content: Severe autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathy characterized by absent (beta-0) or severely reduced (beta-plus) synthesis of beta-globin chains, leading to an excess of unpaired alpha-globin chains that precipitate in erythroid precursors, causing profound ineffective erythropoiesis and severe peripheral hemolysis. Management: 1. Lifelong, regular, Transfusion-Dependent protocol: packed RBC transfusions every 2-4 weeks to maintain pre-transfusion Hb 9.5-10.5 g/dL; 2. MANDATORY Iron Chelation Therapy (oral Deferasirox, Deferiprone, or subcutaneous Deferoxamine) initiated after 10-20 transfusions or when serum ferritin exceeds 1000 ng/mL to prevent fatal hemochromatotic heart failure; 3. Definitive cure: Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (Allo-HSCT) or gene therapy.

topic: Polycythemia Vera (JAK2 V617F Mutation & Aquagenic Pruritus)
red_flags: major arterial or venous thrombosis (stroke, mi, budd-chiari, dvt)
clinical_hallmarks: pathognomonic symptom: AQUAGENIC PRURITUS (intense, intractable, excruciating itching, burning, or stinging sensation triggered by warm water, showers, or baths, without any visible cutaneous rash)
plethoric appearance: ruddy cyanosis ('red face'), engorged conjunctival vessels, and dusky redness of palms and soles
Erythromelalgia: episodic, intense burning pain and erythema in the distal hands and feet, relieved by aspirin or cold application
symptoms of hyperviscosity: dull throbbing headache, dizziness, visual scotomas, tinnitus, and epistaxis
moderate splenomegaly on palpation (70%)

laboratory hallmarks: Markedly elevated Hemoglobin (> 16.5 g/dL in men, > 16.0 g/dL in women) and Hematocrit (> 49% in men, > 48% in women), associated leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, SUPPRESSED SERUM ERYTHROPOIETIN (EPO < normal), and positive JAK2 V617F mutation in > 95% of patients
pertinent_negatives: suppressed serum EPO distinguishes primary PV from secondary polycythemia (where EPO is elevated)
content: Clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by autonomous, erythropoietin-independent trilineage hematopoietic hyperplasia, driven by the somatic gain-of-function JAK2 V617F mutation (valine-to-phenylalanine substitution at codon 617) in exon 14. WHO diagnostic criteria (3 major, or 2 major + 1 minor). Treatment: 1. Therapeutic Phlebotomy (removal of 450-500 mL blood regularly) to STRICTLY MAINTAIN HEMATOCRIT < 45% (demonstrated to reduce cardiovascular death and major thrombotic events by fourfold); 2. Low-dose Aspirin (75-100 mg daily); 3. Cytoreductive therapy (Hydroxyurea) for high-risk patients (age > 60 or prior thrombosis); 4. JAK1/2 inhibitor (Ruxolitinib) for hydroxyurea-resistant cases.

clinical_hallmarks: insidious, progressive early symptoms: persistent, vague postprandial epigastric fullness, early satiety, anorexia, and unintentional marked weight loss
unexplained iron deficiency anemia and occult GI blood loss in an adult > 50 years

pathognomonic metastatic lymph node and peritoneal stigmata: 1. VIRCHOW'S NODE (hard, non-tender enlargement of the LEFT SUPRACLAVICULAR lymph node / Troisier sign); 2. SISTER MARY JOSEPH NODULE (palpable metastatic nodule in the umbilicus); 3. BLUMER'S SHELF (metastatic ridge palpable on digital rectal exam in the rectovesical or rectouterine pouch); 4. KRUKENBERG TUMOR (bilateral metastatic ovarian enlargement with mucin-rich signet ring cells)
Linitis Plastica: diffuse infiltrative adenocarcinoma causing a rigid, non-distensible, thickened 'leather bottle' stomach on barium swallow/CT
pertinent_negatives: symptoms refractory to empirical PPI courses warrant immediate endoscopy
content: Malignant epithelial tumor of the stomach, categorized by Lauren classification into Intestinal type (associated with chronic H. pylori atrophic gastritis, smoking, dietary nitrosamines) and Diffuse type (infiltrative, E-cadherin/CDH1 gene mutation, signet-ring cells). Diagnostic gold standard: Upper GI Endoscopy (EGD) with multiple oriented biopsies (minimum 6-8 biopsies for high diagnostic yield); Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) and Contrast CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for TNM staging. Treatment: Resectable disease: Radical Subtotal or Total Gastrectomy with D2 Lymphadenectomy + Perioperative FLOT Chemotherapy; Targeted Trastuzumab for HER2-positive metastatic disease; Nivolumab for PD-L1 positive tumors.

red_flags: trousseau syndrome of malignancy (migratory superficial thrombophlebitis)
clinical_hallmarks: cardinal clinical presentation: PROGRESSIVE, INSIDIOUS, PAINLESS OBSTRUCTIVE JAUNDICE (yellow sclerae, deep dark tea-colored urine, pale clay-colored acholic stools, and generalized pruritus)
epigastric ache radiating through to the mid-back, characteristically partially relieved by sitting upright and leaning forward
rapid, marked, unintentional weight loss and profound anorexia

COURVOISIER'S SIGN (pathognomonic): A PALPABLE, ENLARGED, NON-TENDER GALLBLADDER in the presence of obstructive jaundice (indicates malignant distal common bile duct obstruction, as chronic gallstone disease causes a fibrotic shrunken non-distensible gallbladder)
Trousseau syndrome: migratory, superficial thrombophlebitis presenting as recurrent tender inflammatory cords in superficial veins
sudden, new-onset diabetes mellitus in an elderly patient without risk factors
pertinent_negatives: absence of biliary colic and absence of fever (distinguishes from acute gallstone cholangitis)
content: Highly lethal malignancy arising from the ductal epithelium of the exocrine pancreas (70% located in the head of the pancreas). Diagnostic workup: Multiphase Thin-Cut Pancreatic Protocol CT of abdomen (shows hypoattenuating pancreatic mass, loss of peripancreatic fat planes, and pathognomonic 'DOUBLE DUCT SIGN' [simultaneous dilation of both the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct]); Serum CA 19-9 tumor marker (useful for monitoring, sensitivity 80%); EUS with fine-needle biopsy. Treatment: Resectable head tumors: Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple Procedure) followed by adjuvant modified FOLFIRINOX chemotherapy; Endoscopic biliary stenting (metal stent) for jaundice palliation.

red_flags: spontaneous tumor rupture with catastrophic hemoperitoneum
portal vein tumor thrombosis with variceal hemorrhage
clinical_hallmarks: develops almost exclusively (> 85-90%) in patients with underlying CHRONIC CIRRHOSIS (chronic Hepatitis B, chronic Hepatitis C, alcoholic cirrhosis, or NASH/MASH)
clinical presentation is often subtle: rapid, unexplained decompensation of previously stable cirrhosis (new-onset refractory ascites, worsening encephalopathy, or variceal bleed)
unintentional weight loss, anorexia, and dull right upper quadrant dragging pain
physical examination: hard, nodular, enlarged liver; an audible hepatic arterial bruit over the tumor
laboratory hallmark: Markedly elevated serum Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP > 400-500 ng/mL is strongly suggestive in high-risk cirrhotic patient)

pathognomonic dynamic multiphasic imaging criteria (CT/MRI): ARTERIAL PHASE HYPERENHANCEMENT (intense enhancement in late arterial phase) FOLLOWED BY 'WASHOUT' in the venous or delayed phase with an enhancing pseudocapsule (LI-RADS 5)
pertinent_negatives: biopsy is NOT required for diagnosis in cirrhotic patients if dynamic CT/MRI meets definitive non-invasive LI-RADS 5 criteria
content: Primary malignant neoplasm of hepatocytes. Surveillance standard: Biannual (every 6 months) liver ultrasound + serum AFP in all cirrhotic patients. Staged using the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system. Treatment options: Very early / Early stage (BCLC 0/A): Surgical Resection (for non-cirrhotic or preserved Child-Pugh A), Orthotopic Liver Transplantation (Milan criteria: 1 lesion <= 5 cm or up to 3 lesions <= 3 cm), or Radiofrequency / Microwave Ablation (RFA/MWA); Intermediate stage (BCLC B): Transarterial Chemoembolization (TACE); Advanced stage (BCLC C): Systemic immunotherapy combination (Atezolizumab + Bevacizumab is first-line).

clinical_hallmarks: predominantly affects young women of childbearing age (female:male ratio 9:1)

pathognomonic cutaneous signs: MALAR RASH (erythematous 'butterfly' maculopapular eruption across bridge of nose and cheeks, characteristically SPARING THE NASOLABIAL FOLDS) and marked photosensitivity
inflammatory, non-erosive polyarthritis primarily affecting hands and wrists (Jaccoud arthropathy with reversible joint deformities)
serositis: pleurisy and pericarditis with friction rub
Lupus Nephritis: persistent proteinuria (> 0.5 g/day) and active urinary sediment (RBC casts)

laboratory hallmarks: ANA positive in > 98% (entry criterion); High specificity markers: Anti-dsDNA (correlates with disease activity and nephritis) and Anti-Smith (Sm) antibodies; Depressed serum complement levels (low C3 and C4 during active flare)
pertinent_negatives: malar rash strictly spares the nasolabial folds (distinguishes from seborrheic dermatitis or rosacea)
content: Prototypic chronic multisystem autoimmune disease characterized by immune complex deposition, autoantibody production against nuclear antigens, and complement activation (EULAR/ACR 2019 criteria: ANA >= 1:80 plus >= 10 points). Protocol: 1. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ: <= 5 mg/kg/day) is RECOMMENDED FOR ALL LUPUS PATIENTS (improves survival and prevents flares); 2. Systemic Corticosteroids for acute flares; 3. Lupus Nephritis: Renal biopsy mandatory for ISN/RPS classification; Induction: IV Methylprednisolone pulses + Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF) or IV Cyclophosphamide; Belimumab or Voclosporin for refractory active nephritis.

topic: Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma - Diffuse vs Limited CREST)
red_flags: scleroderma renal crisis (malignant hypertension, microangiopathic anemia)
clinical_hallmarks: Limited Cutaneous Scleroderma (CREST syndrome): 1. Calcinosis cutis (painful calcium deposits in finger pads); 2. Raynaud's phenomenon; 3. Esophageal dysmotility (reflux and dysphagia); 4. Sclerodactyly (tight, shiny, thickened skin of fingers distal to MCPs, loss of normal skin folds, flexion contractures); 5. Telangiectasias (mat-like red spots on face, lips, hands)
Diffuse Cutaneous Scleroderma: rapid skin thickening extending PROXIMAL TO ELBOWS/KNEES and involving trunk, with early severe visceral fibrosis (ILD, renal crisis)
facial changes: 'bird-like facies', pinched beaked nose, radial perioral furrows, and microstomia (restricted mouth opening)

pathognomonic serology: Limited SSc: Anti-Centromere Antibodies (ACA in 70-80%); Diffuse SSc: Anti-Scl-70 (Anti-Topoisomerase I in 40%) and Anti-RNA Polymerase III (associated with high risk of Scleroderma Renal Crisis)
pertinent_negatives: ACE INHIBITORS (Captopril) are life-saving in Scleroderma Renal Crisis; HIGH-DOSE STEROIDS (> 15 mg/day) are strictly contraindicated because they precipitate renal crisis
content: Systemic connective tissue disease characterized by immune dysregulation, microvascular obliterative vasculopathy, and progressive tissue fibrosis of skin and internal organs. Diagnostic workup: Nailfold capillaroscopy, ANA, Anti-Scl-70, Anti-Centromere, HRCT thorax, Echocardiogram with Doppler estimated PAP, PFTs. Treatment: Organ-specific: Raynaud: CCBs (Nifedipine); Scleroderma Renal Crisis: STAT immediate ACE inhibitor (Captopril); ILD: Mycophenolate Mofetil or Cyclophosphamide or Nintedanib; PAH: Endothelin receptor antagonists (Bosentan) + PDE-5 inhibitors (Sildenafil).

clinical_hallmarks: develops in up to 30% of patients with cutaneous psoriasis (cutaneous lesions precede joint disease by years in 70%, but can be concurrent or rarely postdate arthritis)

cardinal clinical features: 1. DACTYLITIS ('sausage digit' - diffuse, uniform, painful erythematous swelling of an entire finger or toe from tenosynovitis); 2. Distinctive involvement of the DISTAL INTERPHALANGEAL (DIP) JOINTS; 3. Psoriatic nail dystrophy (nail pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, and 'oil-drop' spots); 4. Enthesitis (Achilles tendon, plantar fascia)

five clinical patterns (Moll and Wright): asymmetric oligoarthritis (most common 70%), symmetric polyarthritis (mimicking RA), DIP joint predominant, spondylitis, and Arthritis Mutilans (telescoping digits)
plain X-ray (pathognomonic): 'PENCIL-IN-CUP' DEFORMITY (narrowing of the proximal articular bone entering the expanded cup-like base of the distal phalanx)
pertinent_negatives: seronegative: Rheumatoid Factor (RF) and Anti-CCP are negative
content: Chronic inflammatory musculoskeletal disease associated with cutaneous psoriasis, classified using the CASPAR (ClASsification criteria for Psoriatic ARthritis: established inflammatory articular disease + >= 3 points from personal/family psoriasis, nail dystrophy, negative RF, dactylitis, and juxta-articular new bone formation). Treatment: Mild: NSAIDs; Peripheral arthritis: Conventional synthetic DMARDs (Methotrexate, Leflunomide); Moderate-severe, axial, or dactylitic disease: Biologic DMARDs (TNF inhibitors [Adalimumab], IL-17 inhibitors [Secukinumab, Ixekizumab], IL-23 inhibitors [Ustekinumab, Guselkumab]) or targeted synthetic JAK inhibitors (Tofacitinib).

keywords: cant see cant pee cant climb a tree
clinical_hallmarks: classic clinical triad (the mnemonic 'CAN'T SEE, CAN'T PEE, CAN'T CLIMB A TREE'): 1. Conjunctivitis / anterior uveitis; 2. Urethritis or cervicitis; 3. Asymmetric, additive oligoarthritis primarily affecting large weight-bearing joints of lower limbs (knees and ankles)
develops 1-4 weeks following a primary mucosal infection: either genitourinary (Chlamydia trachomatis, Ureaplasma) or gastrointestinal dysentery (Campylobacter jejuni, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia)

pathognomonic mucocutaneous lesions: Keratoderma Blennorrhagica (hyperkeratotic, pustular, crusting, vesicular plaques on soles of feet and palms) and Circinate Balanitis (painless shallow serpiginous erosions on the glans penis)
dactylitis ('sausage toes') and intense calcaneal heel pain (enthesitis)
strongly linked to HLA-B27 (> 65-80%)
pertinent_negatives: synovial fluid is STERILE (sterile reactive inflammation, NOT septic arthritis)
content: Sterile autoimmune inflammatory arthropathy developing secondary to an infectious trigger at a distant mucosal site in genetically predisposed individuals. Diagnostic workup: Joint arthrocentesis (rules out septic arthritis or crystals), First-void urine NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis, stool cultures. Treatment: Acute phase: High-dose NSAIDs (Indomethacin 50-75 mg TID) is first-line; Intra-articular corticosteroid injections for monoarthritis; Antibiotic therapy is indicated ONLY to treat active persistent Chlamydia urethral infection (Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 10-14 days - treat partner!), antibiotics do NOT alter arthritis course once established; Sulfasalazine or Methotrexate for chronic persistent arthritis (> 3-6 months).

red_flags: occult underlying malignancy (ovarian, breast, lung, gastric - up to 30% paraneoplastic)
clinical_hallmarks: cardinal motor presentation: PROGRESSIVE, SYMMETRIC, PAINLESS PROXIMAL MUSCLE WEAKNESS involving shoulder girdle (difficulty lifting arms to comb hair or reach high shelves) and pelvic girdle (difficulty rising from low chairs, climbing stairs, or getting out of bath)

pathognomonic cutaneous signs in Dermatomyositis: 1. HELIOTROPE RASH (violaceous/purplish erythema of the upper eyelids, often accompanied by periorbital edema); 2. GOTTRON'S PAPULES (violaceous, flat-topped papules and plaques over the dorsal interphalangeal and MCP joints of hands); 3. Gottron sign (erythema over elbows and knees); 4. Shawl sign (erythema over upper back and shoulders) and V-sign (anterior chest)
Mechanic's hands: hyperkeratotic, cracked, scaling skin along lateral aspect of digits (Antisynthetase syndrome: Anti-Jo-1)

laboratory hallmarks: MASSIVELY ELEVATED SERUM CREATINE KINASE (CK - often 10-50x normal), elevated aldolase, LDH, and AST/ALT; Muscle biopsy shows CD4+ perivascular/perimysial inflammation in DM, CD8+ endomysial infiltration in PM
pertinent_negatives: normal sensory examination and preserved deep tendon reflexes
content: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies characterized by immune-mediated striated muscle injury. Crucial oncological association: Adults with Dermatomyositis have a 3- to 6-fold increased risk of underlying internal malignancy (MANDATORY age-appropriate cancer screening). Diagnostic workup: Serum CK, myositis-specific autoantibodies (Anti-Jo-1, Anti-Mi-2, Anti-TIF1-gamma), Electromyography (EMG), Muscle MRI (STIR shows muscle edema), and Muscle Biopsy. Treatment: First-line: High-dose oral Corticosteroids (Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day); Steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (Methotrexate or Azathioprine); IVIG for refractory weakness or severe dysphagia.

topic: Behçet's Disease (Recurrent Aphthous Ulcers & Pathergy Test)
red_flags: rupture of pulmonary artery aneurysm (massive fatal hemoptysis)
clinical_hallmarks: MANDATORY ENTRY CRITERION (International Study Group criteria): RECURRENT ORAL APHTHOUS ULCERATION (at least 3 episodes in a 12-month period: painful, round, sharply defined shallow ulcers with yellowish-gray necrotic base and erythematous halo on buccal mucosa, tongue, or lips)

PLUS >= 2 of the following cardinal features: 1. Recurrent painful GENITAL ULCERS (scrotal or vulvar punched-out ulcers that heal with scarring); 2. Ocular inflammation (anterior uveitis with pathognomonic shifting HYPOPYON [sterile pus layering in anterior chamber], posterior uveitis, retinal vasculitis); 3. Cutaneous lesions (erythema nodosum-like nodules, pseudofolliculitis, acneiform lesions); 4. POSITIVE PATHERGY TEST (formation of an erythematous sterile papule or pustule >= 2 mm at site of 20-gauge sterile needle prick within 24-48 hours)
strongly associated with HLA-B51 along the ancient Silk Road route
pertinent_negatives: negative ANA and negative ANCA (variable vessel vasculitis)
content: Chronic, relapsing, systemic inflammatory disorder affecting blood vessels of all sizes (arteries and veins) with endothelial activation and neutrophil hyperreactivity. Treatment: Mucocutaneous disease: Topical steroids + oral Colchicine (0.5-1.5 mg daily) or Apremilast; Ocular / Visceral / Neurological disease: High-dose systemic Corticosteroids + Azathioprine; Anti-TNF agents (Infliximab, Adalimumab) are exceptionally effective for severe posterior uveitis and refractory vascular aneurysms. Anticoagulants are controversial in deep vein thrombosis due to high risk of bleeding from coexisting pulmonary aneurysms.

topic: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN - HBV Association & Mononeuritis Multiplex)
clinical_hallmarks: systemic necrotizing vasculitis targeting medium-sized muscular arteries, with strong etiologic association with HEPATITIS B VIRUS (HBV) infection (in up to 30%)

neurological hallmark: MONONEURITIS MULTIPLEX (asymmetric, painful, asynchronous involvement of non-contiguous peripheral nerves, characteristically presenting as acute foot drop [peroneal nerve] or wrist drop [radial nerve])
cutaneous signs: Livedo Reticularis (purplish, mottled, reticular lace-like vascular skin discoloration), tender subcutaneous nodules along the course of arteries, and digital infarctions
severe bilateral or unilateral TESTICULAR PAIN and tenderness in young men without infection
renovascular hypertension (renal artery involvement causing ischemia and renin hypersecretion)
angiography (mesenteric or renal): PATHOGNOMONIC MULTIPLE SEGMENTAL MICROANEURYSMS AND STENOSES resembling 'a string of beads' / rosary beads
pertinent_negatives: SPARES THE PULMONARY CIRCULATION (absence of pulmonary infiltrates distinguishes PAN from microscopic polyangiitis and GPA)
content: Systemic necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that spares arterioles, capillaries, and post-capillary venules, without glomerulonephritis. ACR 1990 criteria (needs >= 3 of 10 criteria). Diagnostic workup: Deep skin/muscle/sural nerve biopsy, Mesenteric/Renal Catheter Angiography (CT/conventional), Hepatitis B serologies (HBsAg, HBeAg, HBV DNA). Treatment: Idiopathic PAN: High-dose oral Prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) + Cyclophosphamide for severe organ-threatening disease (Five-Factor Score >= 1); HBV-associated PAN: Short course of corticosteroids + Plasma exchange + Antiviral therapy (Entecavir or Tenofovir) to clear viral replication.

red_flags: atlantoaxial subluxation with cervical cord compression
clinical_hallmarks: chronic, symmetric, inflammatory polyarthritis characteristically targeting the SMALL JOINTS OF HANDS AND FEET: Metacarpophalangeal (MCP), Proximal Interphalangeal (PIP), and wrist joints (STRICTLY SPARING THE DIP JOINTS)
prolonged morning stiffness lasting GREATER THAN 60 MINUTES that improves with movement and warmth

pathognomonic hand deformities in established disease: 1. Ulnar deviation of fingers at MCP joints; 2. Swan-neck deformity (hyperextension of PIP with flexion of DIP); 3. Boutonnière deformity (flexion of PIP with hyperextension of DIP); 4. Z-deformity of thumb
subcutaneous firm, non-tender Rheumatoid Nodules over extensor surfaces (elbows)

laboratory hallmarks: Anti-Citrullinated Protein Antibodies (Anti-CCP / ACPA: high specificity > 95-98%, correlates with aggressive erosive disease) and Rheumatoid Factor (RF 70-80%); Elevated ESR and CRP
pertinent_negatives: distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints are spared (involvement of DIP points to osteoarthritis or psoriatic arthritis)
content: Systemic autoimmune inflammatory disease characterized by persistent synovial proliferation (pannus formation), leading to cartilage destruction and juxta-articular marginal bone erosions (2010 ACR/EULAR criteria). Treatment (Treat-to-Target Strategy): 1. FIRST-LINE ANCHOR DRUG: Oral Methotrexate (MTX: 15-25 mg once weekly + Folic acid 5 mg weekly); 2. Conventional synthetic DMARD combinations (Sulfasalazine, Leflunomide, Hydroxychloroquine); 3. Biologic DMARDs for inadequate response: TNF inhibitors (Adalimumab, Etanercept), IL-6 receptor antagonists (Tocilizumab), T-cell co-stimulation modulator (Abatacept), or JAK inhibitors (Tofacitinib, Upadacitinib).

clinical_hallmarks: Yamaguchi Diagnostic Criteria (requires >= 5 features with >= 2 major):

Major Criteria: 1. High spiking quotidian or double quotidian fever (>= 39C, typically peaking in evening and returning to baseline); 2. Arthralgias or arthritis lasting >= 2 weeks; 3. Evanescent, non-pruritic, macular or maculopapular SALMON-PINK / SALMON-COLORED CUTANEOUS RASH appearing synchronously with fever spikes and disappearing between spikes (Koebner phenomenon positive); 4. Leukocytosis (WBC >= 10,000 /mcL with >= 80% granulocytes)
Minor Criteria: sore throat (pharyngitis without exudates), lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly, abnormal LFTs, and negative RF and negative ANA
LABORATORY HALLMARK: EXTREME HYPERFERRITINEMIA (serum ferritin levels often > 3,000 - 10,000 ng/mL, occasionally > 50,000 ng/mL) accompanied by a low percentage of glycosylated ferritin (< 20%)
pertinent_negatives: strictly negative Rheumatoid Factor (RF) and negative ANA
content: Rare, systemic autoinflammatory disorder characterized by neutrophil hyperactivation and uncontrolled cytokine storm (IL-1-beta, IL-6, IL-18, and ferritin). Statutory diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out occult infections and hematologic malignancies (lymphoma). Treatment: 1. First-line: High-dose oral Corticosteroids (Prednisone 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day) or IV pulse Methylprednisolone; 2. Conventional DMARD: Methotrexate (15-25 mg/week); 3. Biologic therapy for steroid-refractory disease: IL-1 receptor antagonists (Anakinra, Canakinumab) or IL-6 antagonists (Tocilizumab) induce rapid clinical and biochemical remission.

topic: Takayasu Arteritis (Pulseless Disease & Aortic Arch Syndrome)
clinical_hallmarks: predominantly affects YOUNG FEMALES (< 40 years of age, female:male ratio 8:1), historically high prevalence in Asia

cardinal vascular signs: 1. MARKED BLOOD PRESSURE ASYMMETRY (> 10 mmHg systolic difference between arms); 2. DIMINISHED OR ABSENT UPPER EXTREMITY PULSES ('PULSELESS DISEASE' - impalpable radial or brachial pulses); 3. Arterial bruits audible over subclavian, carotid, or abdominal aorta; 4. Upper extremity claudication (arm fatigue and pain upon exertion)
carotodynia: localized tenderness over the carotid arteries during active inflammatory phase
systemic prodrome: low-grade fever, malaise, night sweats, arthralgias, and weight loss
imaging gold standard: CT/MR Angiography or conventional catheter angiography showing smooth, tapered stenosis, occlusions, and aneurysms of the aorta and its primary branches
pertinent_negatives: age of onset < 40 years distinguishes decisively from Giant Cell Arteritis (> 50 years)
content: Chronic, granulomatous, panarteritic large-vessel vasculitis predominantly affecting the aorta, its major primary branch vessels (subclavian, common carotid, renal arteries), and pulmonary arteries (ACR 1990 criteria). Diagnostic workup: MR Angiography (MRA) or CT Angiography of aorta and branches (concentric vessel wall thickening and luminal stenosis), ESR, CRP. Treatment: 1. High-dose oral Corticosteroids (Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day); 2. Steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (Methotrexate, Azathioprine, Mycophenolate); 3. Biologic anti-TNF agents (Infliximab) or Tocilizumab for refractory inflammation; 4. Surgical bypass grafting or endovascular angioplasty/stenting (PERFORMED ONLY WHEN VASCULAR INFLAMMATION IS IN QUIESCENT REMISSION).

clinical_hallmarks: transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes; name derives from Makonde language meaning 'that which bends up' (reflecting the hunched, contorted posture of suffering patients)
abrupt onset of high fever (> 39C / 102F) accompanied by SEVERE, CRIPPLING, DEBILITATING POLYARTHRALGIA AND POLYARTHRITIS
joint involvement is bilateral and symmetric, characteristically affecting distal joints (wrists, hands, ankles, metatarsals) with visible periarticular swelling
centrifugal maculopapular rash appearing 2-5 days after fever onset
pathognomonic cutaneous pigmentation: Centrofacial brownish/black hyperpigmentation (Chik sign / 'brown nose sign')
prolonged chronic phase: severe chronic inflammatory polyarthritis persisting for months to years in up to 30-40% of patients
pertinent_negatives: absence of severe retro-orbital pain and profound shock (differentiates from severe dengue, though co-infections occur)
content: Arboviral alphavirus infection of the family Togaviridae. Diagnostic workup: RT-PCR for Chikungunya viral RNA (days 1-7 of illness), Chikungunya IgM capture ELISA (positive from day 5 onwards), CBC (lymphopenia, mild thrombocytopenia). Treatment: Acute phase: Strictly supportive: Adequate hydration; Analgesics: Acetaminophen / Paracetamol (avoid NSAIDs and Aspirin until Dengue is definitively excluded to prevent hemorrhage); Chronic persistent arthralgia: NSAIDs, short-course corticosteroids, or Methotrexate / Hydroxychloroquine for chronic destructive arthritis.

red_flags: hypovolemic shock / death within 2-4 hours ('cholera gravis')
clinical_hallmarks: ingestion of water or food contaminated with feces containing Vibrio cholerae (serogroups O1 and O139)
abrupt onset of massive, effortless, painless, profuse watery diarrhea that rapidly loses all fecal character
pathognomonic stool appearance: 'RICE-WATER STOOL' (pale, translucent, turbid grayish-white fluid containing flecks of mucus and intestinal epithelial cells, with a faint non-offensive fishy odor)
volume of fluid loss can exceed 1 Liter per hour (up to 20-30 Liters/day in adults)

profound signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, dry tongue, loss of skin pinch turgor (> 2-3 seconds), 'washerwoman's hands' (wrinkled shriveled skin on fingers), hoarse voice, absent radial pulses, and anuria
pertinent_negatives: absence of fever, absence of tenesmus, and absence of abdominal cramping (painless watery purged stools)
content: Acute diarrheal illness caused by enterotoxigenic bacterium Vibrio cholerae. Cholera enterotoxin (choleragen) binds GM1 ganglioside, irreversibly activating adenylate cyclase, producing massive cAMP and hypersecretion of sodium, chloride, and water. Diagnostic workup: Stool darkfield microscopy (darting motility), Cary-Blair transport medium, TCBS agar culture, rapid dipstick. Emergency Treatment: 1. IMMEDIATE AGGRESSIVE REHYDRATION: IV Ringer's Lactate (100 mL/kg within 3 hours for severe dehydration: 30 mL/kg in first 30 min, then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hours); 2. WHO Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) as soon as patient can drink; 3. Single-dose oral antibiotic: Doxycycline (300 mg single dose) or Azithromycin (1 g single dose) reduces stool volume and shedding.

red_flags: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS: microangiopathic anemia, thrombocytopenia, AKI)
clinical_hallmarks: transmitted via fecal-oral route with an extremely low infectious dose (as few as 10-100 organisms can cause disease)
abrupt onset of high fever, severe colicky lower abdominal pain, and initial watery diarrhea progressing within 24-48 hours to CLASSIC BACILLARY DYSENTERY
frequent, scant-volume stools composed entirely of FRANK BLOOD, PUS, AND MUCUS (up to 20-30 times per day)
severe, agonizing TENESMUS (painful, constant, ineffectual straining to defecate, with rectal burning)
stool microscopy: sheets of Polymorphonuclear Leukocytes (WBCs > 50/hpf) and numerous RBCs
caused by Shigella dysenteriae type 1 (produces Shiga toxin), Shigella flexneri, or Shigella sonnei
pertinent_negatives: high fever and rapid onset distinguish bacillary dysentery from amoebic dysentery (which is gradual with lower fever)
content: Invasive acute bacterial enteritis characterized by mucosal invasion of colonic enterocytes, intracellular multiplication, cell-to-cell spread, and mucosal ulceration. Complications: HUS, toxic megacolon, reactive arthritis. Diagnostic workup: Stool culture (MacConkey or Hektoen enteric agar), stool PCR. Treatment: 1. Strict avoidance of antimotility agents (Loperamide is CONTRAINDICATED as it worsens toxic megacolon); 2. Rehydration therapy; 3. Targeted antimicrobial therapy: Oral Ciprofloxacin (500 mg BID for 3 days) or Azithromycin (500 mg day 1, 250 mg days 2-5) or Ceftriaxone for children.

red_flags: apnea and sudden infant death in infants < 6 months
clinical_hallmarks: caused by Bordetella pertussis, presenting through three distinct sequential clinical phases:
1. Catarrhal Phase (1-2 weeks): insidious onset of mild coryza, sneezing, low-grade fever, and mild occasional cough (most infectious stage, clinically indistinguishable from common cold)

2. Paroxysmal Phase (2-6 weeks): violent, uncontrollable paroxysms of coughing (bursts of 5-15 rapid consecutive staccato coughs during a single expiration) culminating in a PATHOGNOMONIC HIGH-PITCHED INSPIRATORY 'WHOOP' as air is forcefully drawn through narrowed glottis
3. POST-TUSSIVE EMESIS (vomiting immediately following a coughing fit) is highly specific for pertussis in adolescents/adults
facial petechiae and subconjunctival hemorrhages from extreme venous pressure during coughing
laboratory hallmark: MARKED ABSOLUTE LYMPHOCYTOSIS (WBC 20,000-50,000 /mcL with > 60-70% mature lymphocytes, driven by pertussis toxin inhibiting lymphocyte extravasation)
pertinent_negatives: infants < 6 months frequently lack the inspiratory whoop and present instead with life-threatening APNEA
content: Highly contagious bacterial infection of the tracheobronchial tree. Diagnostic gold standard: Nasopharyngeal swab for Bordetella pertussis PCR (high sensitivity) or Regan-Lowe / Bordet-Gengou culture. Treatment: Macrolide antibiotic initiated early: Oral Azithromycin (10 mg/kg day 1, then 5 mg/kg days 2-5; or 500 mg daily for adults) or Clarithromycin; Antibiotics eliminate nasopharyngeal carriage and prevent secondary transmission within 5 days, though paroxysmal cough may persist for weeks ('the 100-day cough'); Mandatory chemoprophylaxis for all household close contacts.

topic: Syphilis (Treponema Pallidum - Primary Chancre to Neurosyphilis)
keywords: secondary syphilis copper rash palms soles
red_flags: tertiary neurosyphilis / tabes dorsalis / general paresis
thoracic aortic aneurysm with tree-bark calcification
clinical_hallmarks: Primary Syphilis: HARD CHANCRE (solitary, painless, indurated, clean-based ulcer with raised, rolled borders on genitalia or oral mucosa) accompanied by painless regional lymphadenopathy; heals spontaneously in 3-6 weeks

Secondary Syphilis (systemic dissemination): diffuse, non-pruritic, symmetrical, coppery-red / bronze maculopapular rash characteristically INVOLVING THE PALMS AND SOLES; CONDYLOMATA LATA (painless, highly infectious, broad, moist, wart-like plaques in intertriginous/perianal regions); mucous patches; 'moth-eaten' patchy alopecia

Tertiary Syphilis: Gummas (destructive granulomatous lesions of skin/bone), cardiovascular syphilis (ascending aortitis), and Neurosyphilis: Tabes Dorsalis (sensory ataxia, lightning pains, Charcot joints) and ARGYLL ROBERTSON PUPILS ('prostitute's pupil': accommodates to near vision but does not react to light)
serological algorithm: Non-treponemal screening tests (VDRL or RPR - titers monitor treatment response) confirmed by Treponemal-specific tests (FTA-ABS or TP-PA)
pertinent_negatives: painless clean base distinguishes primary chancre from painful necrotic chancroid or HSV
content: Chronic, multistage systemic infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum. Diagnostic workup: Darkfield microscopy of chancre exudate, nontreponemal (RPR/VDRL) and treponemal serology, CSF examination for neurosyphilis. Treatment: 1. Primary, Secondary, or Early Latent Syphilis: Benzathine Penicillin G (2.4 million units IM single dose); 2. Late Latent Syphilis or Latent of unknown duration: Benzathine Penicillin G (2.4 million units IM once weekly for 3 consecutive weeks, total 7.2 million units); 3. Neurosyphilis: Continuous IV Aqueous Crystalline Penicillin G (18-24 million units daily as 3-4 million units q4h for 10-14 days); Oral Doxycycline (100 mg BID for 14-28 days) for non-pregnant penicillin-allergic patients.

topic: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (VZV Reactivation & Hutchinson Sign)
clinical_hallmarks: reactivation of latent Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) within the Ophthalmic division of the Trigeminal Nerve (Cranial Nerve V1)
prodromal severe unilateral burning, tingling, or lancinating forehead and scalp pain
pain is followed by a classic unilateral, erythematous, vesicular, crusting dermatomal rash strictly respecting the midline of the forehead and upper eyelid

PATHOGNOMONIC HUTCHINSON SIGN: presence of herpetic vesicles on the TIP, SIDE, OR ROOT OF THE NOSE (indicates involvement of the nasociliary branch of CN V1, carrying a > 75% risk of sight-threatening ocular complications)

slit-lamp ocular manifestations: punctate epithelial keratitis, dendritic pseudoulcer (mucous plaque dendrite lacking terminal bulbs, distinct from HSV), anterior uveitis with raised intraocular pressure, and stromal keratitis
pertinent_negatives: rash strictly respects the vertical anatomical midline of face
content: Sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency. Immediate Treatment Protocol: 1. Early Systemic Antiviral Therapy (MUST BE INITIATED WITHIN 72 HOURS OF RASH ONSET): Oral Valacyclovir (1,000 mg TID for 7-10 days) or Famciclovir (500 mg TID) or oral Acyclovir (800 mg 5x/day); 2. STAT Emergent Ophthalmologist Consultation; 3. Topical Corticosteroid drops (Prednisolone acetate 1%) indicated ONLY under ophthalmology supervision for stromal keratitis/uveitis; 4. Prevention: Recombinant Zoster Vaccine (Shingrix - 2 doses) for adults >= 50 years; 5. Postherpetic neuralgia management: Gabapentin, Pregabalin, or Amitriptyline.

topic: Anthrax (Bacillus Anthracis - Cutaneous Malignant Pustule & Inhalation)
red_flags: inhalation anthrax with acute respiratory failure (near 100% fatal without early therapy)
clinical_hallmarks: history of exposure to infected herbivorous livestock (cattle, sheep, goats) or animal products (hides, wool, bone meal), or biosecurity aerosol threat

Cutaneous Anthrax (95% of cases): painless pruritic papule developing 1-7 days post-exposure, rapidly enlarging into a vesicle surrounded by a ring of satellite vesicles; ruptures to form a characteristic PATHOGNOMONIC COAL-BLACK, DEPRESSED, PAINLESS NECROTIC ESCHAR ('MALIGNANT PUSTULE')
surrounded by EXTENSIVE, GELATINOUS, NON-PITTING EDEMA that is striking and completely out of proportion to lesion size

Inhalation Anthrax (Woolsorter's disease): biphasic illness (initial mild viral-like prodrome followed by abrupt acute dyspnea, cyanosis, stridor, and diaphoresis); Chest Radiograph: PATHOGNOMONIC MARKED WIDENING OF THE MEDIASTINUM and pleural effusions due to hemorrhagic mediastinitis without parenchymal bronchopneumonia
pertinent_negatives: lesion is PAINLESS and has absence of frank pus (distinguishes from staphylococcal carbuncle)
content: Zoonotic infection caused by the spore-forming Gram-positive rod Bacillus anthracis. Virulence factors: Poly-D-glutamic acid antiphagocytic capsule and tripartite exotoxin (Protective Antigen [PA], Lethal Factor [LF], Edema Factor [EF]). Diagnostic workup: Gram stain and PCR of vesicle fluid, blood cultures, chest CT. Treatment: Cutaneous: Oral Ciprofloxacin (500 mg BID for 60 days) or Doxycycline (100 mg BID); Inhalation / Systemic: IV Triple Therapy (IV Ciprofloxacin + Clindamycin/Linezolid [protein synthesis inhibitor to halt toxin production] + Meropenem) + Monoclonal Antitoxin (Raxibacumab or Obiltoxaximab or Anthrax Immune Globulin).

topic: Severe Preeclampsia & HELLP Syndrome (Magnesium Sulfate Protocol)
clinical_hallmarks: new-onset hypertension (Systolic BP >= 140 mmHg or Diastolic BP >= 90 mmHg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart) occurring AFTER 20 WEEKS GESTATION in a previously normotensive woman, with Proteinuria (>= 300 mg/24h or protein-to-creatinine ratio >= 0.3)

Severe Features: Systolic BP >= 160 mmHg or Diastolic BP >= 110 mmHg, persistent severe frontal headache unresponsive to analgesics, scotomas or visual blurring, intractable right upper quadrant / epigastric pain (hepatic capsule stretch), pulmonary edema, thrombocytopenia (< 100,000 /mcL), serum creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL
brisk hyperreflexia with sustained patellar/ankle clonus (heralds impending eclamptic seizure)
HELLP SYNDROME TRIAD: 1. Hemolysis (schistocytes on smear, LDH > 600 U/L, indirect bilirubin > 1.2 mg/dL); 2. Elevated Liver enzymes (AST/ALT >= 2x ULN); 3. Low Platelets (< 100,000 /mcL)
pertinent_negatives: absence of chronic hypertension preceding 20 weeks gestation
content: Multisystem disorder of pregnancy characterized by defective spiral artery remodeling leading to placental hypoperfusion, endothelial dysfunction, and widespread vasospasm. Definitive cure is delivery. Emergency Protocol: 1. SEIZURE PROPHYLAXIS: IV Magnesium Sulfate (Zuspan regimen: 4-6 g IV loading dose over 20 min, followed by 1-2 g/hr continuous IV maintenance; monitor patellar reflexes, respiratory rate > 12/min, and urine output > 30 mL/hr; Calcium Gluconate 1g IV is antidote for Mg toxicity); 2. STAT ANTIHYPERTENSIVE THERAPY for BP >= 160/110 mmHg (IV Labetalol 20 mg bolus, IV Hydralazine 5-10 mg, or oral immediate-release Nifedipine 10-20 mg); 3. Delivery indicated at >= 34 weeks, or immediately at any gestational age if maternal/fetal compromise or HELLP syndrome.

clinical_hallmarks: pathognomonic clinical presentation: SUDDEN, UNPROVOKED, PROFUSE, BRIGHT RED VAGINAL BLEEDING occurring in the third trimester (typically after 28 weeks gestation) that is ENTIRELY PAINLESS
bleeding characteristically starts without warning, often waking the patient from sleep ('sentinel bleed')
physical examination: UTERUS IS SOFT, RELAXED, AND NON-TENDER (in sharp, fundamental contrast to the rigid, wood-hard, agonizingly tender uterus of placental abruption)
fetal heart rate pattern is initially reassuring unless maternal hemorrhagic shock supervenes
high incidence of abnormal fetal lie (transverse, oblique) or floating high unengaged presenting part
imaging gold standard: Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS - completely safe when transducer introduced gently) demonstrates placental tissue overlying or abutting the internal cervical os
pertinent_negatives: DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION IS STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED (can dislodge placental cotyledon and provoke catastrophic, fatal hemorrhage) until ultrasound has ruled out previa
content: Abnormal implantation of the placenta over or near the internal cervical os. Risk factors: prior cesarean delivery, multiparity, advanced maternal age, prior uterine curettage. Classification: complete (covers internal os), marginal (edge <= 2 cm from os). Management: NPO, large-bore IV access (16G x 2), crossmatch packed red blood cells, continuous fetal monitoring, maternal resuscitation; Corticosteroids (Betamethasone) for fetal lung maturity if < 37 weeks; Delivery: Scheduled Cesarean section at 36-37 weeks (or emergent Cesarean delivery at any gestation for severe intractable hemorrhage); Vigilance for Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS).

red_flags: fetal demise / severe prolonged fetal bradycardia
maternal hypovolemic shock out of proportion to visible bleeding
clinical_hallmarks: sudden onset of CONSTANT, SEVERE, AGONIZING ABDOMINAL AND BACK PAIN in the third trimester
vaginal bleeding with DARK, PORT-WINE OR CLOTTED BLOOD (though 20% of abruptions are 'concealed' where blood is trapped behind placenta without external bleeding)
pathognomonic physical examination: UTERUS IS EXQUISITELY TENDER, RIGID, HYPERTONIC, AND 'WOOD-LIKE' OR 'BOARD-LIKE' ('WOODY HARD UTERUS')
uterine tachysystole (frequent, high-frequency, low-amplitude contractions on tocodynamometry)
fetal distress: severe persistent fetal bradycardia, late decelerations, or intrauterine fetal demise
maternal shock that is COMPLETELY OUT OF PROPORTION TO VISIBLE EXTERNAL BLEEDING (due to massive concealed retroplacental hematoma)
Couvelaire uterus (intraoperative finding): widespread myometrial extravasation of blood giving the uterus a purple, bruised, mottled ecchymotic appearance
pertinent_negatives: uterus is rigid and agonizingly tender (distinguishes decisively from painless soft uterus of placenta previa)
content: Premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from the uterine myometrial wall before delivery, initiated by hemorrhage into the decidua basalis. Major risk factors: maternal chronic hypertension, preeclampsia, cocaine use, abdominal trauma, rapid uterine decompression. Complications: Consumptive coagulopathy (DIC in 30% of severe abruptions), renal failure, maternal and fetal mortality. Management: STAT emergent resuscitation (large-bore IV access, aggressive fluids, crossmatch 4-6 units PRBCs, FFP, cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen < 150 mg/dL); IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY CESAREAN DELIVERY for viable fetus with fetal distress or maternal instability; Vaginal delivery permitted only if fetal demise has occurred and mother is hemodynamically stable.

keywords: the 4 ts tone trauma tissue thrombin
clinical_hallmarks: ACOG Definition: cumulative blood loss >= 1,000 mL OR blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours following delivery (regardless of delivery route)

THE 4 Ts ETIOLOGICAL MNEMONIC: 1. TONE (Uterine Atony - accounts for 70-80% of PPH: uterus is soft, flaccid, enlarged, poorly contracted, and 'BOGGY' upon fundal palpation); 2. TRAUMA (20%: lacerations of cervix, vagina, perineum, or uterine rupture); 3. TISSUE (10%: retained placental fragments or succenturiate lobe); 4. THROMBIN (1%: coagulopathy, DIC)
profuse, continuous vaginal blood loss with large clots, accompanied by maternal tachycardia (pulse > 110), hypotension, pallor, cold extremities, and oliguria
pertinent_negatives: firm, well-contracted fundus rules out uterine atony (mandates immediate visual inspection for genital tract lacerations)
content: Leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide. Stepwise Management Protocol: 1. Call for multidisciplinary obstetric emergency help STAT; 2. Vigorous Continuous Bimanual Uterine Compression and Fundal Massage; 3. First-line Uterotonic: IV Oxytocin (10-40 units in 500-1000 mL crystalloid infusion at 250-500 mL/hr or 10 units IM); 4. Second-line Uterotonics: Methylergonovine (Methergine 0.2 mg IM - CONTRAINDICATED in hypertension/preeclampsia), Carboprost (Hemabate 15-methyl PGF2-alpha 250 mcg IM - CONTRAINDICATED in asthma), and rectal/sublingual Misoprostol (800-1000 mcg); 5. STAT Tranexamic Acid (TXA: 1g IV within 3 hours); 6. Intrauterine Balloon Tamponade (Bakri balloon filled with 300-500 mL warm saline); 7. Surgical laparotomy: B-Lynch uterine compression sutures, bilateral uterine artery ligation, or emergent Peripartum Hysterectomy.

red_flags: maternal thyroid storm (due to massive hCG cross-reacting with TSH receptors)
clinical_hallmarks: abnormal, irregular, painless or crampy vaginal bleeding in first trimester (in > 80% of complete moles)
pathognomonic macroscopic sign: passage of clear, swollen, fluid-filled, translucent 'GRAPE-LIKE VESICLES' per vaginam
UTERINE SIZE IS DISPROPORTIONATELY LARGE FOR GESTATIONAL AGE (e.g. fundal height at umbilicus at 10 weeks gestation in complete mole)
severe, intractable hyperemesis gravidarum (intense vomiting requiring IV fluids)
early-onset Preeclampsia developing BEFORE 20 WEEKS GESTATION (highly pathognomonic for hydatidiform mole)
bilateral, massively enlarged, multilocular ovarian THECA LUTEIN CYSTS (due to massive hCG luteinizing ovarian stroma)
laboratory hallmark: ASTRONOMICALLY HIGH QUANTITATIVE SERUM BETA-hCG (frequently > 100,000 mIU/mL, often reaching 500,000 - 1,000,000 mIU/mL)

Pelvic Ultrasound (pathognomonic): 'SNOWSTORM' or 'BUNCH OF GRAPES' appearance (diffuse, echogenic intrauterine mass with innumerable microcystic spaces, with COMPLETE ABSENCE OF FETAL PARTS or amniotic sac in complete mole)
pertinent_negatives: absence of fetal heartbeat and absence of fetal skeleton in complete hydatidiform mole
content: Gestational trophoblastic disease characterized by abnormal fertilization and hydropic villous hyperplasia. Complete Mole (46,XX diploid, all paternal chromosomes from single sperm duplicating in enucleated ovum); Partial Mole (69,XXY triploid, fertilization of normal ovum by two sperm). Treatment Protocol: 1. STAT Suction Curettage (Suction Dilation and Evacuation - D&E) under ultrasound guidance; 2. Post-evacuation Surveillance: Weekly quantitative serum Beta-hCG monitoring until normal for 3 consecutive weeks, then monthly for 6 months; 3. Strict contraception for 6 months; 4. Rising or plateauing hCG indicates Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia (GTN / choriocarcinoma) requiring Single-agent Methotrexate or multi-agent EMA-CO chemotherapy.

red_flags: ovarian gangrene and ischemic necrosis if surgical detorsion delayed
loss of ovary and future fertility
clinical_hallmarks: sudden, acute, excruciating, sharp, unilateral lower quadrant abdominal and pelvic pain, frequently triggered by sudden postural movement, exercise, or coitus
paroxysmal pain: pain waxes and wanes or occurs in waves as the ovary transiently twists and partially untwists
PROFOUND, INTRACTABLE NAUSEA AND REPEATED VOMITING present in > 70-85% of cases (due to autonomic visceral stimulation from twisted infundibulopelvic ligament)
pre-existing ovarian enlargement: > 80% have a benign ovarian cyst or mass measuring >= 5 cm (most frequently a Mature Cystic Teratoma / Dermoid Cyst)
physical exam: unilateral adnexal tenderness and a palpable tender adnexal mass

Pelvic Color Doppler Ultrasound: markedly ENLARGED, EDEMATOUS OVARY (volume > 3x contralateral normal ovary) with peripherally displaced antral follicles ('string of pearls' in stroma) and pathognomonic 'WHIRLPOOL SIGN' (twisting of the vascular pedicle in cross-section)
pertinent_negatives: PRESENCE OF NORMAL DOPPLER BLOOD FLOW DOES NOT RULE OUT TORSION (venous occlusion occurs first; arterial flow can remain preserved intermittently)
content: Complete or partial rotation of the ovary and fallopian tube on its ligamentous vascular axis (infundibulopelvic and utero-ovarian ligaments), obstructing venous and lymphatic outflow followed by arterial thrombosis and hemorrhagic infarction. Statutory gynecological surgical emergency. Diagnostic Mandate: High clinical suspicion warrants emergent diagnostic laparoscopy even if ultrasound appears equivocal. Management: STAT Emergency Laparoscopy with Ovarian Detorsion (unwinding the twisted vascular pedicle); conservative detorsion and ovarian preservation is indicated REGARDLESS OF OVARY APPEARANCE (even dusky blue/black ovaries often recover endocrine and follicular function); Cystectomy is performed electively after detorsion to prevent recurrence.

red_flags: bilateral hydronephrosis / uremia from ureteral encasement (leading cause of death)
clinical_hallmarks: early stage disease is frequently asymptomatic (highlighting the critical imperative for regular screening)
cardinal early symptom: POSTCOITAL VAGINAL BLEEDING (contact spotting or fresh bleeding immediately following sexual intercourse)
intermenstrual bleeding, postmenopausal bleeding, and a persistent, malodorous, watery, blood-tinged vaginal discharge
advanced stage: dull pelvic and deep sciatic back pain radiating down leg, lower extremity unilateral edema (lymphatic/venous compression), and hematuria/fecaluria from fistula
speculum examination: visible exophytic (fungating, friable, cauliflower-like) or endophytic (ulcerative, indurated) lesion on the ectocervix that BLEEDS COPIOUSLY UPON TOUCH
etiological hallmark: Persistent infection with HIGH-RISK HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS (HPV Type 16 in > 50-60%, HPV Type 18 in 10-15%, expressing oncoproteins E6 [degrades p53] and E7 [inactivates pRb])
pertinent_negatives: normal Pap smear cytology without HPV co-testing has up to 30-40% false negative rate; biopsy of any visible suspicious lesion is MANDATORY regardless of Pap result
content: Malignant neoplasm arising from the transformation zone of the cervix, predominantly Squamous Cell Carcinoma (75-80%) or Adenocarcinoma (20-25%). Staging: FIGO Clinical/Pathological Staging (Stage I-IV). Diagnostic workup: Cervical punch biopsy, Colposcopy, Pelvic MRI, PET-CT. Treatment: Early Stage (FIGO IA-IB2): Radical Hysterectomy with Bilateral Pelvic Lymphadenectomy (Wertheim operation); Locally Advanced Stage (FIGO IB3 - IVA): Definitive Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy (CCRT: External Beam Radiotherapy + Intracavitary Brachytherapy + weekly IV Cisplatin); Primary Prevention: 9-valent HPV Vaccine (Gardasil 9) given at age 9-14 years.

clinical_hallmarks: FIGO PALM-COEIN ETIOLOGICAL CLASSIFICATION SYSTEM for Abnormal Uterine Bleeding:

Structural Causes (PALM): 1. POLYP (endometrial/cervical polyps); 2. ADENOMYOSIS (globular enlarged, uniformly tender, 'boggy' uterus); 3. LEIOMYOMA (uterine fibroids - submucosal causing heavy prolonged bleeding, intramural, subserosal); 4. MALIGNANCY and Hyperplasia (endometrial carcinoma - any postmenopausal bleeding is cancer until proven otherwise)

Non-Structural Causes (COEIN): 1. COAGULOPATHY (Von Willebrand disease in adolescents); 2. OVULATORY Dysfunction (PCOS, thyroid disorders, perimenopause); 3. ENDOMETRIAL (primary hemostatic defect); 4. IATROGENIC (IUDs, anticoagulants); 5. NOT yet classified

clinical evaluation: soaking through >= 1 sanitary pad/tampon every 1-2 hours for consecutive hours, passage of large blood clots (> 2.5 cm / quarter size), bleeding lasting > 7-8 days, or intermenstrual spotting
pertinent_negatives: pregnancy test MUST ALWAYS BE PERFORMED FIRST to exclude obstetric complications
content: Bleeding from the uterine corpus that is abnormal in frequency, regularity, duration, or volume outside of pregnancy. Diagnostic workup: Urine pregnancy test, CBC, ferritin, TSH, Transvaginal ultrasound, Saline Infusion Sonohysterography (SIS), and Pipelle Endometrial Biopsy (mandatory in women >= 45 years, or < 45 years with risk factors like obesity or chronic unopposed estrogen). Treatment: Acute Severe Bleeding: High-dose oral Tranexamic Acid (1.3 g TID) OR high-dose IV conjugated estrogens OR oral medroxyprogesterone; Chronic Long-term: Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD (Mirena - reduces blood loss by > 90%), Combined Oral Contraceptives, Tranexamic acid during menses; Surgical: Hysteroscopic polypectomy/myomectomy, Endometrial Ablation, or Hysterectomy.

topic: Infectious Vaginitis (Bacterial Vaginosis vs Trichomoniasis vs Candida)
specialty: Obstetrics & Gynecology / Primary Care / Infectious Disease
red_flags: recurrent intractable candidiasis (screen for diabetes mellitus or HIV)
bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy (increases risk of preterm labor and prom)
clinical_hallmarks: CLINICAL AND MICROSCOPIC TRIAD DIFFERENTIATION OF INFECTIOUS VAGINITIS:

1. Bacterial Vaginosis (BV - Gardnerella vaginalis & anaerobes): thin, homogeneous, off-white/gray discharge that smoothly coats vaginal walls; prominent foul 'FISHY' AMINE ODOR accentuated after intercourse; POSITIVE WHIFF TEST (fishy odor on adding 10% KOH); Vaginal pH > 4.5; Saline wet mount shows pathognomonic CLUE CELLS (vaginal squamous epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria, obscuring cell borders in > 20% of cells) and absent PMNs (Amsel criteria)

2. Trichomoniasis (Trichomonas vaginalis): profuse, thin, FROTHY, greenish-yellow, malodorous discharge; intense vulvar itching and dysuria; pathognomonic 'STRAWBERRY CERVIX' (colpitis macularis: punctate red cervical petechial hemorrhages); Vaginal pH > 4.5; Wet mount shows MOTILE FLAGELLATED OVAL PROTOZOA and sheets of neutrophils

3. Candida Vulvovaginitis (Candida albicans): thick, white, curdy, 'COTTAGE CHEESE-LIKE' adherent vaginal discharge; severe, intense vulvar pruritus, burning, and marked vulvar erythema and edema; NORMAL Vaginal pH (< 4.5); Negative Whiff test; 10% KOH prep reveals budding yeast and PSEUDOHYPHAE
pertinent_negatives: normal vaginal pH (< 4.5) points directly to Candida (rules out BV and Trichomonas)
content: Most common gynecological diagnosis in primary care. Differential Diagnostic Workup: Vaginal pH paper (litmus), Whiff test, saline wet mount, 10% KOH preparation. Treatment: 1. Bacterial Vaginosis: Oral Metronidazole (500 mg BID for 7 days) OR topical 0.75% Metronidazole gel intravaginally daily for 5 days; 2. Trichomoniasis: Oral Metronidazole (500 mg BID for 7 days - MANDATORY concurrent treatment of male sexual partner, sexual abstinence until treatment completed); 3. Candida: Single-dose Oral Fluconazole (150 mg single dose) or topical Clotrimazole/Miconazole cream.

topic: Pelvic Organ Prolapse (Cystocele, Rectocele & Uterine Procidentia)
red_flags: complete procidentia with decubitus ulceration and bleeding
clinical_hallmarks: sensation of a vaginal bulge, lump, protrusion, or 'something falling out of the vagina'
chronic pelvic heaviness, dragging sensation, and lower back pressure that worsens towards the end of the day or after prolonged standing, and relieves upon lying down

Cystocele (Anterior compartment): urinary hesitancy, slow stream, incomplete emptying, and recurrent cystitis; stress urinary incontinence (or 'masked' incontinence unmasked upon reduction of prolapse)

Rectocele (Posterior compartment): constipation, difficult defecation, and pathognomonic 'SPLINTING' (patient must use fingers to press against the posterior vaginal wall or perineum to successfully evacuate stool)
Uterine Procidentia: complete herniation and exteriorization of the entire uterus outside the introitus, showing dry, keratinized, ulcerated vaginal epithelium (decubitus ulcers)
quantified objectively using the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) staging system (Stages 0 to IV)
pertinent_negatives: prolapse reduces or softens in supine non-straining position
content: Herniation of pelvic organs through the vaginal canal resulting from relaxation and damage to the levator ani muscle complex, endopelvic fascia, and uterosacral/cardinal ligament supports. Risk factors: multiparity, vaginal deliveries, operative deliveries (forceps), obesity, chronic coughing/straining, menopause (loss of estrogen). Management: Mild/asymptomatic: Pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel exercises) and lifestyle modifications; Symptomatic Moderate-Severe: 1. Non-surgical: Vaginal Pessary (ring, Gellhorn, shelf pessary fitted individually) + topical vaginal estrogen cream for mucosal health; 2. Surgical: Anterior/posterior colporrhaphy, Sacrocolpopexy (gold standard for apical prolapse), Sacrospinous ligament fixation, or Colpocleisis (obliterative surgery for frail elderly).

clinical_hallmarks: ORAL MUCOSAL LESIONS ARE THE INITIAL PRESENTATION in > 70-80% of patients, preceding cutaneous blisters by months: painful, persistent, non-healing erosions and shallow ulcers on buccal mucosa, palate, and gingiva that make eating agonizing
cutaneous lesions: FLACCID, THIN-WALLED, FRAGILE BLISTERS AND BULLAE arising on normal or erythematous skin (characteristically on scalp, face, chest, and intertriginous folds)
blisters rupture extremely easily, leaving extensive, painful, weeping, raw, denuded areas with crusting and slow healing
PATHOGNOMONIC PHYSICAL SIGN: POSITIVE NIKOLSKY'S SIGN (firm lateral sliding pressure of a finger on normal-appearing perilesional skin causes immediate dislodgement or sloughing of the epidermis)
Asboe-Hansen sign (bulla spread sign): gentle downward pressure on an intact blister causes lateral extension of the fluid wave into adjacent unblistered skin
direct immunofluorescence (pathognomonic): intercellular 'FISHNET' or 'CHICKEN-WIRE' pattern of IgG and C3 deposition throughout the squamous epidermis
pertinent_negatives: flaccid blisters and positive Nikolsky distinguish pemphigus from tense blisters and negative Nikolsky of bullous pemphigoid
content: Potentially fatal autoimmune blistering disease caused by IgG autoantibodies targeting Desmoglein-3 (mucosal-predominant) and Desmoglein-1 (mucocutaneous), causing intraepidermal acantholysis (loss of intercellular keratinocyte adhesion). Histopathology shows suprabasal intraepidermal split with a retained 'row of tombstones' basal layer. Treatment: 1. STAT High-dose Systemic Corticosteroids (Oral Prednisone 1.0-1.5 mg/kg/day); 2. FIRST-LINE BIOLOGIC: Rituximab (anti-CD20: two 1000 mg IV infusions on days 1 and 15 - induces complete remission in > 85-90% and reduces steroid requirements); 3. Adjuvant immunosuppressants (Mycophenolate Mofetil, Azathioprine); 4. Intensive burn-like barrier wound care.

topic: Bullous Pemphigoid (BP180 & BP230 - Negative Nikolsky Sign)
red_flags: iatrogenic steroid complications in frail elderly
clinical_hallmarks: predominantly affects ELDERLY PATIENTS (> 70-80 years of age), frequently with underlying neurological comorbidities (Parkinson's, dementia, prior stroke)
prodromal phase lasting weeks to months: intense, severe, generalized PRURITUS with urticarial, eczematous, or excoriated plaques
bullous phase: widespread eruption of LARGE, TENSE, FIRM, DOME-SHAPED BLISTERS AND BULLAE (1-5 cm) filled with clear or serosanguinous fluid, arising on either normal or erythematous urticarial bases
predilection for flexor aspects of limbs (forearms, thighs, lower abdomen, axillae, groins)
blisters DO NOT RUPTURE EASILY and can remain intact for days
NEGATIVE NIKOLSKY'S SIGN (firm lateral sliding pressure DOES NOT shear the epidermis)
oral mucosal involvement is RARE (< 10-20%) and mild (sharp contrast to pemphigus vulgaris)

histopathology and immunofluorescence: SUBEPIDERMAL BLISTER with eosinophil-rich infiltrate; Direct Immunofluorescence shows CONTINUOUS, SMOOTH, LINEAR BAND OF IgG AND C3 along the dermo-epidermal junction
pertinent_negatives: tense bullae, lack of oral ulcers, and negative Nikolsky distinguish BP from Pemphigus Vulgaris
content: Most common autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease of the elderly, caused by IgG autoantibodies targeting hemidesmosomal proteins at the dermal-epidermal junction: BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230. Diagnostic workup: Perilesional skin biopsy for DIF, serum ELISA for anti-BP180/BP230. Treatment: 1. Extensive disease: High-potency Topical Corticosteroid ointment (Clobetasol propionate 0.05% cream 30-40 g daily applied to whole body - preferred over systemic steroids due to significantly lower mortality in frail elderly); 2. Systemic Corticosteroids (Prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day); 3. Anti-inflammatory antibiotics: oral Doxycycline (100 mg BID) + Nicotinamide; 4. Methotrexate or Rituximab for refractory cases.

topic: Malignant Melanoma (ABCDE Diagnostic Criteria & Breslow Depth)
red_flags: ulceration / spontaneous bleeding of pigmented lesion
clinical_hallmarks: the classic 'ABCDE' CLINICAL SCREENING CRITERIA FOR MELANOMA:
A - ASYMMETRY: one half of the cutaneous pigmented lesion does not match the other half
B - BORDER: irregular, notched, scalloped, ragged, or poorly defined/blurred borders
C - COLOR: variegated, uneven pigmentation with multiple colors within the same lesion (shades of tan, brown, jet black, interspersed with red, white, or slate-blue depigmented areas)
D - DIAMETER: larger than 6 mm (roughly the size of a pencil eraser, though melanomas can be smaller)
E - EVOLVING: any documented change in size, shape, color, surface contour, or new symptoms (itching, bleeding, tenderness)
THE 'UGLY DUCKLING' SIGN: a solitary nevus that looks distinctly different and out of character compared to all other surrounding nevi in that individual
Dermoscopy hallmarks: atypical pigment network, irregular brown/black globules, asymmetric pigmentation, and blue-white veil
pertinent_negatives: EXCISIONAL BIOPSY WITH 1-3 MM MARGINS IS MANDATORY; SHAVE BIOPSY IS STRONGLY DISCOURAGED because it compromises accurate Breslow depth measurement
content: Highly aggressive malignancy arising from epidermal melanocytes, strongly correlated with intermittent intense UV-radiation blistering sun exposure and somatic driver mutations (BRAF V600E in 50%, NRAS, KIT). Single Most Important Histopathological Prognostic Factor: BRESLOW THICKNESS (measured in millimeters from the granular layer to the deepest tumor cell). Management Protocol: 1. Complete full-thickness excisional biopsy with 1-3 mm margins; 2. Wide Local Excision (WLE) with surgical margins based on Breslow thickness (Melanoma in situ: 5 mm margin; <= 1.0 mm depth: 1 cm margin; > 1.0-2.0 mm depth: 1-2 cm margin; > 2.0 mm depth: 2 cm margin); 3. Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) for Breslow depth > 0.8 mm or ulcerated lesions; 4. Adjuvant/Metastatic Therapy: Targeted BRAF/MEK inhibitors (Dabrafenib + Trametinib for BRAF-mutant) OR Dual Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors (Nivolumab + Ipilimumab).

topic: Basal Cell Carcinoma (Nodular BCC & Pearly Telangiectatic Papule)
red_flags: local tissue destruction eroding into cartilage/bone ('rodent ulcer')
clinical_hallmarks: THE MOST COMMON CANCER IN HUMANS worldwide, overwhelmingly arising on chronic sun-exposed areas of the head and neck (> 80%, characteristically nose, eyelids, ears, cheeks)
Nodular BCC (most frequent subtype 60-70%): a smooth, translucent, wax-like, 'PEARLY' OR 'OPALESCENT' PAPULE OR NODULE
prominent, delicate, arborizing branching TELANGIECTASIAS (small dilated blood vessels) coursing distinctly across the lesion surface
central depression with a rolled, raised, translucent 'RODENT' BORDER ('rolled pearly borders')
frequent history of repeated bleeding, ulceration, crusting, and partial temporary healing ('the scab that bleeds when dried with towel and never fully heals')
pigmented BCC variant: brown or black speckled melanin mimicking melanoma
extremely low metastatic potential (< 0.1%), but highly invasive locally with capacity to destructively infiltrate skin, soft tissue, cartilage, and cranial bones
pertinent_negatives: pearly translucent border with arborizing vessels distinguishes BCC from flaky keratotic squamous cell carcinoma
content: Malignant cutaneous neoplasm arising from basal cells of the follicular epithelium and interfollicular epidermis, driven by constitutive activation of the Hedgehog signaling pathway (PTCH1 loss-of-function mutation in Gorlin syndrome and sporadic cases). Diagnostic workup: Punch or shave skin biopsy showing peripheral palisading of basaloid cells with clefting artifact. Treatment: 1.
