Low-risk / Non-facial: Standard surgical excision with 4 mm margins, or electrodessication and curettage (ED&C); 2. High-Risk / Cosmetically Sensitive / Facial (H-zone: nose, eyelids, lips, ears): MOHS MICROGRAPHIC SURGERY (gold standard, achieving 99% cure rate with maximum tissue conservation); 3. Advanced unresectable/metastatic: Oral Hedgehog pathway inhibitors (Vismodegib, Sonidegib) or Cemiplimab (anti-PD-1).

topic: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (Steamy Cornea & Mid-Dilated Pupil)
red_flags: permanent optic nerve ischemia and irreversible blindness within hours
severe headache and vomiting misdiagnosed as acute migraine or intracranial bleed
clinical_hallmarks: sudden onset of excruciating, agonizing, unilateral ocular and peri-orbital pain radiating to ipsilateral forehead and temple
severe visual impairment: profound blurriness and PATHOGNOMONIC COLORED HALOS AROUND LIGHTS (rainbow rings around point sources of light due to corneal epithelial edema)
PROFOUND SYSTEMIC SYMPTOMS: severe nausea, retching, vomiting, and diaphoresis (frequently leading to misdiagnosis as an acute abdominal emergency)
triggered by pupillary dilation in dim lighting (movie theaters, evening dusk) or anticholinergic / sympathomimetic medications

pathognomonic physical examination signs: 1. Conjunctival and ciliary injection ('ciliary flush'); 2. 'STEAMY' OR 'HAZY' CLOUDY CORNEA with loss of normal corneal luster; 3. MID-DILATED, VERTICALLY OVAL, SLUGGISH OR FIXED PUPIL (unresponsive to light); 4. Shallow anterior chamber depth; 5. Palpation of globe: 'ROCK-HARD' / STONY HARD EYEBALL compared to the normal contralateral eye
tonometry hallmark: MASSIVELY ELEVATED INTRAOCULAR PRESSURE (IOP typically 50 to 80 mmHg, normal 10-21 mmHg)
pertinent_negatives: pupil is mid-dilated and unreactive (in sharp contrast to small constricted pupil of acute anterior uveitis)
content: Ophthalmic emergency resulting from pupillary block preventing aqueous humor from draining through the trabecular meshwork, causing acute rise in posterior chamber pressure and anterior displacement of peripheral iris. Statutory emergency requiring immediate IOP reduction to prevent ischemic optic neuropathy. Protocol: 1. STAT Medical IOP Reduction (The Emergency Cocktail): Topical Beta-blocker (Timolol 0.5% 1 drop) + Topical Alpha-2 agonist (Apraclonidine 1% 1 drop) + IV Acetazolamide (500 mg IV STAT) + IV Mannitol (1-2 g/kg of 20% solution over 30 min for IOP > 50 mmHg); 2. Topical Pilocarpine 2% (parasympathomimetic miotic) instilled only when IOP drops < 40 mmHg (high IOP renders iris sphincter ischemic and unresponsive); 3. DEFINITIVE BILATERAL CURE: Nd:YAG Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) to BOTH eyes once cornea clears (prophylactic LPI to unaffected eye is mandatory due to high contralateral attack risk).

topic: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO - Cherry-Red Spot)
red_flags: irreversible retinal ganglion cell necrosis within 90-100 minutes of ischemia
concurrent Giant Cell Arteritis (urgent high-dose steroids needed)
clinical_hallmarks: THE 'OCULAR STROKE': sudden, abrupt, catastrophic, painless, profound monocular visual loss (acuity typically drops to 'counting fingers' or 'light perception')
occurs instantaneously over seconds, often noticed immediately upon waking up
RAPID TESTING: Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil) in affected eye

DILATED FUNDOSCOPY (PATHOGNOMONIC HALLMARK): 1. Diffuse, pale, ground-glass, opaque, milky-white retina (due to acute intracellular edema of ischemic inner retinal layers); 2. PROMINENT 'CHERRY-RED SPOT' AT THE FOVEA (the fovea centralis is thinned with no inner retinal layers, allowing the underlying richly vascular, normal choroid to shine through brightly); 3. Attenuation and narrowing of retinal arterioles with segmented, fragmented blood column ('boxcarring' / cattle-trucking of blood flow)
in 15-20% of patients with a patent cilioretinal artery (arising from ciliary circulation), central foveal island of vision is spared
pertinent_negatives: pain is completely absent (presence of pain suggests optic neuritis or orbital disease)
content: Acute thrombotic or embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery (end-artery of ophthalmic artery supplying inner two-thirds of retina), predominantly originating from ipsilateral carotid artery atheroma or cardiac emboli (or Giant Cell Arteritis in elderly > 50 years). Considered an ischemic stroke equivalent. Urgent Empirical Measures (if presenting < 4-6 hours): 1. Immediate Ocular Massage (firm pressure for 10-15s followed by sudden release using three-mirror contact lens or thumb to dislodge embolus downstream); 2. Anterior Chamber Paracentesis to acutely drop IOP; 3. Sublingual Isosorbide dinitrate or paper-bag breathing (induces hypercapnic vasodilation); 4. Rule out GCA (STAT ESR and CRP; high-dose pulse steroids if GCA suspected); 5. Comprehensive stroke evaluation (Carotid duplex, Echocardiogram, telemetry, Brain MRI/DWI).

topic: Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (Flashes, Floaters & Falling Curtain)
red_flags: macula-off detachment (severe permanent loss of central visual acuity if not repaired rapidly)
clinical_hallmarks: THE CLASSIC PREMONITORY SEQUENCE: 1. Sudden shower of new black 'FLOATERS' (spots, cobwebs, or ring-like shadows floating across visual field, representing vitreous hemorrhage or condensations); 2. PHOTOPsia (recurrent, brief, bright flashes of light in peripheral vision, characteristically in the dark, provoked by eye movement due to vitreoretinal traction)
THE PROGRESSIVE DEFECT: A dark, dense, opaque 'CURTAIN', 'SHADOW', OR 'VEIL' falling across or advancing from the periphery of the visual field into central vision
visual acuity remains 20/20 if the macula is still attached ('macula-on'), but drops catastrophically to legal blindness if detachment advances across the fovea ('macula-off')
Slit-lamp biomicroscopy: positive SHAFER'S SIGN ('TOBACCO DUST' - tiny brownish clumps of pigmented epithelial cells suspended in the anterior vitreous)

Dilated Fundoscopy: elevated, corrugated, translucent, folded, greyish-white billowing retinal sheet with undulating movement on ocular motion, and an identifiable full-thickness retinal tear or horseshoe break
pertinent_negatives: no eye pain or external redness (painless internal neurosensory detachment)
content: Separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) caused by liquefied vitreous passing through a full-thickness retinal tear/break into the subretinal space. Major risk factors: high myopia (nearsightedness), cataract surgery, lattice degeneration, ocular trauma. Time-sensitive Ophthalmic Emergency: A 'Macula-On' retinal detachment is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY that MUST BE REPAIRED EXPEDITIOUSLY (within 24 hours) to preserve central vision. Surgical Techniques: 1. Pneumatic Retinopexy (intravitreal gas bubble injection + cryopexy/laser for superior single tears); 2. Scleral Buckling (external silicone exoplant indenting sclera); 3. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) with endolaser and long-acting gas/silicone oil tamponade.

clinical_hallmarks: strongest risk factor: EXTENDED-WEAR SOFT CONTACT LENSES (sleeping in contacts, poor lens hygiene, cleaning lenses with tap water)
severe, intense, foreign-body pain, copious purulent/mucopurulent discharge, extreme photophobia, and rapid visual drop
Slit-lamp examination: circumcorneal ciliary injection ('red eye') and a DENSE, ROUND, FOCAL WHITE/YELLOWISH CORNEAL INFILTRATE (stromal opacity) with overlying epithelial defect
fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals an intensely bright green epithelial ulceration overlying the stromal infiltrate
Pseudomonas aeruginosa keratitis: rapid, fulminant liquefactive necrosis of corneal stroma ('corneal melting') with thick, soupy, greenish-yellow mucopurulent discharge within 24-48 hours
PATHOGNOMONIC INTRAOCULAR SIGN: HYPOPYON (a horizontal level of creamy white purulent exudate / sterile neutrophils settled at the bottom of the anterior chamber)
pertinent_negatives: TOPICAL CORTICOSTEROID DROPS ARE STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in acute undiagnosed corneal ulcer (potentiates fungal/bacterial replication and causes rapid corneal perforation)
content: Invasive microbial infection of the corneal stroma with epithelial disruption. Common organisms: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (contact lenses), Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae. Statutory corneal emergency. Protocol: 1. STAT Emergency Corneal Scrapings for Gram stain, Giemsa, and bacterial/fungal culture on blood, chocolate, and Sabouraud agar; 2. EMPIRIC INTENSIVE ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN: Fortified Topicals (Fortified Tobramycin 1.4% or Amikacin + Fortified Cefazolin 5% or Vancomycin 5%) OR monotherapy with 4th-generation Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin 0.5% or Gatifloxacin drops) INSTILLED EVERY 30-60 MINUTES AROUND THE CLOCK; 3. Cycloplegic drops (Homatropine 5%) for ciliary spasm pain; 4. Emergent therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty (corneal transplant) for impending perforation.

specialty: ENT / Pediatrics / Emergency Medicine / Critical Care
red_flags: cardiac arrest provoked by oral tongue blade examination
clinical_hallmarks: rapidly progressive, life-threatening inflammation of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures, historically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib - now also Strep pneumoniae, Group A Strep in vaccinated era)

CARDINAL '4 Ds' SYMPTOM COMPLEX: 1. DROOLING (inability to swallow saliva due to agonizing throat pain); 2. DYSPHAGIA (severe difficulty swallowing); 3. DYSPHONIA (muffled, whispery 'hot-potato' voice); 4. DISTRESS (respiratory agitation and air hunger)

PATHOGNOMONIC POSTURE: THE 'TRIPOD POSITION' (child sits upright, leaning forward, supported by outstretched hands on knees, with neck hyperextended and chin thrust forward ['sniffing dog position'] to maximize airway diameter)
inspiratory stridor, tachypnea, and supraclavicular / intercostal retractions
soft tissue lateral neck radiograph: PATHOGNOMONIC 'THUMBPRINT SIGN' (thick, rounded, swollen epiglottis projecting into hypopharynx like an adult thumb, with obliteration of the vallecula)
pertinent_negatives: DO NOT EXAMINE PHARYNX WITH TONGUE BLADE OR AGITATE CHILD (crying, agitation, or tongue depression can trigger fatal acute reflex laryngospasm and immediate complete airway arrest)
content: Life-threatening pediatric and adult supraglottic airway emergency. Absolute Clinical Rule: Keep child calm in parent's arms, provide humidified blow-by oxygen, NO IV lines, NO oral exam until in Operating Room. STAT Protocol: 1. STAT Transfer to Operating Room with Senior Anesthesiologist and ENT Surgeon present; 2. Endotracheal Intubation under inhalation general anesthesia with one size smaller ETT; direct laryngoscopy reveals swollen, edematous, fiery 'CHERRY-RED EPIGLOTTIS'; 3. Emergent surgical cricothyroidotomy equipment open on stand; 4. IV Antibiotics: IV Ceftriaxone (50-100 mg/kg/day) + Vancomycin for 7-10 days; 5. Extubation after 48-72 hours when leak test positive.

red_flags: intracranial extension: Sigmoid Sinus Thrombosis, epidural abscess, meningitis
Bezold's abscess (pus tracking down into sternocleidomastoid sheath)
clinical_hallmarks: develops as a direct complication of untreated or inadequately treated ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA (AOM), most commonly in children < 2 years
persistent or recrudescent high fever, otalgia, irritability, and creamy profuse purulent otorrhea

CARDINAL PHYSICAL SIGNS: 1. POSTAURICULAR ERYTHEMA, TENDER EDEMA, AND FLUCTUATION directly overlying the mastoid process; 2. Loss of the normal postauricular sulcus; 3. FORWARD AND DOWNWARD PROTRUSION / DISPLACEMENT OF THE AURICLE (the ear pinna is visibly pushed forward and outward away from head)
otoscopy: fiery red, bulging, opaque, or perforated tympanic membrane, accompanied by sagging / drooping of the posterosuperior external auditory canal wall
High-Resolution CT (HRCT) of temporal bone (gold standard): clouding/opacification of mastoid air cells with PATHOGNOMONIC LOSS OF MASTOID BONY SEPTA (coalescent mastoiditis)
pertinent_negatives: bony septal breakdown on CT distinguishes true coalescent mastoiditis from simple serous opacification of mastoid in AOM
content: Suppurative infection of the mastoid air cells with osteitis and progressive resorption of the bony trabeculae (coalescence). Predominant pathogens: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Diagnostic workup: HRCT temporal bone with contrast, middle ear fluid culture. Protocol: 1. Hospital admission and STAT IV Antibiotics: IV Ceftriaxone (50-100 mg/kg/day) + Vancomycin; 2. STAT Myringotomy / Tympanocentesis (+/- tympanostomy tube placement) to decompress the middle ear and obtain culture; 3. STAT Cortical Mastoidectomy (Schwartze operation) indicated if no improvement within 24-48 hours, or if subperiosteal abscess, intracranial complications, or coalescent bone erosion are present.

topic: Acute Compartment Syndrome (The 5 Ps & Emergency Fasciotomy)
specialty: Orthopedic Surgery / Trauma Surgery / Emergency Medicine
keywords: the 5 ps pain out of proportion
red_flags: myonecrosis and irreversible nerve damage after 6 hours
clinical_hallmarks: history of high-energy tibial shaft fracture, crush injury, tight circumferential cast/bandage, or revascularization
EARLIEST AND MOST RELIABLE CLINICAL HALLMARK: SEVERE, AGONIZING PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION TO INJURY, recalcitrant to high-dose opioids

PATHOGNOMONIC PHYSICAL EXAMINATION SIGN: EXCRUCIATING PAIN ELICITED BY PASSIVE STRETCH OF THE MUSCLES traversing the affected compartment (e.g. passive toe extension for deep posterior compartment of calf)
palpation: TENSE, WOODEN, BOARD-LIKE, SHINY SWELLING of the muscular compartment

THE TRADITIONAL '5 Ps': 1. Pain (early, reliable); 2. Paresthesias (early nerve ischemia); 3. Pallor; 4. Paralysis (late, indicates muscle death); 5. Pulselessness (TERMINAL, EXTREMELY LATE SIGN - peripheral pulse is typically PRESERVED because intracompartmental pressure rarely exceeds systolic arterial pressure)
intracompartmental pressure manometry: absolute pressure > 30 mmHg, OR DELTA PRESSURE (Diastolic BP minus Compartment Pressure) <= 30 mmHg confirms diagnosis
pertinent_negatives: PULSELESSNESS IS A TERMINAL SIGN, NOT A SENSITIVE SCREENING CRITERION; presence of a distal pulse DOES NOT rule out compartment syndrome
content: Life-threatening surgical emergency where increased tissue pressure within an enclosed non-distensible osteofascial compartment exceeds capillary perfusion pressure (approx 30 mmHg), causing microvascular occlusion, tissue hypoxia, and muscle/nerve necrosis. Immediate Surgical Protocol: 1. STAT REMOVAL OF ALL CIRCUMFERENTIAL CASTS, BANDAGES, OR DRESSINGS DOWN TO SKIN (reduces pressure by 50-80%); 2. Maintain limb at heart level (DO NOT ELEVATE, as elevation decreases arterial perfusion pressure; DO NOT DEPEND); 3. STAT EMERGENCY FASCIOTOMY: Urgent full-length dual-incision four-compartment fasciotomy for leg (anterolateral and posteromedial incisions releasing anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, and deep posterior compartments); 4. Re-look at 48 hours and delayed closure or skin grafting.

topic: Fat Embolism Syndrome (Gurd's Criteria & Petechial Rash)
specialty: Orthopedic Surgery / Critical Care / Trauma Surgery
clinical_hallmarks: develops typically 24 to 72 hours following blunt trauma with CLOSED LONG BONE FRACTURES (femur, tibia) or pelvic fractures, or during reamed intramedullary nailing

CLASSIC DIAGNOSTIC TRIAD: 1. Respiratory distress (dyspnea, tachypnea, profound refractory hypoxemia); 2. Neurological dysfunction (acute confusion, agitation, drowsiness, seizures, coma); 3. PATHOGNOMONIC PETECHIAL RASH (in 20-50%: non-palpable, pinpoint petechiae characteristically distributed over the ANTERIOR AXILLAE, CHEST, NECK, FLANKS, AND CONJUNCTIVAE, resolving within days)

Gurd's Diagnostic Criteria (requires >= 1 major + >= 4 minor): Major: petechial rash, hypoxemia (PaO2 < 60 mmHg), CNS depression, pulmonary edema; Minor: tachycardia (HR > 110), fever > 38.5C, retinal fat emboli, fat globules in urine, sudden thrombocytopenia, unexplained drop in hematocrit
chest radiograph: bilateral, diffuse, patchy interstitial and alveolar opacities ('SNOWSTORM APPEARANCE')
pertinent_negatives: rash is absent in simple pulmonary thromboembolism
content: Multisystem microvascular occlusion and systemic inflammatory cascade caused by bone marrow fat globules and free fatty acids entering the torn venous circulation following orthopedic trauma. Treatment: 1. STRICTLY PREVENTIVE: Early, definitive, stable surgical reduction and fixation of long bone fractures within 24 hours of trauma markedly reduces incidence; 2. Supportive Critical Care: High-flow oxygen and early lung-protective mechanical ventilation with PEEP for ARDS; Maintenance of intravascular volume; Systemic corticosteroids (Methylprednisolone) may reduce hypoxemia when given early in high-risk polytrauma.

red_flags: suppurative joint decompression / septic arthritis in infants
chronic osteomyelitis with sinus tract and squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer)
clinical_hallmarks: Acute Hematogenous Osteomyelitis: overwhelmingly affects CHILDREN (< 10 years, male:female 2:1), characteristically localizing to the METAPHYSIS OF RAPIDLY GROWING LONG BONES (distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal humerus)
abrupt onset of high fever, chills, irritability, and REFUSAL TO BEAR WEIGHT OR MOVE THE AFFECTED LIMB (pseudoparalysis of childhood)
EXQUISITE, WELL-LOCALIZED POINT BONE TENDERNESS directly over the metaphysis upon gentle palpation, accompanied by local warmth and soft-tissue edema
Brodie's Abscess: subacute/chronic form presenting as a localized, round or oval radiolucent abscess cavity surrounded by a dense, sclerotic bone margin

late plain radiograph signs (lag behind clinical symptoms by 10-14 days): periosteal reaction, lytic bone destruction, SEQUESTRUM (island of dead, devitalized bone separated from living bone), and INVOLUCRUM (shell of new periosteal bone enclosing dead bone)
MRI of bone (gold standard): bone marrow edema within 24-48 hours
predominant pathogen: STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS (> 80-90% of cases, including MRSA)
pertinent_negatives: early normal plain radiograph DOES NOT rule out acute osteomyelitis; MRI or bone scan is mandatory
content: Suppurative bacterial infection and inflammation of bone and marrow cavity. Diagnostic workup: Blood cultures (positive in 50%), bone aspirate / biopsy for culture, CBC, ESR, CRP, and contrast MRI. Treatment: 1. Empiric IV Antibiotic Therapy: IV Cefazolin or IV Flucloxacillin (or IV Vancomycin / Daptomycin for suspected MRSA) initiated for 2 weeks followed by high-dose oral antibiotics for total 4-6 weeks; 2. Surgical Indications: Subperiosteal abscess, cortical bone perforation, lack of clinical/CRP improvement within 48-72 hours of targeted antibiotics, or chronic sequestrum (requires surgical debridement and sequestrectomy).

topic: Avascular Necrosis of Femoral Head (Crescent Sign & Ficat Staging)
red_flags: subchondral cortical collapse and secondary severe osteoarthritis
clinical_hallmarks: history of high-risk etiologies: prolonged high-dose SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROID THERAPY (most common non-traumatic cause), chronic ALCOHOL ABUSE (> 400 mL/week), sickle cell disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, or prior femoral neck fracture
insidious, progressive, deep groin or anterior thigh pain, aggravated by weight-bearing and relieved by rest
physical examination: restricted and painful internal rotation and abduction of the hip
radiographic hallmarks (Ficat and Arlet Staging):
Stage I: Normal plain radiograph, but MRI reveals diagnostic focal bone marrow edema with a serpentine low-signal band on T1-weighted images ('double-line sign' on T2)
Stage II: Radiographic evidence of sclerosis and osteopenia with preserved spherical femoral head contour
Stage III: PATHOGNOMONIC 'CRESCENT SIGN' (subchondral radiolucent linear fracture line) indicating impending or early structural bone collapse
Stage IV: Flattening, collapse of the femoral head, and joint space narrowing with secondary osteoarthritis
pertinent_negatives: plain radiograph can be completely normal in early disease (Stage I), requiring MRI for definitive early detection
content: Ischemic death of cellular elements of trabecular bone and marrow of the femoral head, caused by compromised microvascular supply from the medial femoral circumflex artery. Diagnostic gold standard: MRI pelvis (sensitivity > 99%). Treatment: 1. Pre-collapse (Stages I-II): Joint-preserving procedures: Core Decompression +/- autologous bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) to reduce intraosseous pressure and promote revascularization; 2. Post-collapse (Stages III-IV): Total Hip Arthroplasty (THA - gold standard, provides definitive pain relief and functional restoration).

topic: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE & Klein's Line)
red_flags: avascular necrosis of femoral head (catastrophic complication of forcible reduction)
clinical_hallmarks: predominantly affects ADOLESCENT CHILDREN during pubertal growth spurt (boys age 12-16, girls age 10-14), characteristically in OBESE or overweight adolescents
INSIDIOUS, DULL, ACHING REFERRED KNEE OR DISTAL THIGH PAIN (in up to 30-50% the hip pain is completely absent, leading to frequent diagnostic delays or missed diagnosis)
limp with antalgic or Trendelenburg gait; foot on affected side is held in external rotation

PATHOGNOMONIC PHYSICAL EXAMINATION SIGN: OBLIGATE EXTERNAL ROTATION DURING PASSIVE HIP FLEXION (as the hip is flexed upward to 90 degrees, the thigh spontaneously and involuntarily externally rotates and abducts)
plain radiographs (AP and Frog-leg lateral pelvis): posterior and inferior displacement of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck ('ice cream slipping off the cone')

PATHOGNOMONIC RADIOGRAPHIC SIGN: ABNORMAL KLEIN'S LINE (a line drawn along the superior border of the femoral neck normally intersects the lateral aspect of the femoral epiphysis; in SCFE, the line FAILS TO INTERSECT the slipped epiphysis / Trethowan sign)
pertinent_negatives: DO NOT ATTEMPT MANIPULATIVE CLOSED REDUCTION (manipulation kinks fragile retinacular blood vessels and drastically increases AVN risk from < 5% to > 50%)
content: Most common hip disorder of adolescents, characterized by displacement of the femoral neck anteriorly and superiorly through the hypertrophic zone of the physeal growth plate while the capital epiphysis remains in the acetabulum. Classified as stable (can bear weight) or unstable (unable to bear weight even with crutches). Statutory orthopedic semi-emergency: Patient MUST BE KEPT STRICTLY NON-WEIGHT-BEARING ON CRUTCHES / WHEELCHAIR IMMEDIATELY upon suspicion. Definitive Treatment: STAT In Situ Single Percutaneous Cannulated Screw Fixation (across the physis into the center of the epiphysis) to arrest slip progression; Prophylactic pinning of contralateral normal hip considered for high-risk endocrine disorders.

specialty: Emergency Medicine / Clinical Toxicology / Critical Care
red_flags: bronchorrhea and bronchospasm with acute asphyxiation
respiratory arrest from central depression and diaphragmatic weakness
clinical_hallmarks: history of ingestion (suicidal), dermal absorption, or inhalation of agricultural insecticides (Chlorpyrifos, Malathion, Diazinon)
characteristic pungent 'GARLIC-LIKE' OR CHEMICAL ODOR to breath and vomitus
FULL CHOLINERGIC TOXIDROME (The 'DUMBELS' Mnemonic):

1. D - Diarrhea; 2. U - Urination; 3. M - Miosis (pathognomonic PINPOINT, CONSTRICTED PUPILS < 1-2 mm); 4. B - BRONCHORRHEA AND BRONCHOSPASM (massive flooding of bronchial tree with copious watery secretions and wheezing - THE PRIMARY CAUSE OF DEATH); 5. E - Emesis; 6. L - Lacrimation (copious tearing); 7. S - Salivation (frothing at mouth) and profound Diaphoresis (drenching sweats)
Nicotinic signs: generalized muscle fasciculations, tremors, muscle weakness, and diaphragmatic paralysis
CNS signs: confusion, seizures, and coma
laboratory hallmark: MARKED DEPRESSION OF SERUM BUTYRYLCHOLINESTERASE (pseudocholinesterase) AND RED BLOOD CELL ACETYLCHOLINESTERASE (< 20-50% normal)
pertinent_negatives: DRY LUNGS, NOT PUPIL SIZE, IS THE PRIMARY ENDPOINT FOR ATROPINIZATION
content: Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase enzyme via phosphorylation of active site serine residue, leading to toxic accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses. Life-Saving Protocol: 1. PPE for medical staff; STAT Decontamination (remove all clothing, soap/water bath); 2. STAT ATROPINE TITRATION: Atropine (2 to 5 mg IV bolus, DOUBLING THE DOSE EVERY 3-5 MINUTES: 2mg, 4mg, 8mg, 16mg... until full 'ATROPINIZATION' is achieved: Clear chest on auscultation [dry lungs], HR > 80 bpm, Systolic BP > 90, dry axillae); 3. STAT Oxime: Pralidoxime (2-PAM: 1-2 g IV loading dose over 30 min followed by 500 mg/hr infusion) initiated BEFORE 'aging' of enzyme occurs; 4. IV Diazepam for seizure control.

specialty: Emergency Medicine / Hyperbaric Medicine / Clinical Toxicology
red_flags: delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae (dns) weeks after recovery
clinical_hallmarks: history of exposure to enclosed combustion sources: house fires, faulty domestic gas heaters/furnaces, indoor charcoal grills, running automobile exhaust, or power generators
multiple co-occupants or pets in the same household presenting simultaneously with identical 'flu-like' symptoms
MILD-TO-MODERATE TOXICITY: dull, throbbing, bilateral frontal headache (most common early symptom), nausea, dizziness, vomiting, fatigue, visual disturbances, and confusion
SEVERE TOXICITY: syncope, seizures, chest pain (ischemia), cardiac arrhythmias, ataxia, coma, and cardiorespiratory arrest
CLASSIC BUT RARE/LATE PHYSICAL SIGN: 'CHERRY-RED' DISCOLORATION of the lips, mucosal membranes, and skin (seen in < 2-3% of living patients, predominantly a post-mortem finding)

PATHOGNOMONIC MONITORING PITFALL: STANDARD PULSE OXIMETRY (SpO2) IS FALSELY NORMAL (standard two-wavelength pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, falsely reading 99-100% despite severe cellular hypoxia)
laboratory gold standard: Venous or Arterial Blood Co-oximetry measuring CARBOXYHEMOGLOBIN (COHb: > 3-5% in non-smokers, > 10% in heavy smokers is diagnostic; severe poisoning typically > 25-40%)
pertinent_negatives: standard SpO2 reading of 100% DOES NOT rule out lethal carbon monoxide poisoning
content: CO binds to hemoglobin with an affinity 200-250 times greater than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and shifting the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve sharply to the left (Haldane effect), blocking oxygen unloading. Also inhibits mitochondrial Cytochrome c Oxidase. Treatment: 1. STAT 100% High-Flow Normobaric Oxygen via tightly fitting non-rebreather reservoir mask (reduces COHb half-life from 320 minutes on room air to 74 minutes on 100% O2); 2. HYPERBARIC OXYGEN (HBO: 100% O2 at 2.5-3.0 atmospheres reduces COHb half-life to 20 minutes and prevents Delayed Neuropsychiatric Sequelae); HBO Indications: COHb > 25% (> 15% in pregnancy), loss of consciousness, neurological deficits, cardiac ischemia, or severe acidosis.

topic: Snakebite Envenomation (Neurotoxic vs Vasculotoxic - Polyvalent ASV)
specialty: Emergency Medicine / Clinical Toxicology / Critical Care
red_flags: acute kidney injury and renal cortical necrosis
clinical_hallmarks: history of bite by a venomous snake (The Indian 'Big Four': Russell's Viper, Saw-Scaled Viper, Common Krait, Spectacled Cobra)
presence of visible fang puncture marks, with or without localized swelling

VASCULOTOXIC / HEMOTOXIC ENVENOMATION (Russell's & Saw-scaled Viper): rapid, progressive, severe local edema and tissue necrosis; spontaneous systemic bleeding (hematuria, gingival bleeding, epistaxis, hematemesis); PATHOGNOMONIC BEDSIDE TEST: POSITIVE 20-MINUTE WHOLE BLOOD CLOTTING TEST (20WBCT: 2 mL of fresh blood placed in clean glass tube fails to clot firmly after 20 minutes, indicating venom-induced consumptive coagulopathy)

NEUROTOXIC ENVENOMATION (Common Krait & Cobra): minimal or ABSENT local signs (Krait bite can be completely painless with invisible puncture marks during sleep); progressive descending flaccid motor paralysis: EARLIEST SIGN IS BILATERAL PTOSIS (drooping eyelids), followed by diplopia, ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria, dysphagia, pooling of saliva, and RAPID RESPIRATORY ARREST within 1-6 hours
Russell's Viper adds: acute renal failure, hypopituitarism (Sheehan-like pituitary infarction)
pertinent_negatives: TOURNIQUETS, CUTTING, SUCTION, AND HERBAL PASTES ARE STRICTLY PROHIBITED (accelerate tissue necrosis and gangrene)
content: Life-threatening biological envenomation. Immediate Protocol: 1. Strict immobilization of bitten extremity in splint (DO NOT apply tourniquet or pressure immobilization for viper bites); 2. STAT INDICATIONS FOR POLYVALENT ANTI-SNAKE VENOM (ASV): systemic envenomation (abnormal 20WBCT, systemic bleeding, neurotoxicity [ptosis], shock) or severe local swelling (> 1/2 limb); 3. ASV DOSING: Initial 10 vials of lyophilized Polyvalent ASV reconstituted in 500 mL normal saline infused over 1 hour; 4. Neurotoxic rescue: Neostigmine (0.5 mg IV) + Atropine (0.6 mg IV) trial (acts as antidote for Cobra post-synaptic neurotoxin; Krait pre-synaptic toxin requires mechanical ventilation); 5. Repeat ASV based on persistent 20WBCT abnormality at 6 hours.

topic: Toxic Alcohol Ingestion (Methanol vs Ethylene Glycol - Fomepizole)
keywords: high anion gap and osmolar gap
red_flags: permanent optic atrophy and irreversible bilateral blindness (Methanol)
clinical_hallmarks: history of ingesting bootleg/illicit liquor, moonshine, windshield washer fluid (Methanol) or automotive radiator antifreeze (Ethylene Glycol)
LABORATORY CORNERSTONE: HIGH OSMOLAR GAP (> 10-15 mOsm/kg) in early stages, evolving into a SEVERE HIGH ANION GAP METABOLIC ACIDOSIS (HAGMA with bicarbonate often < 5-10 mEq/L)

METHANOL SPECIFIC HALLMARKS: 1. Visual disturbances described as 'BEING IN A SNOWSTORM' or 'looking through a white snow blizzard'; 2. Fundoscopy: marked optic disc hyperemia, edema, and subsequent optic atrophy and complete blindness (formic acid retinal toxicity); 3. Bilateral putaminal necrosis on brain CT/MRI

ETHYLENE GLYCOL SPECIFIC HALLMARKS: 1. Acute oliguric/anuric kidney injury (glycolic and oxalic acid toxicity); 2. Urinalysis under polarized light shows pathognomonic 'ENVELOPE-SHAPED' OR DUMBBELL-SHAPED CALCIUM OXALATE MONOHYDRATE CRYSTALS; 3. Urine fluoresces under Wood's lamp (due to added fluorescein dye in antifreeze)
pertinent_negatives: ethanol level can delay toxic metabolite formation; osmolar gap is highest early, while anion gap is highest late
content: Metabolized by Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH) into highly toxic organic acids (Methanol -> Formaldehyde -> Formic Acid; Ethylene Glycol -> Glycolic Acid -> Oxalic Acid). Specific Antidote Protocol: 1. INHIBIT ALCOHOL DEHYDROGENASE IMMEDIATELY: Fomepizole (15 mg/kg IV loading dose over 30 min, then 10 mg/kg q12h; has 8,000x greater affinity for ADH than ethanol) OR Oral/IV Ethanol (target blood level 100-150 mg/dL); 2. STAT Emergency Hemodialysis (clears parent alcohol and toxic acid metabolites; indicated for pH < 7.25, visual symptoms, renal failure, or level > 50 mg/dL); 3. Adjunctive cofactors: IV Folinic acid / Leucovorin (50 mg q4h for methanol) OR IV Thiamine + Pyridoxine (for ethylene glycol).

clinical_hallmarks: overwhelmingly affects PREMATURE, LOW-BIRTH-WEIGHT INFANTS (< 32 weeks gestation, < 1500g birth weight) in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU)
typically develops 1 to 3 weeks after initiation of enteral formula feeding

CARDINAL CLINICAL SIGNS: 1. Feeding intolerance with large gastric aspirates / bilious gastric residuals; 2. Rapid, progressive, tense abdominal distension with visible dilated bowel loops; 3. Abdominal wall erythema, edema, and induration; 4. Gross or occult blood in stools (hematochezia); 5. Systemic signs: temperature instability, apnea, bradycardia, lethargy, and profound hypotension
Plain Abdominal Radiographs (Modified Bell Staging):
PATHOGNOMONIC RADIOGRAPHIC HALLMARK: PNEUMATOSIS INTESTINALIS (linear or bubbly radiolucent gas collections within the subserosal or submucosal layers of the bowel wall);
PORTAL VENOUS GAS (branching radiolucent branching gas arborizing out to the periphery of the liver);
PNEUMOPERITONEUM (free intraperitoneal air under diaphragm or 'Football sign' indicating bowel perforation)
pertinent_negatives: exclusive human breast milk feeding is strongly protective against NEC
content: Acute ischemic and inflammatory mucosal necrosis of the neonatal bowel (predominantly terminal ileum and ascending colon), driven by prematurity, enteral feeding, abnormal bacterial colonization, and mucosal ischemia. Protocol: 1. Strict NPO, continuous low-intermittent nasogastric suctioning; 2. Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and correction of thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy; 3. STAT Broad-Spectrum IV Triple Antibiotics (Ampicillin + Gentamicin + Metronidazole or Meropenem + Vancomycin); 4. Serial abdominal radiographs every 6-8 hours; 5. Emergency Surgical Laparotomy with resection of necrotic bowel and enterostomy, OR bedside Primary Peritoneal Drainage (PPD) for extremely low birth weight infants (< 1000g) with perforation.

red_flags: bacterial tracheitis (toxic, high fever, copious purulent secretions)
biphasic stridor with sternal retractions at rest
clinical_hallmarks: most common cause of acute infectious upper airway obstruction in young children (age 6 months to 3 years, peak incidence in late autumn/winter)
viral etiology: overwhelmingly Human Parainfluenza Virus (Type 1 and 2 in > 75%)
prodrome of mild rhinorrhea, sore throat, and low-grade fever for 1-3 days

CARDINAL CLINICAL TRIAD: 1. HARSH, METALLIC, RESIDUAL 'BARKING COUGH' (universally likened to the barking of a seal); 2. Hoarseness / raspy dysphonia; 3. INSPIRATORY STRIDOR that is characteristically WORSE AT NIGHT and aggravated by crying or agitation
Westley Croup Clinical Score (mild <= 2, moderate 3-7, severe >= 8)
Anteroposterior (AP) soft-tissue neck radiograph: PATHOGNOMONIC 'STEEPLE SIGN' (symmetric subglottic tapering and narrowing of the upper tracheal airway shadow resembling a church steeple)
pertinent_negatives: absence of drooling and absence of toxic prostration distinguishes croup from acute epiglottitis
content: Viral inflammation producing edema of the subglottic mucosa and vocal cords within the rigid cricoid ring. Treatment Protocol: 1. SINGLE-DOSE ORAL DEXAMETHASONE (0.15 - 0.60 mg/kg orally or IM) IS RECOMMENDED FOR ALL CHILDREN WITH CROUP (even mild cases, reducing ED visits and hospitalizations); 2. Moderate-to-Severe Croup (stridor at rest or retractions): NEBULIZED RACEMIC EPINEPHRINE (0.5 mL of 2.25% solution or 5 mL of 1:1,000 L-epinephrine in saline) provides rapid subglottic mucosal vasoconstriction and stridor relief within 10-30 minutes; 3. Mandatory observation for minimum 2-4 hours post-epinephrine to monitor for rebound airway edema; 4. Humidified air/mist and keeping child calm.

clinical_hallmarks: history of initiating, titrating, or taking high-potency first-generation antipsychotics (Haloperidol, Fluphenazine) or atypical antipsychotics, OR abrupt withdrawal of dopamine agonists (Levodopa)

THE CARDINAL TETRAD: 1. HYPERTHERMIA (severe fever typically > 38.0 - 40.0C); 2. EXTREME 'LEAD-PIPE' MUSCLE RIGIDITY (generalized, uniform resistance to passive joint movement throughout range of motion); 3. AUTONOMIC INSTABILITY (profuse diaphoresis, tachycardia, labile fluctuating blood pressure, tachypnea, urinary incontinence); 4. ALTERED MENTAL STATUS (confusion, delirium, mutism, stupor, coma)
LABORATORY HALLMARK: MASSIVE ELEVATION OF SERUM CREATINE KINASE (CK typically > 1,000 - 100,000 IU/L) and leukocytosis (WBC 10,000-40,000 /mcL)
hyporeflexia or normal reflexes (fundamental contrast to hyperreflexia and clonus of Serotonin Syndrome)
pertinent_negatives: absence of hyperreflexia, ocular clonus, or shivering distinguishes NMS from Serotonin Syndrome
content: Life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to central dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the corpus striatum and hypothalamus. Immediate Protocol: 1. STAT DISCONTINUATION OF ALL ANTIPSYCHOTIC MEDICATIONS; 2. Aggressive physical cooling and IV hydration (Normal Saline 200-300 mL/hr to prevent myoglobinuric renal failure); 3. STAT SPECIFIC PHARMACOTHERAPY: Dantrolene Sodium (1-2.5 mg/kg IV push, repeated up to 10 mg/kg/day - direct skeletal muscle relaxant) PLUS Bromocriptine (2.5-5 mg orally TID - dopamine agonist) OR Amantadine; 4. IV Lorazepam for agitation and catatonic rigidity; 5. Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) for refractory NMS.

clinical_hallmarks: history of co-administration of >= 2 pro-serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAO inhibitors, Tramadol, Linezolid, MDMA/Ecstasy, Triptans, St. John's Wort) or overdose
HUNTER TOXICITY CRITERIA (patient must have taken a serotonergic agent PLUS >= 1 of the following):
1. SPONTANEOUS CLONUS (rhythmic, involuntary muscular contractions);
2. INDUCIBLE CLONUS PLUS AGITATION OR PROFUSE DIAPHORESIS;
3. OCULAR CLONUS (slow, rhythmic, involuntary horizontal oscillatory eye movements) PLUS AGITATION OR DIAPHORESIS;
4. TREMOR PLUS HYPERREFLEXIA;
5. HYPERTONIA PLUS HYPERTHERMIA (> 38C) PLUS OCULAR OR INDUCIBLE CLONUS;
prominent NEUROMUSCULAR ABNORMALITIES ARE STRIKINGLY MORE PRONOUNCED IN LOWER EXTREMITIES (brisk ankle clonus, patellar hyperreflexia, and lower limb rigidity) than upper extremities
autonomic hyperactivity: hyperactive 'rumbling' bowel sounds (borborygmi) and watery diarrhea
pertinent_negatives: hyperreflexia, clonus, and diarrhea distinguish Serotonin Syndrome from lead-pipe hyporeflexic NMS
content: Life-threatening excess intrasynaptic serotonin activating 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors. Protocol: 1. STAT CESSATION OF ALL SEROTONERGIC AGENTS; 2. IV Benzodiazepines (Lorazepam 2-4 mg IV) to control agitation and muscle hyperactivity; 3. STAT SPECIFIC 5-HT2A ANTAGONIST: Cyproheptadine (12 mg orally/NG initial dose, followed by 2 mg q2h if symptoms persist); 4. Severe Hyperthermia (> 41.1C): STAT Endotracheal Intubation, Neuromuscular Paralysis with Vecuronium (NON-DEPOLARIZING blocker - Succinylcholine strictly contraindicated), and ICU cooling.

red_flags: permanent cerebellar and neurological damage (SILENT syndrome)
cardiac arrhythmias and sinus node arrest
clinical_hallmarks: narrow therapeutic index of Lithium (normal maintenance therapeutic range: 0.6 - 1.2 mEq/L)
frequently precipitated by VOLUME DEPLETION OR DRUG INTERACTIONS that reduce renal lithium excretion (NSAIDs, Thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, dehydration, febrile illness)
MILD TOXICITY (1.5 - 2.0 mEq/L): nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, lethargy, muscle weakness, and progression from fine tremor to a PROMINENT COARSE HAND TREMOR
MODERATE TOXICITY (2.0 - 2.5 mEq/L): marked cerebellar signs (ataxia, unsteady stumbling gait, dysarthria, nystagmus), hyperreflexia, and diffuse fasciculations
SEVERE TOXICITY (> 2.5 mEq/L): delirium, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, non-convulsive status epilepticus, coma, and cardiorespiratory arrest
laboratory hallmark: SERUM LITHIUM LEVEL > 1.5 mEq/L
pertinent_negatives: activated charcoal DOES NOT bind lithium (ineffective)
content: Toxic intracellular accumulation of monovalent lithium cations replacing sodium and inhibiting cellular inositol monophosphatase. Management: 1. STAT IV Fluid Resuscitation: 0.9% Normal Saline at 200-250 mL/hr (sodium-rich hydration restores volume and promotes renal lithium excretion); 2. Whole Bowel Irrigation with PEG for sustained-release formulations; 3. DEFINITIVE ELIMINATION: STAT EMERGENCY HEMODIALYSIS (Indications: Lithium level > 4.0 mEq/L regardless of symptoms; Level > 2.5 mEq/L with severe neurological symptoms or renal failure); 4. Post-dialysis rebound monitoring (lithium slowly redistributes from intracellular stores, often requiring repeated hemodialysis).

topic: Delirium Tremens & Severe Alcohol Withdrawal (CIWA-Ar Protocol)
red_flags: fatal circulatory collapse / malignant ventricular arrhythmias
clinical_hallmarks: history of chronic, heavy, continuous alcohol dependence followed by abrupt cessation or marked reduction in drinking (e.g. hospitalized surgical or trauma patient)
TIMELINE OF ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL:
1. Minor Withdrawal (6-12 hours): fine tremor ('the shakes'), insomnia, anxiety, diaphoresis, palpitations, GI upset;
2. Withdrawal Seizures (12-48 hours): generalized tonic-clonic convulsions (typically 1-3 seizures, non-focal);
3. Alcoholic Hallucinosis (12-48 hours): visual, auditory, or tactile hallucinations (FORMICATION: sensation of insects crawling on skin) with PRESERVED CLEAR SENSORIUM;
4. DELIRIUM TREMENS (DTs - develops 48 to 96 hours post-cessation):

THE FULL DELIRIUM TREMENS SYNDROME: PROFOUND CLOUDING OF CONSCIOUSNESS (fluctuating disorientation, confusion, agitation) COMBINED WITH A MASSIVE AUTONOMIC STORM (high fever, severe tachycardia > 120 bpm, marked hypertension, profuse drenching diaphoresis, and severe coarse tremor)
pertinent_negatives: clear orientation distinguishes simple alcoholic hallucinosis from delirium tremens (where orientation is profoundly shattered)
content: Life-threatening rebound hyperexcitability of the central nervous system resulting from sudden removal of chronic GABA-A receptor facilitation and uninhibited NMDA/glutamate receptor activation. Untreated mortality is 15-20%. Emergency Protocol: 1. STAT High-Dose IV Benzodiazepines (SYMPTOM-TRIGGERED CIWA-Ar DOSING: IV Diazepam 10-20 mg IV every 10-15 minutes OR IV Lorazepam 2-4 mg until patient is calm, lightly sleeping, but easily arousable); 2. IV Thiamine (500 mg IV TID for 3-5 days) BEFORE ANY GLUCOSE to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy; 3. Aggressive fluid and electrolyte replacement (correct hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia); 4. IV Phenobarbital or Dexmedetomidine infusion for refractory DTs.

red_flags: command auditory hallucinations directing violence or self-harm
severe self-neglect and water intoxication (psychogenic polydipsia)
clinical_hallmarks: DSM-5 CRITERIA: >= 2 of the following present for significant portion of time during a 1-MONTH PERIOD (with continuous disturbance lasting >= 6 months), where AT LEAST ONE must be Delusions, Hallucinations, or Disorganized Speech:
1. DELUSIONS: fixed, false, idiosyncratic beliefs impervious to contradictory logic (persecutory, referential [news anchor is sending coded messages], or somatic);
2. HALLUCINATIONS: perception in the absence of external stimulus, overwhelmingly AUDITORY (hearing distinct voices talking to or about the patient);
SCHNEIDER'S FIRST-RANK PATHOGNOMONIC SYMPTOMS:

1. Auditory hallucinations: Voices discussing or arguing about the patient in the THIRD PERSON; Voices commenting continuously on the patient's thoughts or actions (running commentary); Thought echo (thoughts spoken aloud);
2. Delusions of Passivity and Control: feeling bodily movements, sensations, or impulses are completely controlled by an outside alien force;
3. Thought Alienation: THOUGHT WITHDRAWAL (alien agency pulling thoughts out), THOUGHT INSERTION (outside thoughts placed in mind), and THOUGHT BROADCASTING (thoughts radiating openly to others);
Negative Symptoms (The '5 As'): Affective flattening, Alogia (poverty of speech), Avolition, Anhedonia, and Asociality
pertinent_negatives: absence of prominent primary mood episode concurrent with active psychosis (distinguishes from schizoaffective disorder)
content: Chronic, disabling neuropsychiatric brain disorder with neurodevelopmental and neurochemical origins (excess mesolimbic dopamine D2 activity causing positive symptoms; mesocortical dopamine deficit causing negative symptoms). Treatment: 1. First-line: Second-Generation (Atypical) Antipsychotics (Risperidone 2-6 mg, Olanzapine 10-20 mg, Aripiprazole) have lower extrapyramidal side-effect risk; 2. Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia (failed >= 2 adequate antipsychotic trials): CLOZAPINE (the only antipsychotic proven superior for refractory illness and suicide reduction; MANDATORY weekly/monthly CBC monitoring for agranulocytosis and absolute neutrophil count [ANC]); 3. Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotics (LAIs) for non-adherence; 4. Assertive Community Treatment.

keywords: fear of impending doom heart attack
red_flags: severe agoraphobia causing complete home confinement
recurrent emergency room visits for presumed MI / coronary angiograms
clinical_hallmarks: DSM-5 CRITERIA: Recurrent UNEXPECTED PANIC ATTACKS (abrupt surge of intense fear or intense discomfort that REACHES A PEAK WITHIN MINUTES), followed by AT LEAST 1 MONTH of persistent worry about having additional attacks or their consequences ('fear of the fear')
CARDINAL SYMPTOMS OF A PANIC ATTACK (requires >= 4 of 13 symptoms):

1. Palpitations, pounding heart, or tachycardia; 2. Profuse sweating; 3. Trembling or shaking; 4. Sensation of shortness of breath, smothering, or choking; 5. Chest pain or discomfort (frequently mimicking acute myocardial infarction); 6. Nausea or abdominal distress; 7. Dizziness, unsteadiness, lightheadedness, or feeling faint; 8. Chills or heat sensations; 9. Paresthesias (numbness or tingling sensations, especially circumoral and fingers from hyperventilation-induced respiratory alkalosis); 10. Derealization (feelings of unreality) or Depersonalization (being detached from oneself); 11. Fear of losing control or 'going crazy'; 12. SENSATION OF IMPENDING DOOM OR FEAR OF DYING

Agoraphobia (in > 50%): marked fear or avoidance of situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable in the event of a panic attack (public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, lines, crowds)
pertinent_negatives: normal ECG, normal high-sensitivity troponins, and normal D-Dimer rule out organic cardiopulmonary disease
content: Anxiety disorder driven by catastrophic misinterpretation of normal somatic arousal sensations mediated by a hypersensitive amygdala and 'fear network'. Treatment: 1. FIRST-LINE PHARMACOTHERAPY: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs: Sertraline, Paroxetine, Escitalopram) or SNRIs (Venlafaxine) started at HALF the usual initial dose to avoid paradoxical initial activation/anxiety; 2. Short-term bridging: Low-dose Benzodiazepines (Clonazepam, Alprazolam) for acute severe attacks (limit to 2-4 weeks to prevent dependence); 3. FIRST-LINE PSYCHOTHERAPY: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT: interoceptive exposure exercises, cognitive restructuring, and diaphragmatic breathing retraining has > 75-80% durable cure rate).

red_flags: fatal Refeeding Syndrome (hypophosphatemic cardiac arrest upon rapid refeeding)
malignant arrhythmias from severe hypokalemia and prolonged QTc
suicide (second leading cause of death in anorexia)
clinical_hallmarks: DSM-5 CRITERIA: 1. Restriction of energy intake relative to requirements leading to a SIGNIFICANTLY LOW BODY WEIGHT in context of age, sex, and developmental trajectory; 2. Intense, irrational fear of gaining weight or becoming fat; 3. Disturbance in the way body weight/shape is experienced, with undue influence on self-evaluation or denial of the seriousness of current low weight
severity by Body Mass Index (BMI in adults): Mild (>= 17), Moderate (16-16.99), Severe (15-15.99), Extreme (< 15 kg/m2)

CARDINAL PHYSICAL SIGNS OF PROFOUND EMACIATION: 1. LANUGO (fine, soft, downy hair growing on back, arms, and cheeks); 2. Profound sinus bradycardia (resting HR < 40-50 bpm), hypothermia (< 35.5C), and hypotension; 3. Carotenemia (yellow-orange pigmentation of palms and soles due to impaired hepatic conversion of carotene); 4. Secondary amenorrhea and loss of axillary/pubic hair; 5. Parotid gland enlargement and Russell sign (knuckle calluses in purging subtype)

REFEEDING SYNDROME RISK: rapid carbohydrate refeeding causes massive insulin surge, driving phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, precipitating FATAL HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA, heart failure, and arrhythmias
pertinent_negatives: patient perceives themselves as 'overweight' despite objective extreme emaciation
content: Psychiatric eating disorder with highest mortality of any psychiatric illness (5-10% per decade). Inpatient Hospitalization Indications: BMI < 13-14, HR < 40 bpm, BP < 80/50, QTc > 460 ms, K+ < 3.0 mEq/L, or acute refusal to eat. Management: 1. CAREFUL, GRADUAL NUTRITIONAL REHABILITATION: 'Start low and advance slow' (begin feeds at 1,000-1,200 kcal/day, increasing by 200 kcal every 2-3 days); 2. Daily monitoring of serum PHOSPHATE, potassium, and magnesium for first 1-2 weeks; oral/IV phosphate repletion is mandatory; 3. Psychotherapy: Family-Based Treatment (FBT / Maudsley approach) for adolescents; Specialist Supportive Clinical Management (SSCM) or CBT-E for adults; 4. Atypical antipsychotic (Olanzapine 2.5-10 mg) facilitates weight gain and reduces obsessive eating rumination.

red_flags: Malignant Catatonia (hyperthermia, autonomic storm, cardiovascular collapse - lethal if untreated)
pulmonary embolism from prolonged complete immobility
clinical_hallmarks: neuropsychiatric motor syndrome occurring secondary to mood disorders (bipolar mania/depression in 60%), schizophrenia, or general medical/neurological conditions
DSM-5 requires >= 3 of 12 cardinal signs (quantified by Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale):
1. STUPOR (complete immobility and unresponsiveness with preserved awareness of environment);
2. MUTISM (complete absence or minimal verbal output);
3. CATALEPSY (passive induction of a posture held against gravity for extended periods);
4. WAXY FLEXIBILITY (slight, even resistance to positioning by examiner, resembling the bending of a warm candle);
5. NEGATIVISM (motiveless resistance or opposition to instructions or passive movements, or doing the exact opposite);
6. POSTURING (spontaneous, active maintenance of a bizarre, uncomfortable posture against gravity, such as the 'psychological pillow' - head held 2 inches above bed for hours);
7. ECHOLALIA (mimicking examiner's words) and ECHOPRAXIA (mimicking examiner's movements);
8. Stereotypy, Mannerisms, Grimacing, and Agitation

DIAGNOSTIC AND THERAPEUTIC TEST: THE LORAZEPAM CHALLENGE TEST (administration of IV Lorazepam 1-2 mg produces DRAMATIC, NEAR-COMPLETE TEMPORARY RESOLUTION OF CATATONIC MUTISM AND STUPOR WITHIN 10-15 MINUTES, with patient sitting up and speaking normally)
pertinent_negatives: response to lorazepam confirms catatonia and decisively rules out coma
content: Neurochemical motor dysregulation characterized by top-down cortical GABA-A hypoactivity and dopamine-glutamate imbalance. STAT Protocol: 1. STAT LORAZEPAM CHALLENGE AND TITRATION: IV Lorazepam (2 mg IV bolus; if partial response, repeat 2 mg in 30 min; titrated up to 8-16 mg/day in divided doses); 2. Malignant Catatonia (fever, autonomic instability) or Lorazepam-Refractory Catatonia (after 48-72 hours): STAT EMERGENCY ELECTROCONVULSIVE THERAPY (Bilateral ECT is life-saving, achieving > 85-95% remission); 3. Prophylactic LMWH anticoagulation to prevent DVT/PE; 4. Strictly AVOID all antipsychotic medications (precipitate fatal malignant catatonia).

topic: Incarcerated & Strangulated Inguinal Hernia (Taxis vs Surgery)
red_flags: bowel gangrene and ischemic perforation within 4-6 hours
clinical_hallmarks: history of a pre-existing groin lump or bulge (indirect, direct, or femoral hernia) that previously reduced spontaneously or with gentle manual pressure
acute presentation: SUDDEN, AGONIZING, SEVERE PAIN IN THE GROIN BULGE that has become COMPLETELY IRREDUCIBLE / INCARCERATED
CARDINAL DIFFERENTIATION: INCARCERATION VS STRANGULATION:
1. Incarceration: non-reducible groin mass with local discomfort; overlying skin is normal and non-tender; patient may develop mechanical small bowel obstruction (vomiting, distension, obstipation)

2. STRANGULATION (ISCHEMIC TISSUE NECROSIS - STAT SURGICAL EMERGENCY): groin mass becomes EXQUISITELY TENDER, TENSE, FIRM, ERYTHEMATOUS, DUSKY, PURPLISH, OR HOT; systemic signs of toxicity (high fever, marked tachycardia, leukocytosis, and peritonitis)

MANDATORY CLINICAL RULE: MANUAL REDUCTION (TAXIS) IS STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED IF STRANGULATION IS SUSPECTED (reducing gangrenous, non-viable, necrotic bowel into the peritoneal cavity causes catastrophic generalized peritonitis and septic shock / 'reduction en masse')
pertinent_negatives: erythema, warmth, and exquisite tenderness confirm strangulation (taxis is strictly prohibited)
content: Entrapment of herniated abdominal contents (omentum, small bowel) through the internal or external inguinal ring or femoral canal, with subsequent vascular compromise. Femoral hernias have highest rate of strangulation (up to 40%). Emergency Protocol: 1. Strangulated Hernia: NPO, large-bore IV resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole), STAT Emergency Surgical Exploration (groin incision, inspection of bowel viability before and after releasing constriction ring, bowel resection and anastomosis if non-viable, hernia repair without synthetic mesh if infected); 2. Simple Incarceration (< 2 hours, no signs of strangulation): gentle manual reduction (taxis) under IV analgesia and Trendelenburg position.

specialty: General Surgery / Colorectal Surgery / Emergency Medicine
red_flags: sigmoid gangrene and perforation with feculent peritonitis
endoscopic detorsion contraindicated if mucosal ischemia present
clinical_hallmarks: predominantly affects ELDERLY, BEDRIDDEN, INSTITUTIONALIZED PATIENTS or those with chronic constipation, neuropsychiatric disease (Parkinson's, schizophrenia on psychotropics), or high-fiber diets
MASSIVE, ENORMOUS, ASYMMETRICAL ABDOMINAL DISTENSION (often described as a 'tympanitic balloon' filling the entire abdomen, predominantly on the right and upper abdomen)
severe constipation and complete obstipation for several days, accompanied by dull colicky lower abdominal pain and late vomiting
percussion: universal loud, drum-like TYMPANY over the distended sigmoid loop

Plain Abdominal Radiograph (PATHOGNOMONIC): 'COFFEE-BEAN SIGN' OR 'BENT INNER TUBE SIGN' (a massively distended, smooth, ahaustral loop of sigmoid colon originating from the left pelvis and curving upwards towards the right upper quadrant, with its two medial walls apposed to form a central thick radiodense cleft resembling the seam of a coffee bean)
barium/Gastrografin enema: pathognomonic smooth tapered 'BIRD'S-BEAK' appearance at the site of twist
pertinent_negatives: absence of signs of gangrene (peritonitis, bloody rectal discharge, fever, leukocytosis) is a mandatory prerequisite for non-operative detorsion
content: Twisting of a redundant, mobile sigmoid colon on its elongated, narrow-based mesentery through >= 180-360 degrees, producing a closed-loop large bowel obstruction. Treatment Protocol: 1. First-line Emergency Decompression (for uncomplicated volvulus without gangrene/peritonitis): BEDSIDE RIGID SIGMOIDOSCOPY OR COLONOSCOPY WITH INSERTION OF A FLATUS TUBE (soft rectal tube passed gently under direct vision beyond the twist into the distended loop, producing an EXPLOSIVE EVACUATION OF PENT-UP GAS AND LIQUID FECES with instant abdominal deflation and decompression in > 80-90%); 2. Leave flatus tube in place for 24-48 hours; 3. Definitive Cure: Elective Semi-Urgent Sigmoid Colectomy (Hartmann or primary anastomosis) during the same hospital admission (because recurrence rate after detorsion alone exceeds 50-70%); 4. Emergency Laparotomy with Hartmann's Procedure for frank gangrene or peritonitis.

keywords: no one is dead until warm and dead
red_flags: ventricular fibrillation / asystole provoked by rough handling or endotracheal suction
clinical_hallmarks: history of cold weather exposure, cold-water immersion, elderly fall on cold floor, or severe malnutrition/intoxication
Swiss Staging System based on Core Temperature (measured with low-reading esophageal or bladder thermistor):
Stage I (Mild: 32 - 35C): conscious, vigorous intense shivering, tachycardia, ataxia, cold pale skin;
Stage II (Moderate: 28 - 32C): impaired consciousness, apathy, dilated sluggish pupils, CESSATION OF SHIVERING (body exhausts metabolic shivering at < 30-32C), progressive bradycardia;
Stage III (Severe: 24 - 28C): unconscious, comatose, profound bradycardia (HR < 30), severe hypotension, barely detectable respirations;
Stage IV (Apparent Death: < 24C): absent vital signs, asystole or ventricular fibrillation, fixed dilated pupils, cold stiff body mimicking rigor mortis;

PATHOGNOMONIC ECG HALLMARK: THE OSBORN J-WAVE (a prominent, dome-shaped positive deflection at the J-point [junction of QRS complex and ST segment], amplitude directly proportional to depth of hypothermia), accompanied by PR/QT prolongation and baseline shivering artifact
pertinent_negatives: RESUSCITATION MANDATE: 'NO ONE IS DEAD UNTIL WARM AND DEAD' (resuscitative CPR must be continued until core temperature is rewarmed to >= 32-35C)
content: Drop in involuntary core body temperature below 35.0C (95.0F). Rewarming Protocol: 1. Extreme gentle handling (rough movements easily trigger intractable Ventricular Fibrillation in the irritable, cold myocardium); 2. Stage I: Passive External Rewarming (dry clothes, warm blankets, warm sweet drinks); 3. Stage II: Active External Rewarming (forced-air warming blankets [Bair Hugger], radiant heat applied to trunk/core); 4. Stage III/IV: Active Internal Core Rewarming: Humidified warm O2 (40-42C), IV fluids warmed to 42C, warm pleural or peritoneal lavage, and ECMO / Cardiopulmonary Bypass (gold standard for hypothermic cardiac arrest); 5. Withhold IV epinephrine and defibrillation attempts if core temp < 30C.

topic: Acute Erysipelas vs Cellulitis (Milian's Ear Sign & Peau d'Orange)
red_flags: necrotizing fasciitis (pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, skin anesthesia)
clinical_hallmarks: CLINICAL AND ANATOMICAL DIFFERENTIATION: ERYSIPELAS VS CELLULITIS:

1. ERYSIPELAS (Superficial Dermis & Lymphatics - Streptococcus pyogenes / Group A Strep): abrupt onset of high fever and chills followed by a FIERY RED, GLISTENING, SHINY, TENSE, INDURATED PLAQUE with SHARPLY DEMARCATED, DISTINCT, ELEVATED BORDERS; rapidly advancing; PATHOGNOMONIC MILIAN'S EAR SIGN (involvement of the ear pinna confirms erysipelas, because the earlobe has skin and dermis but NO deep subcutaneous tissue, making deep cellulitis impossible);

2. CELLULITIS (Deep Dermis & Subcutaneous Fat - Strep pyogenes & Staphylococcus aureus): gradual onset of erythema, edema, warmth, and tenderness with POORLY DEMARCATED, INDISTINCT, DIFFUSE BORDERS that blend gradually into surrounding normal skin; PATHOGNOMONIC PEAU D'ORANGE APPEARANCE (dimpled, orange-peel cutaneous pitting caused by cutaneous lymphatic obstruction around hair follicles)
predominantly affects lower extremities (> 80%), followed by face, arms, and surgical sites
unilateral presentation; associated with tinea pedis (cracked toe webs as entry portal) or chronic lymphedema
pertinent_negatives: sharply demarcated raised margin and ear involvement confirm superficial erysipelas (distinguishes from indistinct deep cellulitis)
content: Acute bacterial infection of dermis and subcutaneous tissues. Diagnostic workup: Clinical diagnosis; outline advancing border with skin marker to track therapy. Protocol: 1. Elevate the affected limb continuously (accelerates resolution of edema); 2. Treat portal of entry (antifungal cream for tinea pedis); 3. Antimicrobial Therapy: Erysipelas (Group A Strep): Oral Penicillin V (500 mg QID) OR Amoxicillin OR IV Aqueous Penicillin G; Cellulitis (covering Strep + MSSA): Oral Flucloxacillin (500 mg QID for 5-7 days) OR Cephalexin (500 mg QID) OR IV Cefazolin; Add Vancomycin or Linezolid if MRSA suspected or purulent drainage present.

topic: Acute & Chronic Arsenic Toxicity (Raindrop Pigmentation & Mees Lines)
red_flags: malignancy: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of skin, bladder cancer, lung cancer
clinical_hallmarks: chronic ingestion of arsenic-contaminated groundwater from shallow tube-wells (widespread in Ganga-Brahmaputra delta: West Bengal, Bangladesh, Bihar) or occupational exposure

ACUTE POISONING: Pungent 'GARLIC-LIKE' ODOR to breath; severe, agonizing burning abdominal pain, profuse 'rice-water' bloody diarrhea, vomiting, dehydration, and QTc prolongation (Torsades de Pointes)
CHRONIC ARSENICOSIS (PATHOGNOMONIC CUTANEOUS HALLMARKS):

1. 'RAINDROP' HYPERPIGMENTATION: mottled, diffuse, dark brown hyperpigmentation interspersed with small, pale, macules of normal/depigmented skin resembling 'raindrops on a dusty road', characteristically on trunk, chest, and abdomen;

2. ARSENICAL PALMOPLANTAR KERATOSIS: rough, hard, punctate, corn-like hyperkeratotic papules and plaques over the PALMS AND SOLES (high propensity for transformation into invasive Bowen's disease and Squamous Cell Carcinoma);
3. MEES' LINES: transverse, non-palpable, white, parallel bands across the entire width of all fingernails and toenails
chronic peripheral sensorimotor 'glove-and-stocking' axonal neuropathy (painful burning dysesthesias in feet)
pertinent_negatives: 24-hour urinary arsenic collection (> 50-100 mcg/L) confirms exposure (patient must avoid seafood for 48 hours prior to test to exclude non-toxic organic arsenobetaine)
content: Toxic cellular poisoning by trivalent arsenite (As3+) which binds lipoic acid sulfhydryl groups, inhibiting pyruvate dehydrogenase and Krebs cycle ATP synthesis. Diagnostic gold standard: 24-hour urinary arsenic excretion, hair and nail arsenic levels. Treatment Protocol: 1. STAT PROVISION OF ARSENIC-FREE DRINKING WATER (filters, deep aquifers); 2. Acute Poisoning Chelation: STAT Intramuscular Dimercaprol (BAL - British Anti-Lewisite: 3-5 mg/kg IM q4h in peanut oil) OR oral Succimer (DMSA: 10 mg/kg TID for 5 days, then BID for 14 days); 3. Chronic Keratoses: Topical keratolytics (20% urea cream, topical retinoic acid); 4. Strict lifelong surveillance for cutaneous, bladder, and pulmonary malignancies.

topic: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (Phalen Sign, Tinel Sign & Median Neuropathy)
red_flags: irreversible thenar motor atrophy and loss of thumb opposition
clinical_hallmarks: most common compressive focal mononeuropathy of the human body, with strong female predilection (female:male 3:1)

burning pain, tingling paresthesias, and numbness strictly confined to the MEDIAN NERVE SENSORY DISTRIBUTION (palmar aspect of THUMB, INDEX FINGER, MIDDLE FINGER, and radial half of RING FINGER, with STRICT SPARING of the little finger)

symptoms are CHARACTERISTICALLY WORST AT NIGHT, waking the patient from sleep with agonizing numbness; PATHOGNOMONIC 'FLICK SIGN' (patient vigorously shakes, flicks, or wrings their hand to relieve symptoms, like shaking down a thermometer)
PROVOCATIVE PHYSICAL EXAMINATION SIGNS:
1. PHALEN'S TEST (positive: complete flexion of wrists at 90 degrees for 60 seconds reproduces paresthesias in median distribution);
2. TINEL'S SIGN (positive: light percussion over the volar carpal tunnel produces electric-shock sensations radiating into the fingers);
3. DURKAN'S TEST (Carpal Compression Test - most sensitive: direct thumb pressure over carpal tunnel reproduces tingling within 30 seconds);
severe chronic disease: VISIBLE ATROPHY AND FLATTENING OF THE THENAR EMINENCE (abductor pollicis brevis weakness with weak thumb opposition / 'ape-hand' deformity)
pertinent_negatives: palmar cutaneous branch spares the proximal palm (dermatome over thenar base is normal because nerve branches proximal to carpal tunnel)
content: Increased pressure within the unyielding fibro-osseous carpal tunnel leading to ischemia and demyelination of the median nerve. Predisposing factors: repetitive wrist flexion, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis. Diagnostic confirmation: Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS: prolonged median distal motor and sensory latencies). Treatment: 1. Conservative (mild-moderate): Volar neutral wrist splinting worn strictly at NIGHT for 6-8 weeks + ergonomic modification; 2. Local Carpal Tunnel Corticosteroid Injection (Triamcinolone 20-40 mg) provides substantial temporary relief; 3. Definitive Surgical Cure: Carpal Tunnel Release (open or endoscopic division of the transverse carpal ligament / flexor retinaculum, achieving > 90-95% long-term cure).

topic: Plantar Fasciitis (First-Step Morning Heel Pain & Windlass Mechanism)
red_flags: rupture of plantar fascia (sudden pop with ecchymosis, often post-steroid injection)
clinical_hallmarks: most common cause of inferior heel pain in adults (affecting runners, dancers, obese individuals, and workers with prolonged standing on hard surfaces)
CARDINAL PATHOGNOMONIC SYMPTOM: EXCRUCIATING, SHARP, STABBING HEEL PAIN EXPERIENCED WITH THE VERY FIRST FEW STEPS OUT OF BED IN THE MORNING, or after prolonged periods of sitting and inactivity
the pain gradually eases and warms up after walking for 5-10 minutes, but characteristically worsens again towards the end of the day or after prolonged standing
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION HALLMARK: EXQUISITE, SHARPLY LOCALIZED POINT TENDERNESS OVER THE ANTEROMEDIAL ASPECT OF THE CALCANEAL TUBEROSITY (the origin of the plantar fascia)

PATHOGNOMONIC BIOMECHANICAL SIGN: POSITIVE WINDLASS TEST (passive, forced dorsiflexion of the hallux / big toe stretches the plantar fascia over the metatarsal head, reproducing the sharp inferior heel pain)
plain lateral foot radiographs: calcaneal traction spur present in 50% (spur is an incidental traction finding, NOT the cause of pain)
pertinent_negatives: absence of resting night pain (persistent night pain raises suspicion of calcaneal tumor or infection)
content: Chronic degenerative micro-tearing and failed healing response (plantar fasciosis, rather than acute inflammation) at the enthesis of the plantar aponeurosis into the calcaneus. First-Line Conservative Protocol (effective in > 90-95% of patients over 6-12 months): 1. Plantar Fascia and Achilles Tendon Specific Stretching Exercises (performed multiple times daily, especially before the first morning step); 2. Footwear modifications: cushioned shoes with rigid arch support and silicone heel cups; 3. Night Splints (maintains foot in 5 degrees dorsiflexion overnight to prevent fascia shortening); 4. Short-course oral NSAIDs; 5. Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy (ESWT) for chronic refractory cases (> 6 months); 6. Plantar fascia release surgery reserved only for severe failed cases.

topic: De Quervain's Tenosynovitis (Finkelstein Test & Radial Styloid)
keywords: extensor pollicis brevis abductor pollicis longus
red_flags: superficial radial nerve injury from steroid injection or surgery
clinical_hallmarks: stenosing tenosynovitis of the FIRST DORSAL EXTENSOR COMPARTMENT of the wrist, containing the tendons of the ABDUCTOR POLLICIS LONGUS (APL) and EXTENSOR POLLICIS BREVIS (EPB)

predominantly affects women (female:male 6:1), classically NEW MOTHERS ('Mother's Wrist' - repeatedly lifting an infant with thumbs extended and wrists deviated) and individuals with repetitive thumb texting or forceful gripping
constant, severe, aching pain localized directly over the RADIAL STYLOID PROCESS, radiating proximally into forearm or distally into thumb
pain is aggravated by thumb extension, abduction, and pinching motions
palpation: well-circumscribed tenderness and visible fusiform swelling over the first dorsal compartment at the radial styloid

PATHOGNOMONIC DIAGNOSTIC MANEUVER: POSITIVE FINKELSTEIN'S TEST (the patient folds their thumb into the palm, clasps their fingers tightly over the thumb to make a fist, and the examiner gently ulnarly deviates the wrist: this reproduces EXCRUCIATING, SHARP PAIN over the radial styloid)
pertinent_negatives: pain is strictly over the radial styloid (pain at anatomical snuffbox indicates scaphoid pathology)
content: Thickening and stenosing friction of the fibrous sheath enclosing the APL and EPB tendons over the radial styloid. Treatment Protocol: 1. First-line Conservative: Rigid THUMB SPICA SPLINT (immobilizing thumb IP and MCP joints and wrist) worn continuously for 4-6 weeks + oral NSAIDs + activity modification; 2. Local Corticosteroid Injection: Ultrasound-guided injection of Triamcinolone (20 mg) into the first dorsal extensor compartment sheath (success rate > 80-90% cure, take care to identify multiple sub-compartments); 3. Surgical Decompression: Surgical release of the first dorsal extensor retinaculum with identification of separate EPB slip and protection of superficial radial sensory nerve branches.

topic: Lumbar Spinal Canal Stenosis (Neurogenic Claudication & Shopping Cart Sign)
red_flags: cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence)
clinical_hallmarks: predominantly affects OLDER ADULTS (> 60-65 years of age) resulting from chronic degenerative spondylosis (facet joint osteoarthritis, disc bulging, and pathognomonic HYPERTROPHY OF THE LIGAMENTUM FLAVUM)
CARDINAL PATHOGNOMONIC SYMPTOM: NEUROGENIC CLAUDICATION (PSEUDOCLAUDICATION):
bilateral (or unilateral) dull ache, heaviness, numbness, tingling paresthesias, and weakness in the buttocks, thighs, and calves TRIGGERED BY WALKING OR PROLONGED STANDING

PATHOGNOMONIC RELIEF MANEUVER: SYMPTOMS ARE PROMPTLY AND DRAMATICALLY RELIEVED BY BENDING FORWARD OR SITTING DOWN (flexing the lumbar spine widens the canal cross-sectional area by up to 25% and reduces venous congestion);

THE 'SHOPPING CART SIGN': patients walk with a forward-stooped posture and can walk long distances without pain IF LEANING FORWARD OVER A GROCERY SHOPPING CART OR BICYCLE (in sharp contrast to vascular claudication where posture makes no difference)
MRI of Lumbar Spine (gold standard): central canal cross-sectional area < 75-100 mm2, lateral recess narrowing, and ligamentum flavum thickening (characteristically L4-L5 and L3-L4)
pertinent_negatives: normal pedal pulses and absence of skin trophic changes distinguish neurogenic from vascular claudication
content: Mechanical compression of lumbosacral nerve roots within the narrowed spinal canal. Treatment: 1. Conservative (mild-moderate): Physical therapy focusing on flexion-based core exercises, stationary cycling, NSAIDs, Gabapentin; 2. Epidural Corticosteroid Injections (interlaminar or transforaminal) provide intermediate-term symptomatic relief; 3. Definitive Surgical Treatment: Lumbar Decompressive Laminectomy (flavectomy and partial medial facetectomy +/- instrumented fusion if spondylolisthesis present) provides dramatic and durable walking endurance and pain relief.

topic: Acute Rhabdomyolysis (Crush Injury & Serum Creatine Kinase > 5000)
red_flags: fatal hyperkalemic cardiac arrest within hours of extrication
oliguric acute tubular necrosis (acute renal failure)
clinical_hallmarks: precipitating causes: crush injuries / prolonged immobilization (elderly 'found down' on floor), strenuous unaccustomed exercise (marathon, crossfit), seizures, heat stroke, electrocution, or statin-fibrate interactions
CLASSIC CLINICAL TRIAD (present in < 50%): 1. Severe muscle pain (myalgias); 2. Muscle weakness; 3. DARK, TEA-COLORED, COLA-COLORED, OR REDDISH-BROWN URINE (MYOGLOBINURIA)
affected muscle groups (thighs, calves, lower back) are swollen, exquisitely tender, and indurated

PATHOGNOMONIC URINALYSIS DISCREPANCY: URINE DIPSTICK POSITIVE FOR 'BLOOD', BUT URINE MICROSCOPY SHOWS VIRTUALLY NO RED BLOOD CELLS (the orthotolidine dipstick reagent cannot differentiate between hemoglobin and myoglobin; absence of intact RBCs confirms myoglobinuria)
LABORATORY GOLD STANDARD: SERUM CREATINE KINASE (CK) ELEVATED TO >= 5 TIMES UPPER LIMIT OF NORMAL (typically > 5,000 - 50,000 IU/L, often exceeding 100,000 IU/L)

early lethal metabolic derangements: HYPERKALEMIA (massive release of intracellular potassium from lysed myocytes), hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and early hypocalcemia followed by late hypercalcemia
pertinent_negatives: dipstick positive for blood with negative microscopic RBCs is the classic signature of myoglobinuria
content: Rapid breakdown and necrosis of skeletal muscle tissue resulting in leakage of intracellular myocyte contents (myoglobin, CK, potassium, phosphate, aldolase) into the systemic circulation. Myoglobin causes acute tubular necrosis through renal vasoconstriction, tubular cast obstruction, and direct iron-catalyzed oxidative cytotoxicity. STAT Emergency Resuscitation Protocol: 1. IMMEDIATE AGGRESSIVE INTRAVENOUS FLUID RESUSCITATION: IV Crystalloids (0.9% Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate initiated at 1.0 - 1.5 L/hr, maintaining a target urine output of 200 - 300 mL/hr until CK drops < 1,000-5,000 IU/L); 2. STAT TREATMENT OF HYPERKALEMIA (IV Calcium Gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilization, IV Insulin + Dextrose, nebulized Albuterol); 3. Urine alkalinization (IV Sodium Bicarbonate targeting urine pH > 6.5) prevents myoglobin cast precipitation; 4. Emergency Hemodialysis for refractory hyperkalemia or anuric renal failure.

clinical_hallmarks: history of incomplete immunization in an endemic or outbreak region, spread via fecal-oral transmission
minor illness: non-specific prodrome of fever, headache, pharyngitis, nausea, and vomiting for 1-3 days
major illness: abrupt resurgence of high fever followed by severe muscle myalgias, spasms, and ASYMMETRIC, PROXIMAL-PREDOMINANT LOWER EXTREMITY WEAKNESS

CARDINAL PHYSICAL EXAMINATION SIGNS: 1. PURE LOWER MOTOR NEURON (LMN) WEAKNESS (flaccidity, hypotonia, and total loss of deep tendon reflexes / areflexia); 2. ASYMMETRIC DISTRIBUTION (typically one leg or one arm, proximal muscles weaker than distal); 3. COMPLETE PRESERVATION OF SENSATION (normal light touch and pinprick sensation); 4. Tripod sign (child sits with hands braced behind on bed for spinal support); 5. Positive kiss-the-knee sign (inability to flex neck to touch knee)
stool viral culture (gold standard): isolation of poliovirus from 2 stool specimens collected 24 hours apart
pertinent_negatives: completely normal sensory examination confirms pure anterior horn cell motor lesion
content: Poliovirus infection (Enterovirus C family) with selective tropism for the anterior horn motor neurons of the spinal cord and motor nuclei of the brainstem. Treatment: No curative antiviral therapy exists; Supportive care: Bed rest, gentle analgesia, hot moist packs for muscle spasms, tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation for bulbar respiratory failure; Orthopedic splinting and long-term physiotherapy to minimize contractures; Universal Prevention: Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine (IPV - Salk) and Bivalent Oral Poliovirus Vaccine (bOPV - Sabin).

specialty: Infectious Disease / Neurology / Critical Care / Toxicology
keywords: the 4 ds diplopia dysarthria dysphonia dysphagia
red_flags: acute respiratory failure from diaphragmatic paralysis
complete paralysis with fully preserved consciousness
clinical_hallmarks: history of consuming home-canned vegetables, cured meats, or fermented fish (Foodborne Botulism) OR infant under 12 months fed raw honey (Infant Botulism / 'floppy baby syndrome')
CARDINAL PATHOGNOMONIC MOTOR SEQUENCE: SYMMETRICAL, DESCENDING, FLACCID MOTOR PARALYSIS AFFECTING BULBAR MUSCLES FIRST

THE '4 Ds' OF CRANIAL NERVE BULBAR PALSY: 1. DIPLOPIA (double vision) and ptosis; 2. DYSARTHRIA (slurred speech); 3. DYSPHONIA (hoarse or absent voice); 4. DYSPHAGIA (inability to swallow saliva, choking)

PATHOGNOMONIC PUPILLARY AND AUTONOMIC FINDING: BILATERALLY FIXED, DILATED PUPILS UNRESPONSIVE TO LIGHT (in > 50-70% of foodborne cases - cholinergic blockade of pupillary sphincter); severe dry mouth (xerostomia), paralytic ileus, and urinary retention
weakness advances sequentially downward from head/neck -> upper extremities -> respiratory diaphragm -> lower extremities
ALERT, CLEAR SENSORIUM MAINTAINED THROUGHOUT (patient remains completely awake and mentally intact inside a paralyzed body)
pertinent_negatives: normal sensory examination and preserved consciousness confirm neuromuscular junction toxin
content: Most lethal biological toxin known, produced by anaerobic spore-forming Clostridium botulinum. Botulinum neurotoxin is a zinc metalloprotease that cleaves SNARE proteins (SNAP-25, Syntaxin, Synaptobrevin), irreversibly blocking presynaptic acetylcholine exocytosis at neuromuscular junctions. Statutory emergency. Protocol: 1. STAT Emergency Airway Protection and ICU mechanical ventilation based on serial vital capacity; 2. STAT BOTULINUM ANTITOXIN ADMINISTRATION: Equine Heptavalent Botulinum Antitoxin (HBAT: serotypes A-G) for adults OR Botulism Immune Globulin Intravenous (BabyBIG / BIG-IV) for infants (neutralizes circulating free toxin before it binds; does not reverse existing paralysis); 3. Wound debridement + IV Penicillin G for wound botulism; AVOID aminoglycosides.

topic: Chagas Disease (Trypanosoma Cruzi - Romaña Sign & Megadisease)
red_flags: apical left ventricular aneurysm rupture / fatal ventricular tachycardia
clinical_hallmarks: transmission via feces of infected triatomine bugs ('kissing bugs' / reduviid bugs) in endemic regions (Latin America) or congenital/transfusion spread

ACUTE CHAGAS (in 5%): PATHOGNOMONIC ROMAÑA'S SIGN (unilateral, painless, brawny, purplish periorbital edema with conjunctivitis and preauricular lymphadenopathy developing when bug feces is rubbed into eye) OR Chagoma (erythematous subcutaneous skin nodule at bite site)
CHRONIC CHAGAS (develops decades after initial silent infection in 20-30%):

1. CARDIAC CHAGAS: progressive Dilated Cardiomyopathy with biventricular heart failure, Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB) + Left Anterior Fascicular Block (LAFB) on ECG, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, and PATHOGNOMONIC THIN-WALLED APICAL LEFT VENTRICULAR ANEURYSM (apical thinning with mural thrombus formation and high stroke risk);

2. GASTROINTESTINAL CHAGAS: progressive destruction of the enteric myenteric plexus of Auerbach leading to 'MEGADISEASE': MEGAESOPHAGUS (severe progressive dysphagia and regurgitation mimicking achalasia) and MEGACOLON (intractable severe constipation, fecaloma, and sigmoid volvulus)
pertinent_negatives: apical LV aneurysm with RBBB is the classic signature of Chagasic cardiomyopathy
content: Zoonotic protozoan infection caused by Trypanosoma cruzi. Diagnostic workup: Acute: Direct blood smear (motile trypomastigotes); Chronic: Two distinct positive serological assays (ELISA + indirect immunofluorescence). Treatment: 1. Anti-parasitic pharmacotherapy: Benznidazole (5-7 mg/kg/day for 60 days) OR Nifurtimox (8-10 mg/kg/day for 60-90 days) - highly effective in acute, congenital, and early chronic infection; 2. Cardiac: Guideline-directed heart failure therapy, ICD for ventricular tachycardia, anticoagulation for apical aneurysm; 3. GI: Endoscopic pneumatic dilatation / laparoscopic Heller myotomy for megaesophagus; Sigmoidectomy for megacolon.

topic: Acute Hepatitis B Virus Infection (HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc & Serology)
red_flags: acute fulminant hepatic failure (coagulopathy INR > 1.5, encephalopathy)
progression to chronic hepatitis B with cirrhosis/HCC risk
clinical_hallmarks: transmitted parenterally, sexually, or vertically via blood and bodily fluids; incubation period 30 to 180 days (mean 75 days)
prodromal serum-sickness-like syndrome (in 10-20%): fever, transient urticarial rash, and symmetrical polyarthralgias (immune complex deposition)
ICTERIC PHASE: insidious onset of deep fatigue, malaise, anorexia, nausea, dull right upper quadrant discomfort, dark tea-colored urine, and frank scleral/cutaneous icterus
physical examination: smooth, tender, enlarged liver margin and mild splenomegaly
