laboratory hallmarks: MASSIVE TRANSAMINASE ELEVATION (serum ALT and AST typically > 1,000 - 3,000 IU/L, with ALT > AST)
PATHOGNOMONIC SEROLOGICAL PROFILE OF ACUTE HEPATITIS B:
1. Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg): FIRST serological marker to appear, indicating active infection;

2. IgM Antibody to Hepatitis B Core Antigen (IgM anti-HBc): THE ABSOLUTE DIAGNOSTIC MARKER OF ACUTE HBV INFECTION (present in high titer during acute phase and sole marker present during the 'WINDOW PERIOD' when HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared);
3. Hepatitis B e-Antigen (HBeAg): indicates active high-level viral replication and extreme infectivity;
4. Hepatitis B Surface Antibody (anti-HBs): indicates recovery, clinical cure, and protective lifelong immunity (also sole marker positive after recombinant vaccination)
pertinent_negatives: IgM anti-HBc distinguishes acute hepatitis B from acute flare of chronic hepatitis B (where IgG anti-HBc is present)
content: Partially double-stranded DNA virus of the family Hepadnaviridae. Greater than 95% of immunocompetent adults achieve spontaneous clearance and lifelong immunity (by contrast, > 90% of perinatally infected neonates develop chronic HBV). Management: 1. Uncomplicated Acute HBV: Supportive care, rest, adequate hydration, avoidance of alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs; 2. Severe Acute / Fulminant HBV (INR > 1.5, encephalopathy, or protracted course): STAT Oral Nucleoside/Nucleotide Analogue (Entecavir 0.5 mg daily OR Tenofovir alafenamide / TDF) initiated immediately to reduce mortality and need for liver transplant; 3. Universal Prevention: 3-dose recombinant Hepatitis B vaccine + Hepatitis B Immune Globulin (HBIG) administered within 12 hours of birth to infants of HBsAg-positive mothers.

topic: Acute Hepatitis C Virus Infection (HCV RNA & DAA Cure)
red_flags: high rate of chronicity (75-85% progress to chronic hepatitis C)
clinical_hallmarks: predominantly transmitted via percutaneous blood exposure: injection drug use (sharing needles/syringes in > 70%), contaminated medical injections, occupational needle-stick injury, or unscreened blood transfusions
ACUTE INFECTION IS ASYMPTOMATIC IN > 75-80% OF CASES ('the silent epidemic')
symptomatic acute hepatitis C (20-25%): mild fatigue, low-grade fever, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and jaundice developing 2 to 12 weeks post-exposure
LABORATORY AND DIAGNOSTIC ALGORITHM:

1. Hepatitis C Viral RNA by quantitative RT-PCR (HCV RNA): THE EARLIEST AND MOST SENSITIVE DIAGNOSTIC MARKER, detectable in serum within 1 to 2 weeks post-exposure (well before anti-HCV antibodies develop);

2. Anti-HCV Antibody (ELISA): becomes positive 4 to 12 weeks post-exposure; a positive anti-HCV antibody WITH a positive HCV RNA confirms active viremic infection; a positive antibody with NEGATIVE HCV RNA indicates resolved/cured prior infection;
serum ALT fluctuates characteristically with episodic spikes
unlike Hepatitis B, SPONTANEOUS CLEARANCE OCCURS IN ONLY 15-25%; THE REMAINING 75-85% DEVELOP CHRONIC HEPATITIS C
pertinent_negatives: negative anti-HCV antibody DOES NOT rule out acute infection during the first 4-8 weeks; HCV RNA PCR is mandatory for acute diagnosis
content: Positive-sense single-stranded enveloped RNA virus of the Flaviviridae family. Modern Revolution in HCV Therapy: Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs) achieve Sustained Virologic Response (SVR12 - undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks post-therapy, representing a COMPLETE CLINICAL AND VIROLOGICAL CURE in > 95-98% of patients across all genotypes). Pan-Genotypic DAA Regimens (First-Line): Oral Sofosbuvir / Velpatasvir (Epclusa: 400/100 mg one tablet daily for 12 weeks) OR Glecaprevir / Pibrentasvir (Mavyret: 3 tablets daily for 8 weeks). No vaccine exists; post-exposure prophylaxis with DAAs is not currently recommended; test HCV RNA at 4 weeks post-exposure.

topic: Acute Hepatitis E Virus (Waterborne Epidemic & Pregnancy Mortality)
red_flags: FULMINANT HEPATIC FAILURE IN PREGNANCY (case fatality rate 20-25% in third trimester)
obstetric catastrophe: DIC, eclampsia, massive PPH, and intrauterine fetal demise
chronic HEV in solid-organ transplant recipients
clinical_hallmarks: epidemiological hallmark: LARGE WATERBORNE EPIDEMICS in developing countries (Indian subcontinent, Africa) resulting from fecal contamination of municipal drinking water supplies during monsoon seasons or floodings
transmission is primarily fecal-oral (Genotypes 1 and 2 in humans); zoonotic transmission via undercooked pork/game meat (Genotypes 3 and 4 in industrialized nations)
incubation period 2 to 10 weeks (mean 40 days)

clinical presentation in general population: self-limiting acute icteric hepatitis (fatigue, anorexia, nausea, fever, dark urine, and jaundice with elevated transaminases) with low overall mortality (< 0.5-1%)
CATASTROPHIC PATHOGNOMONIC VULNERABILITY: EXTREME, UNEXPLAINED HIGH MORTALITY IN PREGNANT WOMEN (approaching 20-25% case fatality rate, peaking in the THIRD TRIMESTER)

pregnant women experience rapid, catastrophic progression from mild jaundice to FULMINANT HEPATIC FAILURE within days, accompanied by massive hepatic encephalopathy, severe coagulopathy, DIC, and spontaneous abortion / stillbirth
diagnostic hallmark: Serum anti-HEV IgM antibodies (high specificity) or HEV RNA in stool/serum
pertinent_negatives: does NOT progress to chronic carrier state or cirrhosis in immunocompetent individuals (unlike HBV and HCV)
content: Non-enveloped positive-sense RNA virus of the Hepeviridae family. High pregnancy mortality is linked to high viral loads, hormonal changes (progesterone/estrogen downregulating cell-mediated immunity), and altered cytokine profiles. Management: 1. Strict supportive care in ICU for pregnant women with acute HEV; 2. Monitoring of coagulation profile, transaminases, and neurological sensorium; 3. Prompt management of cerebral edema, hypoglycemia, and coagulopathy; 4. Ribavirin (oral 600-1000 mg daily for 12 weeks) is effective for chronic HEV in immunocompromised patients (STRICTLY TERATOGENIC, CONTRAINDICATED IN PREGNANCY); 5. Prevention: Clean drinking water sanitation, boiling water, and recombinant HEV vaccine (Hecolin - approved in China).

keywords: dysphagia to both solids and liquids
clinical_hallmarks: insidious, progressive DYSPHAGIA TO BOTH SOLIDS AND LIQUIDS SIMULTANEOUSLY from symptom onset (in sharp, fundamental contrast to mechanical esophageal obstruction/cancer which begins with solids and only later advances to liquids)
nocturnal regurgitation of undigested, foul, non-acidic food consumed hours earlier (often soiling the pillow, causing nighttime coughing or choking)
substernal chest pressure and gradual unintentional weight loss
Eckardt Clinical Symptom Score (weight loss, dysphagia, retrosternal pain, regurgitation: 0-12)

Barium Esophagram (PATHOGNOMONIC RADIOGRAPHIC SIGN): dilated, tortuous, aperistaltic esophagus tapering smoothly at the gastroesophageal junction into a sharp, symmetrical 'BIRD'S-BEAK' OR 'RAT-TAIL' APPEARANCE, with delayed emptying into stomach
HIGH-RESOLUTION ESOPHAGEAL MANOMETRY (DIAGNOSTIC GOLD STANDARD - Chicago Classification v4.0):

1. Elevated Integrated Relaxation Pressure (IRP > 15 mmHg) indicating failure of Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES) relaxation; 2. Complete absence of normal coordinated peristalsis in the esophageal body (100% failed peristalsis)
pertinent_negatives: dysphagia to liquids from day one rules out simple peptic esophageal stricture
content: Primary esophageal motor disorder characterized by loss of inhibitory nitrergic ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus (Auerbach's plexus) of the distal esophagus and LES, leading to uninhibited cholinergic tone, failure of LES relaxation, and loss of peristalsis. UPPER ENDOSCOPY IS MANDATORY IN ALL PATIENTS to exclude pseudoachalasia (malignancy at GE junction). Definitive Treatment Options: 1. Endoscopic Pneumatic Balloon Dilatation (graded 30, 35, 40 mm balloons disrupting circular LES muscle fibers); 2. Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy (surgical division of LES circular muscle down to mucosa combined with Dor/Toupet partial fundoplication); 3. Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM - endoscopic submucosal tunneling and myotomy); 4. Botulinum toxin injection into LES (reserved for elderly/frail patients unfit for surgery).

topic: Acute Opioid Overdose (The Opioid Toxidrome & Naloxone Titration)
specialty: Emergency Medicine / Clinical Toxicology / Critical Care
red_flags: apneic hypoxemic cardiac arrest within minutes
clinical_hallmarks: history of recreational illicit opioid abuse (Heroin, Fentanyl, Oxycodone, Methadone, Morphine) or iatrogenic postoperative opioid oversedation
THE CLASSIC DIAGNOSTIC 'OPIOID TRIAD':
1. SEVERE RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION (slow, shallow, irregular, or agonal breathing with respiratory rate typically < 8-10 breaths/min, progressing to complete apnea and profound cyanosis);
2. CNS DEPRESSION (unconsciousness, stupor, or deep unarousable coma);
3. PINPOINT PUPILS (marked, bilateral, symmetrical, extreme MIOSIS: pupils constricted to < 1-2 mm, responding poorly to light)
physical examination: cold, clammy skin, profound muscle flaccidity, bradycardia, hypotension, and hypothermia

PATHOGNOMONIC MONITORING PITFALL: Fentanyl and high-potency synthetic fentanyl analogues can induce acute 'WOODEN CHEST SYNDROME' (severe, rigid chest wall muscle rigidity preventing manual bag-valve-mask ventilation)
PATHOGNOMONIC THERAPEUTIC RESPONSE: RAPID, COMPLETE REVERSAL OF COMA AND RESUMPTION OF NORMAL SPONTANEOUS RESPIRATION WITHIN 1-3 MINUTES OF INTRAVENOUS OR INTRANASAL NALOXONE
pertinent_negatives: pupils may be normal or dilated if concomitant severe cerebral hypoxia, hypothermia, or co-ingestion with sympathomimetics/anticholinergics
content: Agonism of central mu-opioid receptors in the brainstem medullary respiratory center, blunting normal hypercapnic and hypoxemic ventilatory drives. Statutory life-saving emergency. STAT Treatment Protocol: 1. AIRWAY AND VENTILATION FIRST: Immediate Bag-Valve-Mask (BVM) ventilatory support with 100% high-flow oxygen; 2. SPECIFIC COMPETITIVE OPIOID ANTAGONIST: NALOXONE (Narcan): IV/IM/SC/Intranasal (Titrated Dosing Protocol: begin with 0.04 - 0.4 mg IV in non-arrested patients, titrating upward every 2-3 minutes to RESTORE ADEQUATE SPONTANEOUS BREATHING [RR > 10-12/min] WITHOUT precipitating severe, violent acute opioid withdrawal and sympathetic surge; Intranasal Narcan: 4 mg single nasal spray into one nostril for community bystanders); 3. CRITICAL OBSERVATION MANDATE: Naloxone half-life is short (30-90 minutes); long-acting opioids (Methadone, extended-release Oxycodone) frequently outlast naloxone, causing RECURRENT APNEA AND RESEDATION requiring continuous IV Naloxone infusion.

topic: Salicylate (Aspirin) Toxicity (Mixed Respiratory Alkalosis & Metabolic Acidosis)
specialty: Clinical Toxicology / Emergency Medicine / Critical Care
red_flags: cerebral edema and coma (indicates neuroglycopenia and CNS acid toxicity)
severe refractory metabolic acidosis and hyperpyrexia
clinical_hallmarks: history of acute ingestion of > 150 mg/kg of Acetylsalicylic Acid (Aspirin) or chronic ingestion in elderly with renal impairment
EARLIEST AND MOST COMMON SYMPTOM: TINNITUS (ringing or buzzing in the ears) and subjective mild sensorineural hearing impairment, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and diaphoresis
PATHOGNOMONIC ARTERIAL BLOOD GAS (ABG) SIGNATURE: MIXED ACID-BASE DISORDER:
1. Primary RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS (direct salicylate stimulation of the medullary respiratory center producing rapid, deep hyperventilation / tachypnea, low PaCO2, and early high pH);

2. Concomitant Primary HIGH ANION GAP METABOLIC ACIDOSIS (HAGMA: uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation leading to anaerobic glycolysis, accumulation of lactic acid, ketoacids, and salicylate organic acid ions, depressing serum bicarbonate);

late and severe toxicity signs: hyperpyrexia / hyperthermia (due to uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation dissipating energy as raw heat), marked dehydration, delirium, hallucinations, pulmonary edema, and coma
laboratory hallmarks: Serum Salicylate Level > 30-40 mg/dL (severe toxicity typically > 80-100 mg/dL); Positive Ferric Chloride urine test (purple color)
pertinent_negatives: normal or near-normal pH on ABG with simultaneously low PaCO2 and low HCO3 confirms a classic mixed respiratory alkalosis / metabolic acidosis
content: Salicylate uncouples mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, impairs Krebs cycle enzymes, and causes lipid and carbohydrate catabolism. Emergency Treatment Protocol: 1. STAT Gastric Decontamination: Activated Charcoal (1 g/kg orally, repeated in 2-4 hours); 2. URINE ALKALINIZATION (THE MAINSTAY OF MEDICAL MANAGEMENT): IV Sodium Bicarbonate infusion (100-150 mEq NaHCO3 in 1 L D5W at 150-250 mL/hr, maintaining urine pH >= 7.5 - 8.0 and blood pH < 7.55; 'ion-trapping' ionizes salicylate into lipid-insoluble form, preventing CNS entry and accelerating renal clearance by tenfold); 3. MANDATORY Potassium Repletion (hypokalemia prevents urine alkalinization because kidneys exchange H+ for Na+); 4. STAT EMERGENCY HEMODIALYSIS INDICATIONS: Serum salicylate > 90-100 mg/dL acute (> 60 mg/dL chronic), severe acidosis (pH < 7.20), neurological impairment/coma, pulmonary edema, or renal failure.

topic: Acute Cyanide Poisoning (Bitter Almond Breath & Hydroxocobalamin)
specialty: Clinical Toxicology / Emergency Medicine / Critical Care
red_flags: rapid cardiorespiratory collapse and death within 5-15 minutes
clinical_hallmarks: history of exposure to smoke inhalation from enclosed structure fires (combustion of polyurethane, synthetic wool, plastics), industrial electroplating, jewelry manufacturing, or ingestion of cyanogenic plants (cassava, apricot kernels / amygdalin)
abrupt onset within seconds to minutes of inhalation: flushing, rapid tachypnea, severe headache, dizziness, nausea, followed rapidly by convulsions, coma, severe hypotension, and respiratory arrest
PATHOGNOMONIC CLINICAL ODOR: FAINT 'BITTER ALMOND' ODOR to breath or gastric contents (genetically detectable by only 40-60% of people)
PATHOGNOMONIC LABORATORY AND METABOLIC HALLMARKS:
1. SEVERE, EXPLOSIVE ANION GAP LACTIC ACIDOSIS (serum lactate typically > 8-10 mmol/L in smoke inhalation victims is highly sensitive and specific for cyanide toxicity);

2. NORMAL OR HIGH ARTERIAL PO2 WITH NARROWED ARTERIOVENOUS OXYGEN DIFFERENCE (cells are completely unable to extract oxygen from blood; venous blood remains fully oxygenated, producing bright pink skin and retinal veins appearing as bright red as retinal arteries on fundoscopy)
pertinent_negatives: pulse oximetry and arterial PaO2 remain normal (cellular asphyxiation, NOT arterial hypoxemia)
content: Cyanide binds with extreme affinity to the ferric (Fe3+) iron atom of mitochondrial Cytochrome c Oxidase (Complex IV of electron transport chain), completely halting cellular aerobic respiration and ATP production, triggering catastrophic anaerobic metabolism. Statutory emergency. Life-Saving Protocol: 1. STAT 100% High-Flow Oxygen via non-rebreather mask; 2. FIRST-LINE SPECIFIC ANTIDOTE OF CHOICE: HYDROXOCOBALAMIN (Cyanokit: 5 grams IV infusion over 15 minutes; binds cyanide directly to form non-toxic Cyanocobalamin / Vitamin B12, safely excreted in urine; causes harmless transient red discoloration of skin and urine); 3. Alternative Cyanide Antidote Kit (if Cyanokit unavailable): Sodium Nitrite (induces methemoglobinemia which binds cyanide - CONTRAINDICATED in smoke inhalation with carbon monoxide) followed by IV Sodium Thiosulfate.

specialty: Emergency Medicine / Trauma Surgery / Critical Care
clinical_hallmarks: history of sudden collapse during an outdoor thunderstorm (direct strike, side flash, ground current / step voltage, or contact)

PATHOGNOMONIC DERMATOLOGICAL SIGN: LICHTENBERG FIGURES (FERN-LIKE / FEATHER-LIKE ARBORESCENT PATTERN: transient, non-palpable, reddish-brown, branching, dendritic cutaneous arborization patterns resembling a fern plant or tree; caused by electron showering along dermal pathways, appearing within 1 hour and completely fading within 24-48 hours)

PATHOGNOMONIC NEUROLOGICAL SIGN: KERAUNOPARALYSIS (transient, temporary, flaccid paralysis and sensory loss with pale, cold, pulseless extremities, predominantly affecting the lower limbs; caused by extreme autonomic vasospasm, resolving spontaneously within hours)
BLAST TRAUMA SIGNS: BILATERAL TYMPANIC MEMBRANE RUPTURE (in > 50-80% due to acoustic shock wave) and melted metallic jewelry or scorched clothing
late ocular complication: BILATERAL LIGHTNING CATARACTS developing months after injury

REVERSE TRIAGE PROTOCOL: In mass-casualty lightning strikes, VICTIMS WHO APPEAR DEAD (APNEIC AND PULSELESS) RECEIVE PRIORITY RESUSCITATION FIRST ('REVERSE TRIAGE'), because the heart's intrinsic automaticity can spontaneously restart, but persistent diaphragmatic spasm/apnea leads to secondary fatal anoxic arrest unless ventilated immediately
pertinent_negatives: Lichtenberg figures are not true thermal burns and require no surgical debridement
content: Massive, instantaneous, direct-current electrical discharge (up to 10-100 million volts, delivering 30,000 amperes in 1/10,000 of a second). Emergency Protocol: 1. IMMEDIATE CPR AND VENTILATION: Aggressive resuscitation of apneic and pulseless victims (high survival rates > 70-80% with immediate CPR); 2. Full Trauma Protocol: Cervical spine immobilization, FAST exam, secondary survey for blast injuries, intracranial hemorrhages, and fractures from violent tetanic muscular contractions; 3. Baseline 12-lead ECG, cardiac enzymes, urinalysis for myoglobinuria; 4. Comprehensive burn care and ophthalmology follow-up.

specialty: Colorectal Surgery / General Surgery / Emergency Medicine
red_flags: pelvic sepsis and horseshoe abscess extension
clinical_hallmarks: acute onset of constant, agonizing, throbbing, severe perianal or buttock pain that is MARKEDLY AGGRAVATED BY SITTING, WALKING, COUGHING, OR DEFECATION
fever, chills, and malaise; difficulty and pain during micturition
Perianal Abscess (most common 60%): visible, tender, erythematous, warm, FLUCTUANT SWELLING directly at the anal verge

Ischiorectal Abscess (20-25%): deep, diffuse, brawny, exquisitely tender induration in the ischiorectal fossa; may lack superficial redness in early stages but produces excruciating pain on gentle rectal digital examination or buttock pressure
predominant etiology: acute bacterial infection of the intersphincteric anal crypt glands (cryptoglandular hypothesis) involving E. coli, Bacteroides fragilis, and Enterococcus
pertinent_negatives: presence of fluctuant perianal mass warrants immediate drainage without waiting for antibiotic trial
content: Suppurative infection arising in anal glands within the intersphincteric space, tracking downwards (perianal) or through external sphincter into ischioanal fossa. Emergency Rule: Abscesses in the anal region MUST BE SURGICALLY DRAINED IMMEDIATELY upon diagnosis; antibiotics alone are ineffective and lead to extensive tissue necrosis. Protocol: 1. STAT Emergency Incision and Drainage (I&D): Cruciate or elliptical skin excision over point of maximum fluctuance as close as possible to the anal verge (to minimize fistula tract length); 2. Breakdown of all internal loculations with gentle gloved finger; 3. Loose packing with iodophor gauze (removed at 24 hours); 4. Twice-daily warm sitz baths; 5. Antibiotics indicated only for concomitant cellulitis, diabetes, immunosuppression, or systemic sepsis.

topic: Lateral Epicondylitis (Tennis Elbow - Cozen's Test & ECRB)
red_flags: radial tunnel syndrome (posterior interosseous nerve entrapment)
osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum in young throwing athletes
clinical_hallmarks: predominantly affects adults aged 35 to 55 years (racquet athletes, manual laborers, typists, carpenters involving repetitive wrist extension and forearm pronation/supination)
insidious onset of aching pain over the LATERAL PROMINENCE OF THE ELBOW, radiating down the extensor surface of the forearm
pain is aggravated by gripping objects, shaking hands, turning doorknobs, or lifting a coffee cup ('coffee cup sign')

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION HALLMARK: EXQUISITE, SHARPLY LOCALIZED POINT TENDERNESS DIRECTLY OVER THE LATERAL EPICONDYLE and approximately 1-2 cm distal into the tendon of the Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB)
PATHOGNOMONIC PROVOCATIVE TESTS:
1. COZEN'S TEST (positive: with elbow flexed to 90 degrees and forearm pronated, resisted active wrist extension with radial deviation reproduces severe lateral elbow pain);
2. MILL'S TEST (passive wrist flexion with elbow extended stretches extensor muscles, reproducing pain);
3. Resisted active extension of the middle finger (Maudsley test - stresses ECRB/EDC)
pertinent_negatives: normal passive elbow range of motion distinguishes epicondylitis from true intra-articular elbow arthritis
content: Angiofibroblastic tendinosis (repetitive micro-tearing and degenerative vascular/collagen breakdown) at the origin of the Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB) muscle at the lateral humeral epicondyle. Treatment Protocol: 1. First-line Conservative: Activity modification, ergonomic adjustments, ice massage, and oral NSAIDs; 2. Counterforce Forearm Strap / Tennis Elbow Brace (worn 2-3 cm distal to epicondyle to dissipate muscle tension); 3. Eccentric extensor strengthening physiotherapy (Tyler twist using flexible resistance bar); 4. Ultrasound-guided Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) or Autologous Blood injection for chronic recalcitrant tendinosis (> 6 months); 5. Corticosteroid injections provide short-term pain relief but worsen long-term recurrence rates; 6. Surgical ECRB debridement and release for refractory cases.

topic: Acute Meniscal Tear (Joint Line Tenderness & McMurray Test)
red_flags: locked knee (bucket-handle tear wedged in intercondylar notch requiring urgent arthroscopy)
clinical_hallmarks: history of a twisting / rotational injury to a weight-bearing, flexed knee in athletes OR trivial squatting/turning in older adults with degenerative meniscal tissue
patient frequently describes feeling a 'POP' OR 'TEARING' SENSATION on either medial or lateral side of the knee

CARDINAL MECHANICAL SYMPTOMS: 1. MECHANICAL TRUE LOCKING (sudden inability to fully straighten or extend the knee due to a displaced bucket-handle fragment mechanically jamming the joint); 2. Catching, clicking, or giving way sensation during pivoting movements
EFFUSION EVOLUTION: MILD-TO-MODERATE KNEE EFFUSION DEVELOPING GRADUALLY OVER 24 TO 48 HOURS post-injury (in sharp contrast to immediate hemarthrosis of ACL tear)
DIAGNOSTIC CLINICAL TESTS:
1. JOINT LINE TENDERNESS (SINGLE MOST SENSITIVE CLINICAL SIGN > 85%): exquisite point tenderness on firm palpation along the medial or lateral tibiofemoral joint line;

2. MCMURRAY'S TEST (positive: with patient supine and knee flexed, axial loading with internal/external tibial rotation while extending the knee elicits a PALPABLE OR AUDIBLE 'CLICK' AND SHARP PAIN at the joint line);
3. Apley's Compression Test and Thessaly Test (dynamic weight-bearing rotation at 20 degrees flexion)
MRI of Knee (gold standard, accuracy > 90%): linear high signal traversing the meniscal substance and contacting an articular surface
pertinent_negatives: absence of true mechanical locking distinguishes stable tears from displaced bucket-handle tears
content: Disruption of the fibrocartilaginous medial (more common, C-shaped) or lateral (O-shaped) meniscus. Tears in the peripheral vascularized 'red-red zone' (outer 10-25%) have high intrinsic healing capacity; tears in the avascular 'white-white zone' cannot heal spontaneously. Protocol: 1. Locked Knee: Urgent Arthroscopic Reduction and Meniscal Repair/Debridement; 2. Degenerative non-obstructive tears: Non-operative physical therapy and quadriceps strengthening; 3. Acute athletic tears: Arthroscopic Meniscal Repair (inside-out or all-inside suture fixation) is the preferred gold standard to preserve long-term chondroprotective joint biomechanics; Partial Meniscectomy performed only when tear is non-repairable.

topic: Morton's Neuroma (Interdigital Perineural Fibrosis & Mulder's Click)
red_flags: metatarsal stress fracture (swelling and dorsal bone tenderness)
intractable chronic foot pain with walking limitation
clinical_hallmarks: predominantly affects women (female:male 5:1), strongly associated with wearing NARROW, POINTED-TOE SHOES OR HIGH HEELS

CARDINAL PATHOGNOMONIC SYMPTOM: BURNING, ELECTRIC-SHOCK, OR SHARP SHOOTING PAIN IN THE FOREFOOT, radiating into the adjacent toes, universally described as 'WALKING ON A PEBBLE OR FOLDED SOCK IN MY SHOE'
pain is characteristically relieved by removing shoes, resting, and vigorously massaging the forefoot

PATHOGNOMONIC ANATOMICAL LOCATION: THIRD INTERMETATARSAL SPACE (between the 3rd and 4th metatarsal heads in > 80-85% of cases, because the 3rd common digital nerve receives anastomotic branches from both medial and lateral plantar nerves, making it thicker and tethered under the deep transverse metatarsal ligament)

PATHOGNOMONIC PHYSICAL EXAMINATION SIGN: POSITIVE MULDER'S SIGN / MULDER'S CLICK (with the examiner's thumb and index finger applying direct plantar-to-dorsal pressure in the 3rd intermetatarsal space, the other hand squeezes the metatarsal heads transversely together: this produces a PALPABLE, AUDIBLE 'CLICK' AND SHARP PAIN as the enlarged neuroma subluxes plantarly)
pertinent_negatives: dorsal metatarsal tenderness with swelling indicates metatarsal stress fracture, NOT interdigital neuroma
content: Perineural fibrosis, endoneurial edema, and demyelination of the common plantar digital nerve as it passes beneath the rigid deep transverse metatarsal ligament. Treatment Protocol: 1. Conservative (cures 70-80%): Wide toe-box shoes with low heels, metatarsal pads (placed proximal to metatarsal heads to elevate and splay them apart), and activity modification; 2. Ultrasound-Guided Corticosteroid Injection (Triamcinolone 20-40 mg + local anesthetic into the 3rd web space via dorsal approach) provides marked long-term pain relief; 3. Surgical Neurectomy: Excision of the Morton's neuroma via dorsal longitudinal incision for chronic refractory pain.

keywords: diffuse gas small and large bowel
clinical_hallmarks: develops typically following abdominal surgery (physiologic postoperative ileus resolves: small bowel 24h, stomach 24-48h, colon 48-72h; prolonged ileus persists > 3-5 days)
secondary etiologies: SEVERE HYPOKALEMIA, hypomagnesemia, high-dose IV opioids, retroperitoneal hematoma, acute pancreatitis, or sepsis
diffuse, dull abdominal fullness, bloating, mild non-colicky discomfort, nausea, and bilious vomiting upon feeding attempt
complete absence of passage of flatus and feces
PATHOGNOMONIC PHYSICAL EXAMINATION FINDING: COMPLETE AND PROFOUND ABSENCE OF BOWEL SOUNDS ON PROLONGED AUSCULTATION ('THE SILENT ABDOMEN' - auscultate for minimum 2-3 full minutes in each quadrant)
abdomen is diffusely distended and non-tender (or mild generalized discomfort without peritoneal guarding)

Plain Abdominal Radiograph: DIFFUSE, UNIFORM GAS AND FLUID DISTENSION THROUGHOUT BOTH SMALL INTESTINE AND LARGE INTESTINE (including stomach, small bowel loops, colon, and rectum) without any distinct cutoff or transition point
pertinent_negatives: uniform gas in both small AND large bowel with a silent abdomen distinguishes ileus from mechanical SBO (which has localized distension, no colonic gas, and high-pitched sounds)
content: Temporary failure of coordinated gastrointestinal smooth muscle motility and peristalsis in the absence of mechanical obstruction, driven by sympathetic hyperactivity, local peritoneal macrophage inflammation, and mu-opioid receptor stimulation. Treatment Protocol: 1. Supportive: NPO, Nasogastric tube decompression for vomiting, IV fluid replacement; 2. AGGRESSIVE CORRECTION OF ELECTROLYTES: Replete serum Potassium (target K+ > 4.0 mEq/L) and Magnesium (target Mg > 2.0 mg/dL); 3. Minimization / cessation of systemic opioids (switch to multimodal non-opioid analgesia: IV Acetaminophen, Ketorolac, epidural analgesia); 4. Peripherally-acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist: Alvimopan (oral 12 mg BID) significantly accelerates gastrointestinal recovery; 5. Chewing gum (sham feeding stimulates cephalic-vagal motility) and early ambulation.

red_flags: severe nosocomial transmission to healthcare workers
clinical_hallmarks: history of tick bite by hard ticks of the genus Hyalomma, or direct contact with fresh blood/tissues of infected livestock (butchers, slaughterhouse workers, veterinarians), or nosocomial exposure in hospital
incubation period 1 to 9 days
abrupt onset of high spiking fever, rigors, severe frontal headache, dizziness, neck pain, and severe back and generalized myalgias
facial flushing, conjunctival suffusion, and enanthem on soft palate
HEMORRHAGIC PHASE (develops abruptly on day 3-5 of illness in severe disease):
widespread cutaneous petechiae and massive ecchymoses, spontaneous epistaxis, gingival oozing, hematemesis, melena, macroscopic hematuria, and uncontrolled bleeding from venipuncture injection sites

LABORATORY HALLMARKS: PROFOUND THROMBOCYTOPENIA (platelets often < 20,000 /mcL), leukopenia, prolonged PT/INR and aPTT, elevated transaminases (AST > 1,000 U/L indicates high mortality), and elevated D-Dimer
high case-fatality rate: 30% to 50%
pertinent_negatives: requires strict Level 4 biosafety / contact and airborne isolation precautions
content: Tick-borne zoonotic bunyavirus belonging to the genus Orthonairovirus (Nairoviridae family). Diagnostic workup: RT-PCR for CCHF viral RNA (days 1-7), IgM ELISA, CBC, coagulation profile. Statutory medical emergency with strict isolation. Protocol: 1. Strict barrier nursing and contact/droplet isolation in negative-pressure room; 2. Aggressive supportive replacement: Fresh Frozen Plasma, Cryoprecipitate, and Platelet transfusions; 3. SPECIFIC ANTIVIRAL THERAPY: Oral or IV Ribavirin (loading dose 30 mg/kg, then 15 mg/kg q6h for 4 days, then 7.5 mg/kg q8h for 6 days) initiated within the first 5 days of illness significantly reduces mortality.

topic: Bubonic Plague (Yersinia Pestis & Axillary / Inguinal Bubo)
specialty: Infectious Disease / Emergency Medicine / Critical Care
red_flags: secondary Pneumonic Plague (airborne transmission, rapid fatal respiratory failure within 24 hours)
Septicemic Plague with purpura fulminans / acral gangrene ('Black Death')
clinical_hallmarks: transmitted by the bite of an infected rodent flea (Xenopsylla cheopis / oriental rat flea) following rodent die-offs, or contact with infected wild rodents (marmots, prairie dogs, rats)
incubation period 2 to 6 days
abrupt onset of high fever (> 39-40C), shaking chills, severe headache, tachycardia, and profound prostration

PATHOGNOMONIC PHYSICAL SIGN: THE 'BUBO' (an exquisitely painful, tender, tensely swollen, non-fluctuant lymph node measuring 1 to 10 cm, surrounded by brawny gelatinous erythematous edema, characteristically in the INGUINAL / FEMORAL REGION [60-70%], followed by axilla and neck)
the pain in the bubo is so excruciating that the patient holds the affected limb in a fixed, motionless abducted posture to avoid any compression
microscopic hallmark: Wayson or Giemsa stain of bubo aspirate demonstrates Gram-negative coccobacilli with characteristic BIPOLAR 'SAFETY-PIN' STAINING
pertinent_negatives: exquisite tenderness and surrounding non-pitting gelatinous edema distinguish plague bubo from painless venereal lymphadenopathy
content: Zoonotic infection caused by the Gram-negative bacillus Yersinia pestis. Statutory Class A bioterrorism agent and global quarantine disease. Untreated bubonic plague has 50-60% mortality; pneumonic plague is 100% fatal without early antibiotics. STAT Treatment Protocol (MUST BE INITIATED IMMEDIATELY ON SUSPICION): 1. First-line Aminoglycosides: IM/IV Streptomycin (1g q12h) OR IV Gentamicin (5 mg/kg once daily for 10-14 days); 2. Alternative agents: IV Doxycycline (100 mg q12h) OR IV Chloramphenicol (for plague meningitis); 3. Droplet respiratory isolation for suspected pneumonic plague; 4. Chemoprophylaxis with oral Doxycycline (100 mg BID for 7 days) for all close contacts.

topic: Paratyphoid Fever (Salmonella Paratyphi A, B, C)
red_flags: intestinal perforation from Peyer's patch ulceration (acute peritonitis)
clinical_hallmarks: transmitted via food or water contaminated with feces of human cases or carriers; endemic in South Asia (accounting for up to 20-40% of all enteric fever cases)
incubation period 1 to 10 days (typically shorter and milder course than Salmonella Typhi, but clinically indistinguishable)
STEP-LADDER FEVER PATTERN: insidious, stepwise rise in body temperature over 3-5 days, peaking at 39-40C with headache, dry cough, malaise, and anorexia

PATHOGNOMONIC PHYSICAL SIGNS: 1. FAGET'S SIGN (relative bradycardia: pulse rate is inappropriately slow for the height of temperature, e.g. pulse 80 with temp 39.5C); 2. ROSE SPOTS (in 10-30%: faint, transient, salmon-pink, blanching maculopapular spots [2-4 mm] appearing in crops on the upper abdomen and chest, resolving in 2-4 days); 3. Coated tongue with red tip and edges; 4. Soft, mild, palpable splenomegaly and hepatomegaly
bowel habit: constipation is more frequent initially in adults; pea-soup diarrhea in children
laboratory hallmarks: Leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis, mild transaminitis; Blood culture is positive in 60-80% during first week; Bone marrow culture has highest sensitivity (> 90%)
pertinent_negatives: absence of leukocytosis (leukopenia or normal WBC is typical; marked leukocytosis suggests secondary intestinal perforation)
content: Systemic intracellular bacterial infection caused by Salmonella enterica serovars Paratyphi A (most common in India), Paratyphi B, or Paratyphi C. S. Paratyphi A lacks the Vi capsular polysaccharide antigen, rendering the standard Vi Typhoid vaccine completely ineffective against paratyphoid fever. Treatment: High rate of fluoroquinolone resistance in South Asia. Protocol: 1. Uncomplicated Outpatient: Oral Azithromycin (20 mg/kg/day or 1g day 1, then 500 mg daily for 7 days); 2. Inpatient Severe Enteric Fever: IV Ceftriaxone (2g IV daily for 10-14 days); 3. High-dose IV Dexamethasone for toxic encephalopathy or shock.

topic: Severe Nodulocystic Acne (Acne Conglobata & Oral Isotretinoin)
red_flags: Acne Fulminans (sudden painful ulcerating nodules with fever, leukocytosis, and polyarthritis)
permanent disfiguring keloidal and ice-pick scarring
clinical_hallmarks: severe, recalcitrant, highly inflammatory follicular disorder of the pilosebaceous units of the face, neck, chest, shoulders, and upper back

ELEMENTARY LESIONS: widespread open comedones ('blackheads'), closed comedones ('whiteheads'), inflammatory erythematous papules, pustules, and LARGE (> 5 mm), PAINFUL, DEEP, FLUCTUANT, ERYTHEMATOUS INFLAMMATORY NODULES AND CYSTS
Acne Conglobata (most severe form): widespread burrowing interconnected abscesses, draining sinus tracts discharging foul, purulent, serosanguinous fluid, and prominent multi-pore giant comedones
heals with severe, permanent, disfiguring cutaneous scars: 'ice-pick' pitted scars, 'boxcar' scars, rolling atrophic scars, and hypertrophic/keloidal bridging scars
pathophysiological tetrad: 1. Follicular epidermal hyperkeratinization; 2. Hyperseborrhea (androgen-mediated); 3. Cutibacterium acnes colonization; 4. Host innate/adaptive immune inflammation
pertinent_negatives: TERATOGENICITY MANDATE: ORAL ISOTRETINOIN IS 100% TERATOGENIC (causes catastrophic craniofacial, cardiac, and thymic malformations); strict contraception with two forms is legally mandatory
content: Severe nodulocystic acne refractory to oral antibiotics. FIRST-LINE DEFINITIVE THERAPY: ORAL ISOTRETINOIN (13-cis-retinoic acid - the ONLY medication that targets all four pathogenic acne factors simultaneously). Protocol: 1. Baseline liver function tests, fasting lipid panel, and two negative serum pregnancy tests (enrolled in iPLEDGE / pregnancy prevention program); 2. Dosing: 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/day orally taken with high-fat meals for 20-24 weeks, achieving a TARGET CUMULATIVE DOSE OF 120 TO 150 MG/KG (ensures permanent long-term cure and prevents relapse in > 80-85%); 3. Monthly monitoring of LFTs, triglycerides, and depression screening; 4. Mandatory dry lips/skin barrier emollients.

topic: Tinea Pedis & Onychomycosis (Athlete's Foot & Trichophyton Rubrum)
red_flags: secondary bacterial cellulitis (entry portal for Group A Strep in diabetics)
tinea incognito from misuse of topical steroids
clinical_hallmarks: most common superficial fungal dermatophyte infection worldwide, overwhelmingly caused by the anthropophilic dermatophyte TRICHOPHYTON RUBRUM (70-80%) or Trichophyton mentagrophytes
THREE DISTINCT CLINICAL PATTERNS OF TINEA PEDIS:
1. Interdigital Type (most common): peeling, fissuring, scaling, and white, boggy MACERATION IN THE 4TH AND 3RD TOE WEB SPACES, accompanied by intense itching and burning;

2. Moccasin Type (Hyperkeratotic): fine, silvery-white scale overlying diffuse erythema covering the soles, heels, and lateral borders of both feet in a slipper-like distribution ('two feet, one hand syndrome');
3. Vesiculobullous Type: intensely pruritic vesicles on the instep/sole

ONYCHOMYCOSIS (Tinea Unguium in > 80% with chronic tinea pedis): Distal Subungual pattern: thickened, opaque, yellow-brown dystrophic toenail, subungual crumbly hyperkeratotic debris, and onycholysis (separation of nail plate from bed)
DIAGNOSTIC BEDSIDE TEST: 10% or 20% POTASSIUM HYDROXIDE (KOH) MOUNT of skin scrapings or subungual debris demonstrating CLEAR, REFRACTILE, BRANCHING, SEPTATE HYPHAE
pertinent_negatives: TOPICAL STEROIDS (Betamethasone, Clobetasol) ARE STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED ALONE (cause 'Tinea Incognito' - masking symptoms while promoting rampant fungal spread)
content: Dermatophyte infection utilizing epidermal and ungual keratin. Diagnostic workup: KOH preparation with fungal culture on Sabouraud agar or nail clipping PAS stain. Treatment: 1. Tinea Pedis (uncomplicated): Topical Allylamine (Terbinafine 1% cream applied BID for 1-2 weeks - superior mycological cure rate > 80%) or topical Imidazoles (Clotrimazole, Ketoconazole); 2. Onychomycosis / Extensive Moccasin Tinea: ORAL TERBINAFINE (250 mg daily orally for 12 weeks for toenails, 6 weeks for fingernails - check baseline ALT/AST; gold standard cure rate 70-80%); Alternative: Oral Itraconazole pulse therapy; Foot hygiene and keeping toe webs dry.

topic: Pathological Bone Fracture (Osteolytic Metastasis & Mirels' Score)
red_flags: spinal cord compression from vertebral pathological collapse
clinical_hallmarks: bone fracture occurring as a result of MINIMAL, TRIVIAL TRAUMA (e.g. rolling over in bed, standing up, coughing) or spontaneously during activities of daily living, in bone weakened by pre-existing disease
patient frequently reports weeks to months of PRECEDING DULL, DEEP, CONSTANT ACHING BONE PAIN THAT IS CHARACTERISTICALLY WORST AT NIGHT and not relieved by rest
PRIMARY SITES OF ORIGIN (The 'BLT with a Kosher Pickle' Mnemonic):
1. Breast; 2. Lung; 3. Thyroid; 4. Kidney (Renal Cell); 5. Prostate (osteoblastic); 6. Multiple Myeloma / Lymphoma
plain radiograph: focal, well-defined or permeative radiolucent 'PUNCHED-OUT' OSTEOLYTIC DESTRUCTION, cortical erosion, or sclerotic (blastic) lesion with sudden cortical break
MIRELS' OBJECTIVE RATING SCORE (assesses risk of impending pathological fracture in long bones to indicate prophylactic surgery; score >= 8 warrants prophylactic surgical stabilization):

Scores 1-3 based on: Location (upper limb=1, lower limb=2, peritrochanteric=3); Pain (mild=1, moderate=2, functional=3); Lesion type (blastic=1, mixed=2, lytic=3); Size (< 1/3 cortex=1, 1/3-2/3=2, > 2/3 cortex=3)
pertinent_negatives: absence of high-energy trauma strongly indicates underlying bone pathology
content: Disruption of osseous continuity occurring through an area of bone structurally compromised by neoplastic, metabolic, or infectious pathology. Management Protocol: 1. Whole-body CT/PET-CT and skeletal survey to identify primary tumor; 2. Biopsy confirmation of bone lesion before definitive instrumentation (avoids spreading sarcoma); 3. Impending Fracture (Mirels >= 8): PROPHYLACTIC SURGICAL FIXATION (Reamed Intramedullary Nailing + polymethylmethacrylate [PMMA] bone cement) PREVENTS CATASTROPHIC DISPLACEMENT; 4. Displaced Fracture: Modular Endoprosthetic Reconstruction or locked intramedullary nail; 5. Palliative External Beam Radiotherapy (8 Gy single fraction) + Bisphosphonates (Zoledronic acid) or Denosumab.

topic: Acute Hemorrhagic Erosive Gastritis & Curling's Ulcer
clinical_hallmarks: history of major physiological physiological stress in ICU (mechanical ventilation > 48h, severe sepsis, extensive burns [CURLING'S ULCER], severe head trauma / intracranial hypertension [CUSHING'S ULCER]) OR ingestion of high-dose NSAIDs, aspirin, or heavy acute alcohol binge
CARDINAL CLINICAL PRESENTATION: sudden, painless or mild burning epigastric discomfort followed by COFFEE-GROUND EMESIS (hematemesis) or spontaneous melena (black, tarry stools)
nasogastric tube aspiration reveals fresh red blood or coffee-ground secretions
vital signs: tachycardia, postural orthostatic hypotension, or frank hypovolemic shock depending on rate of blood loss
URGENT UPPER GI ENDOSCOPY (EGD - DIAGNOSTIC GOLD STANDARD):

reveals MULTIPLE, SUPERFICIAL, PUNCTATE PETECHIAL HEMORRHAGES, ERYTHEMATOUS EROSIONS, AND SHALLOW ULCERATIONS diffusely scattered throughout the gastric fundus and body, with dark subepithelial hemorrhages
pertinent_negatives: mucosal erosions do NOT penetrate the muscularis mucosae (distinguishes erosive gastritis from deep chronic peptic ulcer)
content: Disruption of the gastric mucosal defensive barrier (mucus-bicarbonate layer, mucosal blood flow, prostaglandin synthesis) by systemic hypoperfusion, catecholamines, or COX-1 inhibition, allowing luminal acid and pepsin to cause superficial mucosal necrosis and microvascular hemorrhage. Management: 1. STAT Hemodynamic Resuscitation: IV crystalloids and blood transfusion; 2. STAT HIGH-DOSE IV PROTON PUMP INHIBITOR: IV Pantoprazole or Esomeprazole (80 mg IV bolus followed by 8 mg/hr continuous IV infusion for 72 hours, maintaining intragastric pH > 6.0 to stabilize fibrin clots); 3. Endoscopic Hemostasis (argon plasma coagulation, hemoclips) for focal spurting vessels; 4. Universal ICU Prophylaxis: Enteral or IV PPI / H2-receptor antagonist for all ventilated (> 48h) or coagulopathic patients.

topic: Hymenoptera Envenomation & Anaphylaxis (Bee & Wasp Sting Protocol)
specialty: Allergy & Immunology / Emergency Medicine / Critical Care
red_flags: massive envenomation (> 50-100 stings) causing rhabdomyolysis and acute renal failure
clinical_hallmarks: history of sting by insects of the order Hymenoptera: Apidae (Honeybees - barbed stinger remains in skin; Bumblebees), Vespidae (Yellowjackets, Wasps, Hornets - unbarbed stingers, can sting repeatedly), or Solenopsis (Fire ants)
LOCAL REACTION: immediate, intense, sharp, burning pain, erythema, and a raised wheal with central puncture site, resolving in hours
LARGE LOCAL REACTION: extensive, painful swelling and induration > 10 cm in diameter lasting 3-7 days (IgE-mediated, benign, does NOT predict systemic anaphylaxis)
SYSTEMIC ANAPHYLACTIC REACTION (develops rapidly WITHIN 10 TO 30 MINUTES of sting):
1. Cutaneous: generalized pruritus, flushing, diffuse urticaria (hives), and ANGIOEDEMA (swelling of lips, tongue, uvula, and periorbital tissues);
2. Respiratory: tightness in throat, hoarseness, INSPIRATORY STRIDOR, bronchospasm (expiratory wheezing), and severe dyspnea;
3. Cardiovascular: severe hypotension, dizziness, syncope, diaphoresis, and cardiac arrest;
4. Gastrointestinal: crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and explosive diarrhea
pertinent_negatives: DO NOT SQUEEZE THE HONEYBEE STINGER (scrape it off sideways with a fingernail or credit card to avoid expressing venom sac contents)
content: Type I immediate hypersensitivity reaction mediated by venom-specific IgE antibodies bound to tissue mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine, leukotrienes, and tryptase upon venom re-exposure. STAT Life-Saving Protocol: 1. FIRST-LINE DRUG OF CHOICE: INTRAMUSCULAR EPINEPHRINE (1:1,000 / 1 mg/mL): 0.3 - 0.5 mg IM (0.01 mg/kg in children, max 0.3 mg) INJECTED STAT INTO THE ANTEROLATERAL THIGH (VASTUS LATERALIS); REPEAT EVERY 5-15 MINUTES IF SYMPTOMS PERSIST; 2. High-flow oxygen, aggressive IV fluid bolus (1-2 L Normal Saline for shock); 3. Second-line adjuncts: IV H1-antihistamine (Diphenhydramine 50 mg) + IV H2-blocker (Famotidine 20 mg) + IV Methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg); 4. Discharge with two Epinephrine Autoinjectors (EpiPen 0.3 mg) and referral for Venom Immunotherapy (VIT - achieves > 95% protection against future stings).

red_flags: acute worsening of symptoms or sudden onset severe pain
development of high fever (>102F) or altered sensorium
clinical_hallmarks: Hallmark symptom presentation: high fever, muscle wasting, patches in throat, extra marital contacts
Immediate care precautions: Avoid open cuts, Wear ppe if possible, Consult doctor
pertinent_negatives: absence of focal neurological deficit unless primary intracranial process
content: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Disease / AIDS (ICD-10: B20) is managed under Infectious Diseases / Internal Medicine. AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) is a disease caused by HIV that weakens the immune system. Key clinical features include high fever, muscle wasting, patches in throat, extra marital contacts. Verified therapeutic interventions: Antiretroviral drugs, Protease inhibitors, Integrase inhibitors, Entry inhibitors. Nutritional recommendations: Balanced Diet, Protein-rich foods, Fruits and vegetables, Whole grains. Home care and precautions: Avoid open cuts, Wear ppe if possible, Consult doctor, Follow up.

red_flags: acute worsening of symptoms or sudden onset severe pain
development of high fever (>102F) or altered sensorium
clinical_hallmarks: Hallmark symptom presentation: vomiting, yellowish skin, abdominal pain, fluid overload
Immediate care precautions: Stop alcohol consumption, Consult doctor, Medication
